items.title: U.S., Coalition Partners Strengthen Ties at Egypt International Airshow 2026
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: The core focus regarding the El Alamein International Airshow 2026 is that the combined defense force is built on human networks and interoperability, not just advanced technology. This piece outlines how events on the ground actively strengthen the enduring U.S.-Egypt strategic alliance.
items.body:
AL ALAMEIN, Egypt — U.S. Air Force Airmen assigned to the Texas Air National Guard, alongside forces from U.S. Air Forces Central, joined international military leaders, civil aviation authorities, and defense representatives at Al Alamein International Airport for the Egypt International Airshow 2026.

The multi-day exposition serves as a strategic platform to highlight advanced aerospace technology, align operational capabilities, and reinforce international commitments toward security, stability, and prosperity across the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility.

"Airshows and defense expositions like EIAS 26 drive future interconnectedness across our coalition forces," said U.S. Air Force Brig. Gen. Joshlin Lewis, Special Assistant to The Adjutant General, Headquarters Texas Air National Guard, Camp Mabry, Austin, Texas. "When allies and partners operate similar platforms and share tactical understanding, it translates directly to enhanced operational readiness and collective air power."

Throughout the event, Airmen from the 136th Airlift Wing provided static display tours of a C-130J Super Hercules, giving foreign military partners, international delegations, and media representatives an up-close look at the tactical airlift platform. The display highlighted how shared systems bolster interoperability and support combined defense architecture across the region.

In addition to aircraft displays, members of the AFCENT Band performed for flight line attendees, while U.S. service members conducted bilateral patch exchanges and professional discussions with international aircrew members. Lewis, U. S. Air Force Col. Kurt Anderson, 136th Airlift Wing commander, and U.S. Air Force Command Chief Master Sgt. Paul McGuirk, Texas Air National Guard command chief, met with regional media outlets—including The Egyptian Gazette—to discuss coalition posture and the enduring U.S. commitment to regional stability.

"Interoperability is the cornerstone of any effective coalition," Anderson said. "Events of this scale afford our Airmen the opportunity to build direct relationships with host nation personnel and partner forces, ensuring we remain postured and ready as a credible force."

As part of USCENTCOM's comprehensive approach to complex security challenges, U.S. participation in EIAS 26 reinforces partner nation relationships, supports foreign military sales integration, and demonstrates a collective commitment to long-term regional peace.

items.title: Fort McCoy honors namesake Maj. Gen. Robert Bruce McCoy during 2026 remembrance ceremony
items.author: Scott Sturkol
items.summary: Soldiers, military leaders, students, veterans, community members and descendants of the McCoy family gathered Sept. 10 at Woodlawn Cemetery in Sparta, Wis., to honor the legacy of Maj. Gen. Robert Bruce McCoy, the Wisconsin Citizen-Soldier whose vision more than a century ago helped establish what is now Fort McCoy.
items.body:
Soldiers, military leaders, students, veterans, community members and descendants of the McCoy family gathered Sept. 10 at Woodlawn Cemetery in Sparta, Wis., to honor the legacy of Maj. Gen. Robert Bruce McCoy, the Wisconsin Citizen-Soldier whose vision more than a century ago helped establish what is now Fort McCoy.

The 2026 Maj. Gen. Robert Bruce McCoy Remembrance Ceremony, held at 9:30 a.m. on the north side of Woodlawn Cemetery, marked the second annual remembrance ceremony of its kind. The inaugural event was held in 2025.

The ceremony brought together the U.S. Army Garrison-Fort McCoy community and the local community to remember McCoy’s service, leadership, and vision for creating a large-scale military training area in Monroe County.

Command Sgt. Maj. James Riddle, Fort McCoy Garrison command sergeant major, served as master of ceremonies.

The event included an invocation by Chaplain (Lt. Col.) Raymond Leach of the 88th Readiness Division, the presentation of the colors by the Tomah High School JROTC Color Guard, the Pledge of Allegiance led by students from the Sparta Montessori E-2 classrooms, the National Anthem performed by Sparta High School senior Emaly Sutherland, and TAPS performed by Sparta High School senior Patrick Larson.

Col. Kurt Page, chief of staff of the U.S. Army Reserve’s 88th Readiness Division, served as keynote speaker.

Fort McCoy Garrison Commander Col. Sarah Fraticelli also addressed those attending.

Remembering a Citizen-Soldier

Page opened his remarks by reflecting on his own history with Fort McCoy, dating to 1988 when he arrived at the installation as a young private for annual training and Expert Infantryman Badge training.

He said his first experiences at Fort McCoy helped him develop an appreciation for the installation and the surrounding communities, even though he knew little at the time about the man whose vision had helped create it.

“I fell in love with this area and in love with how much this community supports the veterans and those soldiers that train at Fort McCoy,” Page said.

Page said researching McCoy’s life for the ceremony gave him a greater understanding of how much McCoy contributed to Monroe County and the military.

“This year marks 100 years since General McCoy’s passing and 100 years since the War Department put his name on what we know today affectionately as Fort McCoy,” Page said.

Robert Bruce McCoy was born Sept. 5, 1867, in Kenosha, Wisconsin. His family had a long tradition of military service, including his father, who commanded Company G of the 43rd Wisconsin Volunteer Infantry during the Civil War.

When flooding destroyed the family grain mill in 1876, the McCoy family moved to Sparta, where Robert Bruce McCoy would establish the deep connection with Monroe County that would define much of his life.

Known to friends as “Bob,” McCoy graduated from Sparta High School in 1887. He attended the University of Wisconsin, where he excelled academically and athletically, including as a pitcher and captain of the university baseball team. He later earned a law degree in 1891.

McCoy became active in numerous aspects of civic life. He opened a law practice, edited the Monroe County Democrat , served on the local Board of Education, was elected Monroe County judge in 1897, and later served as mayor of Sparta.

His public service also extended into state politics. In 1920, he was the Democratic nominee for governor of Wisconsin and received more than 200,000 votes.

“Judge, editor, school board, mayor, candidate for governor,” Page said. “Somewhere along the way, nobody ever taught Bob McCoy how to decline a request.”

From citizen to general

McCoy’s military career began when he enlisted as a private in the 3rd Wisconsin Infantry in 1885. Within a year, he received a commission as a captain.

During the Spanish-American War in 1898, McCoy led his Sparta company in Puerto Rico. During the fighting, an artillery shell exploded nearby, permanently damaging his hearing. His military service continued into World War I, when he commanded Wisconsin troops in France.

Page described McCoy's World War I service as the period that “revealed the full measure of the man.”

McCoy commanded infantry regiments during some of the war’s most difficult fighting and was recognized for his valor with the Army Distinguished Service Medal and French military honors, including the Croix de Guerre and Legion of Honor.

After returning home, McCoy continued serving veterans and fellow Soldiers. He helped establish the 32nd Division Veterans Association and eventually became a major general commanding the division.

But Page emphasized that McCoy’s most enduring contribution to the military did not come on a battlefield overseas.

“It was engineered right here, in the low pastures and jack pine ridges of Monroe County,” Page said.

A vision for military training

McCoy understood that the nature of warfare was changing, Page said. Having experienced military operations firsthand, he recognized that future armies would need expansive areas where Soldiers could conduct realistic, large-scale training involving artillery, maneuver and combined arms.

McCoy began purchasing land northeast of Sparta at his own financial risk. He eventually accumulated nearly 4,000 acres and leased portions of the property to help finance additional land purchases.

In 1905, he invited the 7th Field Artillery from Fort Snelling, Minn., to conduct 16 days of live-fire training on his ranch.

“Most landowners would write their representatives when artillery lands near their property line,” Page said. “But Bob McCoy mailed the invitation to come shoot.”

The exercise demonstrated the value of the terrain and McCoy’s concept for a large military training area.

Four years later, the War Department purchased more than 14,000 acres to establish the Sparta Maneuver Tract, laying the foundation for the military installation that eventually became Fort McCoy.

McCoy died Jan. 5, 1926, at age 58, Page said. Later that year, the War Department officially renamed the reservation Camp McCoy in his honor. In 1974, the installation became Fort McCoy.

Page noted the remarkable connection between McCoy’s original vision and the installation’s mission today.

“Today, Fort McCoy spans more than 60,000 acres and trains hundreds of thousands of total force Soldiers, Marines, Sailors, and Airmen, all of them on ground one man bought because he saw that need first,” Page said.

“Kenosha may claim his birth, Sparta claims everything after, and at Fort McCoy, we claim the land and the standard that he set that came with it.”

McCoy’s legacy continues

Fraticelli connected McCoy’s original vision to Fort McCoy's role in the region more than a century later.

“Maj. Gen. McCoy’s dream shaped Monroe County, and today it provides a home for Wisconsin’s only U.S. Army installation,” Fraticelli said.

The original approximately 4,000 acres associated with McCoy’s efforts have grown into an installation encompassing more than 60,000 acres.

Fort McCoy now supports training for the total force and provides a major economic benefit to the surrounding region. Fraticelli noted the installation has a regional economic impact of more than $1.6 billion and employs more than 3,000 military and civilian personnel.

She also highlighted the installation’s modernization and growth during the past decade, including facility improvements, training-area development, increased training and customer-support capabilities, and quality-of-life improvements for Soldiers and their families.

Fort McCoy honors McCoy’s legacy by continuing to provide a four-season training environment for military units from throughout the United States and beyond, Fraticelli said.

The installation supports more than 100,000 U.S. and international service members annually, while remaining a primary training location for Wisconsin National Guard units and an important training site for the U.S. Army Reserve.

“We are confident Maj. Gen. McCoy would be proud to see his mission continuing to impact and shape the U.S. Army and our Department of War,” Fraticelli said.

A legacy shared by a community

The presence of local students and young people at the ceremony provided a tangible connection between McCoy's generation of service and those who will carry that legacy forward.

The Sparta Montessori students led attendees in the Pledge of Allegiance, while Sparta High School students provided the National Anthem and TAPS. The Tomah High School JROTC Color Guard presented the colors.

For Page, the participation of local students and the community reflected an important part of McCoy’s legacy — the relationship between military service and citizenship.

McCoy was not simply a career military officer. He was a lawyer, educator, newspaper editor, judge, mayor, athlete, public servant, community leader and Citizen-Soldier.

His military experience led him to envision a training ground capable of preparing future generations of American service members. His willingness to invest his own resources in that vision ultimately helped transform the landscape of Monroe County.

A century after his death, that vision remains visible every day across Fort McCoy’s training areas, Page said.

Page closed his remarks by challenging those gathered to continue carrying McCoy’s example forward.

“An athlete, jurist, editor, mayor, father, general, Robert Bruce McCoy proved that a citizen in uniform can see farther than the terrain in front of him,” Page said.

“May his legacy keep driving us towards readiness, towards service, and toward the country he loved.”

The 2026 remembrance ceremony served not only as a commemoration of McCoy’s life, but also as a reminder that Fort McCoy’s history is inseparable from the history of Sparta and Monroe County.

From the acreage McCoy purchased at his own risk to the more than 60,000 acres used today, his vision continues to shape the Army's ability to train and prepare for the nation's defense.

And each September, as Soldiers, community members and young people gather to remember him, the story of the Citizen-Soldier who helped make Fort McCoy possible continues to be passed to a new generation.

Fort McCoy’s motto beginning in 2026 is “Training the Total Force and Shaping the Future since 1909.” The installation’s mission: “Fort McCoy strengthens Total Force Readiness by serving as a training center, Mobilization Force Generation Installation, and Strategic Support Area enabling warfighter lethality to deploy, fight, and win our nation’s wars.”

And Fort McCoy’s vision is, “To be the premier training center supporting the most capable, combat-ready, and lethal armed forces.”

Located in the heart of the upper Midwest, Fort McCoy is the only U.S. Army installation in Wisconsin. The installation has provided support and facilities for the field and classroom training of more than 100,000 military personnel from all services nearly every year since 1984.

Learn more about Fort McCoy online athttps://home.army.mil/mccoy, on Facebook by searching “ftmccoy,” on Flickr at https://www.flickr.com/photos/fortmccoywi, and on X (formerly Twitter) by searching “usagmccoy.” Also try downloading the My Army Post app to your smartphone and set “Fort McCoy” or another installation as your preferred base.

Fort McCoy is also part of Army’s Installation Management Command where “We Are The Army’s Home.”

items.title: JOINT TASK FORCE CIVIL SUPPORT CONDUCTS CHANGE OF COMMAND AND HOSTS TECH DEMO DAY
items.author: CPO Eva-Marie Ramsaran
items.summary: JOINT TASK FORCE CIVIL SUPPORT CONDUCTS CHANGE OF COMMAND AND HOSTS TECH DEMO DAY
items.body:
FORT EUSTIS, Virginia - Joint Task Force Civil Support (JTF-CS) marked a significant transition in leadership today during a formal change of command ceremony at the Jacobs Conference Center on Joint Base Langley-Eustis, Virginia, Sept. 10. During the ceremony, presided over by Maj. Gen. Brey Hopkins, Deputy Commanding General, U.S. Army Western Hemisphere Command, U.S. Army Brig. Gen. Tanya S. McGonegal relinquished command to U.S. Army Brig. Gen. Jonathan Ebbert. JTF-CS, a subordinate command of U.S. Northern Command (USNORTHCOM), is the nation’s only standing, no-notice joint task force dedicated to planning, preparing, and executing Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) response and all-hazards Defense Support of Civil Authorities (DSCA) operations. In his remarks as the presiding officer, Hopkins commended the unit’s steadfast posture and praised both incoming and outgoing leadership for their dedication to national resilience. "The mission of Joint Task Force Civil Support is one of the most critical and complex undertakings in the Department of Defense," said Hopkins. "When catastrophe strikes, Americans look to this joint team for rapid, specialized, and decisive aid. Brig. Gen. McGonegal has led this task force with extraordinary distinction, sharpening its operational readiness and strengthening crucial civilian-military partnerships. As we pass the mantle of leadership, I know Brig. Gen. Ebbert has the operational vision, interagency expertise, and proven leadership necessary to carry this no-fail mission forward." McGonegal, who has commanded JTF-CS since February 2024, reflected on her tenure leading the command’s highly specialized, multi-component team of active-duty, reserve, National Guard, and civilian personnel. "Serving alongside the professional Soldiers, Sailors, Airmen, Marines, and civilians of JTF-CS has been the absolute highlight of my military career," said McGonegal. "This team works day in and day out to ensure we are always ready to answer the call on our nation’s worst day. I am incredibly proud of what we have accomplished together to modernize our capabilities and strengthen our partnerships across local, state, and federal levels. I pass the colors to Brig. Gen. Ebbert with complete confidence that this vital, no-fail homeland defense mission remains in the most capable hands." Ebbert joins JTF-CS after most recently serving as the Combatting WMD Division Chief (NGB-J39) at the National Guard Bureau. He brings extensive expertise in domestic emergency response, CBRN enterprise operations, and interagency coordination. "It is a profound honor to assume command of Joint Task Force Civil Support and build upon the exceptional foundation of readiness established by Brig. Gen. McGonegal," said Ebbert. "The mission of JTF-CS is to save lives, mitigate human suffering, and prevent further injury which is a sacred trust we hold with the American people. As threats evolve, we will remain vigilant, agile, and integrated with our civil authority partners. I look forward to working with this outstanding joint force as we continue to refine our readiness to deploy at a moment's notice." The command recently welcomed Col. Scott Welborn, as the new deputy commander. Welborn arrived at Fort Eustis following a successful tour as the Commanding Officer of the Combined Arms Training Center (CATC) Camp Fuji, Japan. His background as an artillery officer and Marine Air-Ground Task Force planner brings valuable joint operational experience to the leadership team. "Joining JTF-CS is a great opportunity to work with this team on an incredibly important mission," said Welborn. "We are grateful for Brig. Gen. McGonegal's leadership these past two plus years and are excited to welcome Brig. Gen Ebbert as the new commander." Prior to the ceremony, JTF-CS hosted its annual Technology Demonstration Day on Fort Eustis. This interactive exhibition showcased the latest advancements in CBRN detection systems, tactical communication units, rapid decontamination systems, and disaster response gear. The event allowed industry partners, civilian emergency responders, and military leaders, including visiting senior commanders, to witness firsthand the cutting-edge capabilities and innovative tools JTF-CS utilizes to accelerate and refine rescue operations during domestic crises. The change of command is a time-honored military tradition that formally symbolizes the transfer of total authority, trust, and responsibility from one commander to the next. Hopkins received the unit colors from McGonegal and passed them to Ebbert, signifying the seamless continuity of leadership and commitment to the JTF-CS mission. For more information about Joint Task Force Civil Support, visit the official website at https://www.jtfcs.northcom.mil , or contact the JTF-CS Public Affairs Office.

items.title: A sacred promise kept: World War II airman returns home after 83 years
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: A World War II pilot who went missing in action over Italy in 1943 has finally been laid to rest in his native Harford County, Maryland. The solemn return of U.S. Army Air Forces 1st Lt. Walter R. Bateman was made possible by the exhaustive recovery efforts of the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency, the seamless teamwork of Army casualty officers from North Carolina to Maryland, and an overwhelming display of local honor.
items.body:
A World War II pilot who went missing in action over Italy in 1943 has finally been laid to rest in his native Harford County, Maryland. The solemn return of U.S. Army Air Forces 1st Lt. Walter R. Bateman was made possible by the exhaustive recovery efforts of the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency , the seamless teamwork of Army casualty officers from North Carolina to Maryland, and an overwhelming display of local honor.

Bateman, who was 22 years old when his B-24D Liberator, "Suzy Q," was shot down on August 16, 1943, was accounted for on May 29, 2026. Because his nearest living family members reside out of state, active-duty soldiers and hundreds of local Maryland citizens stepped forward to serve as his surrogate family during his emotional return to Maryland on August 28, 2026.

The Army's Casualty Assistance Center at Fort George G. Meade , Maryland, coordinated the multi-state support. U.S. Army Capt. Jenelle Smith, a licensed clinical social worker with the 44th Medical Brigade at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, was assigned as the primary Casualty Assistance Officer, or CAO, for Bateman’s niece, Mrs. Hannum, and her husband.

When Smith first met the Hannums, who had recently relocated from Washington State, she connected with them immediately over shared memories of the Pacific Northwest.

"We connected right away over shared memories of farmers’ markets and the community they had called home for decades," said Smith. "They were immediately inviting and patient."

For Smith, guiding a family through a repatriation more than eight decades after the loss required a unique, supportive touch.

"The family was moved that the Army continued to honor 1st Lt. Bateman after all these years, and eager to share their family’s history," said Smith. "My role was simply to give Mrs. Hannum time and space to reflect whenever a memory surfaced. In our two months together, I would listen patiently as she relayed stories passed down about that time of her life."

Because the family could not travel to Maryland for the planeside arrival, U.S. Army Capt. Joseph Chestnut III had the solemn duty of serving as the official escort for Bateman’s remains. For Chestnut, wearing the Army's modern Army Green Service Uniform, which mirrors the World War II-era service uniform, bridged the 83-year history.

"To me, the mission to escort 1st Lt. Bateman back home is my way of recognizing the past sacrifices of my brothers and sisters in arms who came before me," said Chestnut. "It is proof that even when a service member is gone, they are never truly forgotten, not by their family, their community, or their nation. It is a deeply fulfilling experience to be a part of this final act of gratitude to Walter Bateman's service, and it demonstrates to those that enter the Armed Forces and their families that no sacrifice will ever be taken for granted."

The homecoming began at the Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport on August 28, 2026, where the airport came to a standstill as the tarmac transfer took place. The BWI Fire and Rescue Department created a water-cannon arch to salute the fallen airman, while local veterans and active-duty personnel stood in formation.

U.S. Army Maj. John Koehler, chief of the Tri-Service Vision Conservation and Readiness Branch at the Defense Health Agency Public Health-Aberdeen, stepped in as the local courtesy CAO to manage the Maryland-based honors. He described the tarmac atmosphere as "somber, reverent, and deeply respectful."

From BWI, a massive motorcade of approximately 30 Patriot Guard Riders and 30 motorcycle police officers and sheriff's deputies escorted the casket to the Schimunek Funeral Home in Bel Air, Maryland. . Local fire departments and citizens lined highway overpasses to salute.

When the motorcade arrived in Bel Air, several hundred members of the community had gathered with flags and welcome-home signs. For both Chestnut and Koehler, the turn into the funeral home was the most unforgettable moment of the mission.

"Almost a hundred people had gathered there to welcome 1st Lt. Bateman back home, from young children to elders, all from different walks of life, many of whom also serve their nation and their communities," said Chestnut. "The anticipation and the reverence that I saw on their faces as the hearse I traveled on came to a stop was a deeply fulfilling moment for me, something that will stick with me not only during the rest of my career but the rest of my life."

The historical significance of the repatriation inspired immediate community action. Working through APG social networks, Koehler connected with the Jarrettsville VFW, who volunteered to build a custom shadowbox and mount Bateman's newly issued awards from Army Human Resources Command with less than 48 hours’ notice. Bateman was laid to rest with full military honors on Sunday, September 6, 2026, during a private family service at Union Chapel United Methodist Church in Joppa, Maryland. He was buried alongside his parents in the church’s cemetery, where many of his ancestors are interred.

"They were impressed with the level of coordination at every step, and appreciative of the continued efforts of the Army to bring 1st Lt. Bateman home," said Koehler. Though Mrs. Hannum, in her 80s, never had the chance to meet her uncle, the repatriation brought long-sought resolution.

"Many sacrifices are expected not only of service members but also their families: missed birthdays, lonely nights, an empty seat at the dinner table," said Chestnut. "It is a debt that can never be fully repaid by the nation, especially when the service member that family sent to serve their duty gives the ultimate sacrifice, but they all deserve closure at the very least, and I think it is incumbent upon all members of the Armed Forces and the United States Government to do their utmost to provide those families with the closure they deserve." Smith noted that the joint teamwork among the CAOs was completely seamless and that the Hannum family praised the incredible coordination at every step.

"The assignment gave me profound respect for the people working behind the scenes whose dedication I had never fully realized; the intricate history, meticulous recordkeeping, and honors involved were remarkable," said Smith. "Knowing that personnel stand ready to honor a fallen service member decades later, with the same care given to those lost today, was humbling.”

Koehler agreed, noting how the young face in Bateman's WWII portrait bridged the generations. "The photos in his dress uniform contrasted with our modern AGSU made the time gap feel much more immediate for me, as if he could have been any of the lieutenants participating in the welcome home," said Koehler. "The way so many came together to welcome him home across all Services, veterans of conflicts past, family, and community reinforced why I serve this great Nation."

items.title: Army & Air Force Exchange Service Engages Key Military Associations to Protect, Preserve Benefit
items.author: Julie Mitchell
items.summary: Military, retiree groups hear Exchange’s strategic vision for future
items.body:
Military, retiree groups hear Exchange’s strategic vision for future

WASHINGTON – The Army & Air Force Exchange Service (AAFES, the Exchange) is reaffirming its commitment to collaborating with key stakeholders to protect and preserve Exchange benefits for all who served and have served.

Exchange Director/CEO Brad Bingham met Sept. 9 in Washington with members of the Exchange Retiree Advisory Council, a group of key stakeholders that advocate for military community members’ hard-earned Quality-of-Life benefits. The council is composed of 11 organizations focused on matters that affect active-duty service members; Guard members; Reservists; military retirees; Veterans and family members.

The advisory council, established in 1997, now includes:

Air & Space Forces Association

Air Force Retiree Council

Air Force Sergeants Association

Army Retirement Services

Army Chief of Staff’s Retired Soldier Council

Association of the United States Army

Military Officers Association of America

National Military Family Association

Non-Commissioned Officers Association

Reserve Organization of America

The Retired Enlisted Association

“The Exchange is more than a retailer—we are woven into the fabric of military life,” Bingham told council members. “We give back to the military community through dividends to the Services’ Quality-of-Life programs. We hire Veterans, spouses and military family members. And ‘we go where you go,’ where other retailers can’t or won’t. Your members know how vital we are. We want to make sure you know the Exchange is still a great value.”

During the meeting, Bingham reiterated the Exchange’s priorities, including:

Expanding MILITARY STAR card acceptance.

Prioritizing military spouse and Veteran hiring.

Modernizing IT and data capabilities.

Accelerating retail growth.

Strengthening military clothing support.

Optimizing the restaurant portfolio.

Supporting the Army’s Flexible Eating and Expanded Dining (FEED) program.

Bingham also reminded the group that all honorably discharged Veterans can shop tax-free at ShopMyExchange.com, and service-connected disabled Veterans can shop in-store too.

Council members appreciated the opportunity to connect in person with Bingham to learn about the Exchange’s vision for the future.

“It was great to hear about how hard AAFES is working on behalf of Soldiers and families,” said retired Lt. Col. Maria Bentinck, director, Army Retirement Services. “The Exchange is continuing to modernize and enhance support to the entire military community.”

Retired Sgt. Maj. Steve Minyard, director of programs for the Reserve Organization of America, applauded the Exchange’s strategic direction.

“We can take and help spread the message of everything AAFES is doing, including the opportunity for Veterans to shop with the Exchange,” Minyard said. “Many Reserve component members may not realize they are eligible for that benefit.”

Minyard also welcomed the Exchange’s commitment to hiring those connected to the military.

“I appreciate the emphasis on hiring,” he said. “I can tell our members, ‘This is a really good employer that will work well with your Guard and Reserve career.”

Facebook-friendly version: Director/CEO Brad Bingham met with key stakeholders to reinforce the Exchange’s commitment to protecting hard-earned benefits for those who serve and have served. From Veteran and military spouse hiring to tax-free shopping and military-exclusive value, the Exchange remains focused on supporting the military community. https://wp.me/p9Q7PG-3iO

Since 1895, the Army & Air Force Exchange Service has gone where Soldiers, Airmen, Guardians and their families go to improve the quality of their lives by providing valued goods and services at exclusive military pricing. The Exchange is the 51st-largest retailer in the United States. 100% of Exchange earnings support military communities. In the last 10 years, your Exchange benefit has provided $15 billion in earnings that support the military community, including through contributions to critical military Quality-of-Life programs. The Exchange is a nonappropriated fund entity of the Department of War and is directed by a Board of Directors. To find out more about the Exchange history and mission or to view recent press releases please visit our website at http://www.shopmyexchange.com or follow us on X at https://x.com/shopmyexchange.

items.title: Iran attack on base in Jordan damaged American military aircraft, US official says
items.author: Idrees Ali, Reuters
items.summary: Iranian strikes damaged one A-10 Thunderbolt II and eight F-15s this week on the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan.
items.body:
Mideast Africa

Iran attack on base in Jordan damaged American military aircraft, US official says

A U.S. A-10 Thunderbolt II Warthog was damaged in an Iranian strike on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, Jordan, leaving it with a missing wing. (Albert Valladares/U.S. Air Force)

Iranian strikes damaged multiple American military aircraft this week on the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, a U.S. official told Reuters.

The U.S. military, the highest-funded in the world, suffered material damage even before Iran’s strikes on Tuesday. This includes the destruction of more than two dozen drones, Iran striking fighter jets, and aircraft being lost to accidents.

According to a May report from the Congressional Research Service, 42 U.S. military aircraft had already been lost or damaged in the conflict.

Since the Iran war started in February, 18 U.S. service members have been killed and over 800 injured.

A U.S. official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said Iran’s attack hit one A-10 Thunderbolt II, known as the Warthog, leaving it with a missing wing, while roughly eight F-15s sustained light damage and were returned to service.

Iran’s strike on the U.S. base in Jordan came after U.S. forces said they destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers. The U.S. said its strikes were in response to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targeting a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic ​missiles twice over the previous two days.

The Iranian attack required U.S. forces to fire roughly 30 Patriot interceptors to counter the missiles, the U.S. official said, amid increasing concern about the inventory of U.S. air defense interceptors and other missiles.

While specific inventory numbers are classified, the Center for Strategic ​and International Studies has estimated that about 65% of U.S. Patriot interceptors were expended between February and July, with fewer than 850 left on hand, down from 2,330 before the Iran war began.

items.title: No Better Friend: 1st Battalion, 6th Marines Perform Lifesaving Rescue on Southern Border
items.author: 2LT Louis Sosa
items.summary: A routine detection and monitoring mission along the southern border transitioned into a life-saving rescue on Aug. 7, 2026. Service members assigned to Joint Task Force-Southern Border (JTF-SB) in support of Operation Ardent Vanguard, treated and evacuated a suspected illegal alien suffering from severe heat illness near Campo.
items.body:
CAMPO, Calif. - A routine detection and monitoring mission along the southern border transitioned into a life-saving rescue on Aug. 7, 2026. Service members assigned to Joint Task Force-Southern Border (JTF-SB), in support of Operation Ardent Vanguard, treated and evacuated a suspected illegal alien suffering from severe heat illness near Campo.

Under temperatures exceeding 100 degrees, in the mountains of southern California, Lance Cpl. James Brooks and Pfc. Savi Garciamartinez, both infantrymen with 1st Battalion, 6th Marine Regiment, 2nd Marine Division, were manning a static observation post when U.S. Border Patrol radioed them regarding an individual in distress near their position.

Brooks and Garciamartinez left their post to locate the individual. After finding the man, Brooks immediately identified signs of a heat casualty and began cooling procedures. "I was grabbing ice from the cooler, running back and forth with ice packs and putting them in his groin, his armpits and on his neck just trying to cool him down," Brooks said.

Because Brooks did not speak Spanish, the language barrier presented an immediate obstacle. That is when Pfc. Garciamartinez used his ability to speak Spanish and translate what Brooks was doing. "[Pfc. Garciamartinez] was coordinating everything that the [suspected illegal alien] was saying so I could get him the best help as possible. Without him it would have been really hard to do what I did that day," Brooks said.

Garciamartinez translated the individual's symptoms as Brooks administered aid. "He was complaining of chest pains, telling us that he has been out there for three days, said he came all the way from Tijuana and that he had been out of water for so long. I immediately knew that he was heat casing or going to heat case," Brooks recalled.

At the same time, Brooks coordinated with the Sergeant of the Guard and U.S. Border Patrol to facilitate a medical evacuation at the landing zone. U.S. Navy Petty Officer Third Class Valeria Carmona, a hospital corpsman with 1st Battalion, 6th Marine Regiment, 2nd Marine Division, was returning to the command post with the Sergeant of the Guard when they received the radio call. "When I had heard that the patient was no longer sweating and that he was going unconscious, I immediately began in the back seat preparing IVs and my supplies so I was ready to go by the time we got there," Carmona said.

Upon arrival, Carmona evaluated the individual and spoke Spanish to reassure him. "I communicated with him the best I could of what I was going to do,” Carmona said. “It was more so trying to get him to have a level of comfort with me where he would allow me to perform any level of medicine."

The team secured the individual in the SKED litter and transported him up Tecate Peak to a pre-coordinated landing zone. During the climb, Carmona walked alongside the litter and held the IV bag above her head to maintain fluid flow as they traversed the steep terrain of Tecate Peak.

At the landing zone, the team met a Border Patrol Blackhawk helicopter. Due to the severity of the heat illness, Border Patrol agents requested that Carmona stay with the patient. Carmona remained with the patient, providing medical care until transferring the patient to civilian medical professionals.

For their actions that day, Brooks and Carmona received the Navy and Marine Corps Achievement Medal. 1st Lt. Jordan Corpuz, the 3rd Platoon Commander, Charlie Company, 1st Battalion, 6th Marine Regiment, attributed the rescue to the platoon's training culture. He noted that Carmona routinely integrated Tactical Combat Casualty Care (TCCC) training into the platoon's schedule prior to deployment.

"All the Marines of 3rd platoon have benefited from her knowledge and wisdom and the training that she has provided, and I think this is the ultimate pay off of what she’s prepared the Marines to do. It is a testament to their ability to train, to do their rehearsals and to treat every day like you never know what’s going to happen and prepare your best for it."

Corpuz further explained that the service members' actions are a true example of the Marine Corps being no better friend. “Lance Cpl. Brooks recognized that care was needed and that triage needed to be administered to this individual. The sanctity of life is important; I truly believe that and my Marines know that they acted on that and that speaks really about what this mission is about," Corpuz said. "It’s not only about protecting our southern border, it’s also providing aid for human beings."

Beyond the awards and operational success, the rescue left a lasting personal impact on both service members. For Brooks, who was the first to reach the individual and begin treatment, the rescue served as a stark reminder of the value of human life under critical conditions.

"The fact that I could get to him in the time that I could and ultimately save his life [by evacuating] him out of there really rendered well with me,” said Brooks. “It honestly held a special place in my heart for that person. Because I genuinely helped him out and if I wasn’t there or somebody else wasn’t there who knows what would have happened."

Carmona reflected on her role, explaining that a corpsman’s primary duty is to preserve human life and deliver medical aid to anyone in distress.

"It was having to see people regardless of their circumstances as human; they’re individuals,” said Carmona, “That’s our job, it doesn’t matter where they came from or who they are, it is our job to take care of people at the end of the day."

This successful medical evacuation highlights the constant readiness of JTF-SB service members to operate under austere conditions. The coordination between Brooks, Carmona, and U.S. Border Patrol reinforces the dual nature of their mission along the southern border, maintaining security while remaining ready to preserve human life at a moment's notice.

U.S. Northern Command is working side-by-side with the Department of Homeland Security and the U.S. Customs and Border Protection within narrowly defined authorities to provide unique military capabilities to protect the territorial integrity of the U.S. southern border.

items.title: Utah National Guard hosts Panther Strike 2026 at Camp Williams
items.author: SPC Noah Jensen
items.summary: Military intelligence professionals from across the U.S. Army and Canadian Armed Forces gathered at Camp Williams Aug. 5–7, 2026, for Panther Strike, a training event focused on countering hybrid threats, increasing lethality, and enhancing readiness.
items.body:
CAMP WILLIAMS, Utah — Military intelligence professionals from across the U.S. Army and Canadian Armed Forces gathered at Camp Williams Aug. 5–7, 2026, for Panther Strike, a training event focused on countering hybrid threats, increasing lethality, and enhancing readiness.

For more than two decades, Panther Strike has brought human, signal, and counter intelligence together in a single exercise. These elements work toward a single goal- reinforcing collaboration between branches of the MI structure to enable warfighter lethality and readiness to meet the complex nature of the modern hybrid battlefield that extends beyond the front lines, into cyber space, and the civil infrastructure supporting the nation.

The 300th Military Intelligence Brigade (Linguist) planned and executed the mission, focusing on expanding HUMINT skills and proficiencies by conducting assessments, interrogations, and collecting information. They also used role players in simulated environments to help Soldiers build proficiency in an integrated intelligence team in a realistic scenario.

“This is an exercise to refine our intelligence gathering skills and teach us how everything comes together to create a coherent picture," said Sgt. Gregory Thomson, a signal intelligence analyst, assigned to the 300th MI who has participated in Panther Strike twice. “Part of the Panther Strike roleplayer position is being interrogated by the Human Intelligence Collector (35M) soldiers to help get their reps in,” Thomson added.

Among the HUMINT Soldiers participating, Canadian intelligence personnel brought new perspectives to the exercise and gained valuable experience. Working closely with U.S. soldiers, they learned how to operate in a multinational environment and face real-world challenges.

“Attending Panther Strike was incredibly valuable,” said Master Cpl. Suliman Elatrash, 6 Intelligence Company, Canadian Armed Forces. “As an intelligence operator, stepping out of my usual role and directly into the HUMINT collection environment completely shifted my perspective. Forcing myself to operate outside my standard analytical comfort zone ultimately makes me a more versatile asset to the Canadian Armed Forces.”

Panther Strike is an evolving exercise that pushes the boundaries of what intelligence professionals can do. The exercise employs many native speakers as roleplayers during the exercise, several of them are intelligence professionals and this level of intelligence gathering forces the participants to exercise their own language skills and work closely with interpreters. Interpreters add a level of real world complexity to the mission of intelligence gathering that comes with additional costs of time and effort.

“Many of us in the 300th MI have a secondary language that we go to the Defense Language Institute to learn,” said Staff Sgt. Gabriel Cavazos, Panther Strike observer-controller. “A lot of people overlook the importance of working with an interpreter. I utilized an interpreter during a previous deployment of mine in Afghanistan.” Panther Strike prepares every component of intelligence gathering, from increasing lethality, enhancing readiness and working with allied international forces for real-world missions to synchronize efforts to counter hybrid threats.

Covering so many elements of the intelligence environment in one comprehensive exercise trains participants for the real world, where knowing how each piece of the fight functions is the difference between success and failure. Panther Strike is that exercise for the National Guard and continues to ensure the U.S and its allies are trained to fight whenever and wherever they are called.

items.title: Space Force Taps Texas Site for New Deep Space Radar, Targets Operations in 2030
items.author: Greg Hadley
items.summary: The Space Force has selected a site in north Texas as the preferred location for the final site of its new Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability, the service announced Sept. 9. The post Space Force Taps Texas Site for New Deep Space Radar, Targets Operations in 2030 appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

The Space Force has selected a site in north Texas as the preferred location for the final site of its new Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability , the service announced Sept. 9.

Pending final approvals, construction on the new radar and accompanying facilities will start at Lake Kickapoo, Texas, in 2027, according to a Space Force release.

The U.S., United Kingdom, and Australia are working together on the DARC program to boost their ability to monitor geosynchronous orbit, which extends out to 22,000 miles above Earth. Consisting of three radar sites, DARC will give the allies a 24/7, all-weather view of the entire GEO belt—greater coverage than is now possible with any other ground-based system.

“Selecting Texas as the preferred location for the final DARC site keeps us on track to deliver a truly global deep-space sensing network with our closest allies,” new Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas A. Schiess said in a statement. “This capability will improve visibility in our contested domain and reinforce our shared capacity to protect the space systems on which our nations rely.”

Under a trilateral agreement, the U.S. Space Force is leading development, but the agreement allows the U.K. and Australia to operate and host sites and participate in joint operations and exercises. Northrop Grumman is building the radars.

The first DARC site selected is in western Australia. Construction began in 2023 and wrapped up by late 2024 , and the site was cleared for early operational use in 2025, even as testing continues. The second DARC site in Wales was selected in 2024 , and construction is expected to start in April 2026, pending final approvals.

The Space Force hopes to move fast in Texas. The planned timeline is to award a contract and start construction next year, finish building by 2029, and wrap up test and evaluation before accepting the radar for operations in 2030. Those goals were moved up recently —the Government Accountability Office previously reported a 2032 timeline for having all three sites operational.

At one point, it wasn’t entirely clear a third DARC site would even happen. The Space Force indicated in 2025 that it was considering changing course on the DARC acquisition strategy , including potentially cancelling the third location. But the service’s fiscal 2027 budget request funded the full program. That includes $442 million in fiscal ’27 and another $1.6 billion through fiscal ’31.

Lake Kickapoo, about 120 miles northwest of Fort Worth, previously hosted the main transmitter site for the old AN/FPS-133 Space Fence system. That system was initially developed by the Navy, eventually transferred to the Air Force, and was decommissioned in 2013, with a new AN/FSY-3 Space Fence coming online in 2020. The Federation of American Scientists described the Lake Kickapoo site as “the largest continuous wave transmitter in the world” when it was built.

items.title: Forging the Future Fleet: U.S. Naval Academy Developing Tomorrow’s Shipbuilding Leaders From U.S. Naval Academy
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: To answer the President’s and Acting Secretary of the Navy’s call to revitalize American shipbuilding and strengthen the maritime industrial base, the U.S. Naval Academy is executing shipbuilding initiatives of its own. This summer, the Naval Academy selected five midshipmen to participate in its inaugural shipbuilding summer internship program that immersed rising first-class and second-class midshipmen in a multi-shipyard, multi-platform environment in both commercial shipyards and within Nava
items.body:
To answer the President’s and Acting Secretary of the Navy’s call to revitalize American shipbuilding and strengthen the maritime industrial base, the U.S. Naval Academy is executing shipbuilding initiatives of its own.

This summer, the Naval Academy selected five midshipmen to participate in its inaugural shipbuilding summer internship program that immersed rising first-class and second-class midshipmen in a multi-shipyard, multi-platform environment in both commercial shipyards and within Naval Sea Systems Command. Midshipmen not only gained exposure to the maritime industrial base and shipbuilding programs, but they also had the opportunity to conduct academic and operational research alongside experts in the field. During the internships, initial midshipmen research on a submarine concept design proved so impactful that their findings were accepted for presentation at a major industry conference. The midshipmen will build upon their internship experience by bringing forth their newly gained knowledge into their senior capstone projects.

“At the Naval Academy, we have an extraordinary opportunity to connect what midshipmen learn in our classrooms directly to the urgent needs of the fleet,” said U.S. Naval Academy Provost, Dr. Samara Firebaugh. “By pairing rigorous coursework in naval architecture, economics, history, and operations research with hands-on research in active shipyards and command centers, our midshipmen aren't just studying defense production; they are actively delivering solutions that strengthen America’s maritime industrial base before they even graduate.”

Founded in 1845 during the U.S. Navy’s transition from sail to steam propulsion, the U.S. Naval Academy is uniquely suited to address technical revolutions in naval engineering. Having adapted through every major conflict since the Civil War, the U.S. Naval Academy remains one of the new undergraduate institutions offering accredited degree programs in both Naval Architecture and Operations Research, alongside a robust liberal arts and STEM curriculum.

By embedding shipbuilding priorities across both military and academic training, the Academy is ensuring every midshipman steps into the fleet prepared to sustain American sea power.

“Restoring American shipbuilding capacity is a warfighting imperative, and our graduates must step into the fleet ready to fight the most formidable naval force the world has ever known,” said U.S. Naval Academy Superintendent, Lt. Gen. Mike Borgschulte. “Giving midshipmen the opportunity to gain real-world insight into how America builds and sustains that force is not an experience you can get at many other colleges and universities, that is an experience unique to the Naval Academy and our focus on graduating leaders prepared for the demands of naval service.”

In addition to summer training opportunities, the U.S. Naval Academy has also updated portions of its curriculum to emphasize the importance of the maritime industrial base and address the technical, analytical, and economic dimensions of defense production. For example, Professor Marcus Jones is developing a dedicated History of Shipbuilding course for the History Department while Professor Brenda Boultwood currently leads a course of instruction, titled the Economics of National Defense within the Economics Department. Additionally, Interdisciplinary capstones and experimental classes now pair Naval Architecture and Operations Research midshipmen and faculty to tackle the generation of complex requirements.

“Maintaining, modernizing, and expanding the battle fleet depends not only on industrial capacity, but on the technical and strategic competence of the officers who lead, manage, and sustain that capacity throughout their careers,” said U.S. Navy Capt. Li Sung, a Permanent Military Professor within the Naval Architecture and Ocean Engineering Department. “At the U.S. Naval Academy, we graduate leaders who need to understand the necessity for a strong American maritime industrial base and that education and appreciation starts here on the Yard.”

The U.S. Naval Academy is a prestigious four-year service academy that prepares midshipmen morally, mentally, and physically to become professional officers in the naval service. More than 4,400 men and women representing every state in the U.S. and several foreign countries make up the student body known as the Brigade of Midshipmen. U.S. News and World Reports has recognized the Naval Academy as the #1 top public school, #3 national liberal arts college, and #5 best undergraduate engineering programs. Upon graduation, midshipmen earn a Bachelor of Science degree in a choice of 26 different subject majors and go on to serve at least five years of exciting and rewarding service as commissioned officers in the U.S. Navy and U.S. Marine Corps. For more information about the Naval Academy, visit www.usna.edu .

items.title: Sustaining Readiness in The Field: Marines with 1st Maintenance Battalion execute FEX
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: The speed of modern warfare leaves no room for lag between technological innovation and tactical execution. Demonstrating this concept, Marines and Sailors with 1st Maintenance Battalion, 1st Combat Readiness Regiment, 1st Marine Logistics Group, conducted Exercise PHOENIX FEX 2-26 from Aug. 17 -26, 2026 on Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton, California.
items.body:
CAMP PENDLETON, Calif. -- The speed of modern warfare leaves no room for lag between technological innovation and tactical execution. Demonstrating this concept, Marines and Sailors with 1st Maintenance Battalion, 1st Combat Readiness Regiment, 1st Marine Logistics Group, conducted Exercise PHOENIX FEX 2-26 from Aug. 17 -26, 2026 on Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton, California.

By integrating advanced manufacturing and forward-thinking logistics into a rigorous field environment, the battalion operationalized a blueprint for sustaining combat-credible forces against modern pacing threats.

“The ability to organically manufacture new warfighting capabilities in an expeditionary environment is not a future concept; it is our reality, and we are executing it now,” said U.S. Marine Corps Lt. Col. Zachary Pagan, commanding officer of 1st Maintenance Battalion. “We approached this exercise as a full mission rehearsal against a peer adversary. We approached it as if it were our last opportunity to prepare for conflict, because it very well may be.”

The battalion designed a training environment that compelled Marines to operate under persistent adversary intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance; degraded communications; and simulated chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear conditions.

Marines and Sailors quickly adapted and learned to conceal and mask operations for survivability. The unit sustained a strict combat mindset through live-fire ranges, Tactical Combat Casualty Care, and advanced field craft to reinforce that every logistician must remain a warfighter first.

A critical component of the exercise was demonstrating how the Marine Corps can rapidly integrate commercial-off-the-shelf technology to solve tactical problems. Working alongside industry partners like Phillips Federal who provided the advanced hardware, Marines provided the tactical labor to fabricate, produce, and employ small unmanned aerial systems, counter-UAS interceptor drones, and electric dirt bikes for low-signature mobility.

Operating from subterranean facilities, Marines managed self-contained, deployable 3D print farms capable of generating 10 drones per day, while concurrently launching interceptor drones to thwart simulated adversary attacks. These print farms were exercised on 24-hour operations to measure production limitations, demonstrating a potential output of over 1,400 drones a month.

The employment of emerging technology extended to the integration of Artificial Intelligence into supply chain management. By pairing a custom-built proprietary AI platform designed by TAGUP, the battalion’s Reparable Issue Point utilized enterprise data to predict optimal maintenance strategies for secondary reparables. Supply Marines queried embedded Large Language Models to navigate the defense industrial base and source critical repair parts in real time.

Beyond experimentation, the battalion remained focused on its core mission of sustaining the I Marine Expeditionary Force. The battalion generated and deployed over nine Maintenance Support Teams to MEF and TECOM units across Camp Pendleton. In total, 84 maintenance technicians performed more than 4,500 labor hours, repairing over 25 critical equipment items. Prepositioned repair part blocks were delivered via Landing Craft, Air Cushion amphibious connectors to facilitate forward intermediate level equipment repairs in multiple training areas. The flexible and responsive logistics architecture the battalion developed enabled same day repairs and provided supported commands with immediate gains in materiel readiness.

The Marines also spearheaded the repair of Amphibious Combat Vehicle components, by rebuilding unserviceable brake calipers and wheel end assemblies, they returned parts to a like-new condition, generating cost savings of over $20,000 per unit. Over the course of 12 training days, the Marines produced enough brake calipers to restore 60 ACVs to fully operational status. Furthermore, fabrication Marines utilized the newly fielded Advanced Integrated Mobile Machine Shop to machine high-grade tool steel into ACV tool kits that are currently unavailable in the supply system.

Looking toward the requirements of distributed maritime operations, the exercise simulated the need to task-organize multifunctional maintenance capabilities across a contested island chain. Exercise injections drove staff planning and the deployment of an Intermediate Maintenance Company to a secondary location.

Senior leaders were forced to execute maintenance control procedures across unfamiliar weapon system platforms. This dynamic environment provided unique cross-training opportunities, ensuring Marines are prepared for the uncertainty of future equipment platforms and operating environments.

“Our responsibility as leaders is to cultivate realistic training environments that accelerate our Marines’ decision-making and solidify their trust in their equipment and each other,” said 1st. Sgt. Julian Billmair, the acting 1st Maintenance Battalion Sergeant Major. “Adversity builds character and strengthens resiliency. These Marines and Sailors have proven themselves to be ready to support the demands of I MEF with innovation and resolve.”

The establishment of multiple combat service support areas and lines of communication across land and sea enabled the battalion to effectively employ its capacity across the rear, main, and forward areas of the battlespace. Every tactical movement and hybrid capability developed were meticulously captured in embarkation systems, preparing the unit for rapid, no-notice future deployments.

Ultimately, 1st Maintenance Battalion is committed to elevating the readiness of the entire Marine Corps by proving what is possible at the tactical edge today as stated by Pagan, who motivated his unit at the kickoff of the exercise.

“Innovate, dig in, build grit and resiliency, and move the needle on readiness,” he exclaimed.

items.title: Army sergeant caught in undercover operation sentenced to four years in prison for attempted sexual assault of a child
items.author: Michelle McCaskill
items.summary: An Army sergeant caught in a multi-agency law enforcement Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force operation pleaded guilty to attempted sexual assault of a child during his court-martial Aug. 20 at the Wheeler Army Airfield courtroom. Sgt. Joey Walker, 38, an air defense enhanced early warning system operator assigned to the 94th Army Air and Missile Defense Command, Joint Base Pearl Harbor–Hickam, Hawaii, was sentenced by the military judge to four years in prison, reduction in rank to E-1
items.body:
WHEELER ARMY AIRFIELD, Hawaii – An Army sergeant caught in a multi-agency law enforcement Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force operation pleaded guilty to attempted sexual assault of a child during his court-martial Aug. 20 at the Wheeler Army Airfield courtroom.

Sgt. Joey Walker, 38, an air defense enhanced early warning system operator assigned to the 94th Army Air and Missile Defense Command, Joint Base Pearl Harbor–Hickam, Hawaii, was sentenced by the military judge to four years in prison, reduction in rank to E-1 and a dishonorable discharge from the Army.

On Sept. 27, 2025, Walker matched with a female on the dating app Plenty of Fish who was listed as 18 years old. Unbeknownst to him, the profile was operated by an undercover agent with the Naval Criminal Investigative Service.

After they started communicating via text messages, the undercover agent told Walker her age was actually 14. Undaunted, he asked her for a photo and continued to pursue communication.

Walker’s texts eventually became sexually explicit, including sending her a photo of his exposed genitalia. Ultimately, he requested they get together for sex and arranged to meet Oct. 5, 2025, on Schofield Barracks, Hawaii.

That day, an agent with the Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division surveilled Walker as he stopped at the on-post shopette and purchased two bottles of wine, which he promised to bring to the meeting.

Upon arriving at the meet-up location, Walker was arrested by Army CID agents. His phone was seized, and a digital forensic examination confirmed he had been communicating with the undercover agent.

“Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force operations proactively find the child predators who otherwise hide behind electronic screens. This sentence sends a clear warning: the Army will identify, prosecute, and hold accountable those who target children,” said Capt. Catherine Ricci, prosecutor, Eighth Circuit, Army Office of Special Trial Counsel. “We will protect our community.”

“Safeguarding our communities from online predators is an uncompromising mission,” said Special Agent in Charge Michael DeFamio, Army CID’s Asia-Pacific Field Office. “This conviction highlights the dedication of our special agents, digital forensic examiners, and the collaborative strength of military criminal investigative organizations within the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force.”

Walker will serve his prison sentence at the Midwest Joint Regional Confinement Facility at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. Upon release, he will be subject to federal and state sex offender registration requirements.

This case was investigated by Army CID’s Asia-Pacific Field Office and NCIS’s Hawaii Field Office. It was prosecuted by Ricci and Capt. Monica Glenzer, Office of the Staff Judge Advocate, 8th Theater Sustainment Command, Fort Shafter, Hawaii.

About the Army Office of Special Trial Counsel: The Army Office of Special Trial Counsel is composed of specially trained military lawyers, legal professionals and support staff responsible for the expert prosecution of murder, sexual assault, domestic violence, child abuse, kidnapping and other serious criminal offenses. Headquartered at Fort Belvoir, Va., OSTC has eight regional headquarters that oversee 28 field offices located worldwide, including locations in Europe and Korea. For more information visit www.army.mil/ostc.

To Report a Crime: If you would like to report a crime, have information about a crime, or have been the subject or survivor of a crime, you can submit anonymous tips to Army CID at www.p3tips.com/armycid.

items.title: CNO, MCPON Recognize NS Mayport for Installation Excellence Trifecta
items.author: David Holmes
items.summary: During a base-wide all-hands call, Sept. 09, 2026, Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle and Master Chief Petty Officer of the Navy John Perryman recognized Naval Station Mayport for their three distinct installation excellence awards in the past year and presented the base with the inaugural 2025 Shore Battle “E” pennant.
items.body:
NAVAL STATION MAYPORT, Fla. – During a base-wide all-hands call, Sept. 09, 2026, Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle and Master Chief Petty Officer of the Navy John Perryman, recognized Naval Station Mayport for their three distinct installation excellence awards in the past year and presented the base with the inaugural 2025 Shore Battle “E” pennant.

In 2026, Naval Station Mayport was awarded the 2025 Commander, Navy Installations Command Shore Battle “E”; 2026 Commander, Navy Installations Command Installation Excellence Award; and 2026 Commander in Chief's Annual Award for Installation Excellence.

These awards recognize installations for their outstanding performance ensuring Navy readiness around the clock. The three awards honor different aspects of installation performance. The Shore Battle “E” is an operational award that recognizes Navy installations as vital battle forces, specifically for their excellence in generating and supporting combat capabilities. The Installation Excellence Award recognizes overall outstanding performance consistent with Navy Shore enterprise strategic goals, while the Commander in Chief’s Award recognizes overall outstanding performance across all Department of War installations.

“These accolades are a direct result of our incredible Sailors, civilian workforce, and surrounding Jacksonville community. Without them, none of this would be possible. I’m so proud of our warfighters and the families that support them,” said Naval Station Mayport’s commanding officer Capt. Mike Trumbull.

Naval Station Mayport distinguished itself as the most operational base in the Southeast, servicing over 80 supported commands by flawlessly executing more than 71,000 flights and 525 ship movements. They earned top honors for exceptional performance in supporting warfighter readiness while providing a superior quality of life for service members and their families. The installation's commitment to continuous improvement was evident in its award-winning public works, unaccompanied housing, and emergency services departments - setting the standard for shore excellence throughout the Fleet.

Spanning over 3,400 acres, Naval Station Mayport is strategically positioned at the mouth of the St. Johns River and home to Arleigh Burke-class guide-missile destroyers, Freedom-variant littoral combat ships, and three Helicopter Maritime Strike Squadrons.

items.title: NMLPDC’s “Snakes Alive!” Symposium Strengthens Readiness
items.author: PO1 Heath Zeigler
items.summary: Naval Medical Leadership and Professional Development Command’s (NMLPDC) Professional Development Directorate recently hosted the “Snakes Alive!”, a specialized training symposium designed to enhance the operational knowledge and clinical readiness of participants in the Military Tropical Medicine (MTM) program. The symposium, held July 28 at the Uniform Services University of the Health Sciences, provided attendees with practical education on venomous reptiles, envenomation, and unique medical
items.body: Naval Medical Leadership and Professional Development Command’s (NMLPDC) Professional Development Directorate recently hosted the “Snakes Alive!”, a specialized training symposium designed to enhance the operational knowledge and clinical readiness of participants in the Military Tropical Medicine (MTM) program. The symposium, held July 28 at the Uniform Services University of the Health Sciences, provided attendees with practical education on venomous reptiles, envenomation, and unique medical challenges military personnel may encounter while operating in tropical and austere environments. The training directly supports the MTM program’s mission of preparing military professionals to recognize, prevent, and respond to diseases, environmental hazards, and other health threats encountered during operations around the world. For medical personnel deploying to regions where venomous snakes and other reptiles are endemic, understanding these hazards can be critical to protecting the force and delivering timely medical care. Guest speaker Bruce Shwedick, an internationally experienced reptile educator and conservationist, guided participants through the identification, behavior, geographic distribution, and medical significance of some of the world’s most dangerous reptiles. “There are roughly 4,000 types of snakes across the globe, but only about 600 of them are venomous,” said Shwedick. “They range from the Barbados Thread snake, which holds the record as the shortest snake, to the massive, Reticulated Python, the longest snake in the world.” For MTM participants, the diversity of snake species represents more than an academic topic. Military personnel routinely deploy to environments where unfamiliar wildlife and limited access to definitive medical care can complicate the management of bites and envenomation. The ability to recognize regional threats, understand snake behavior, and rapidly identify signs of serious envenomation contributes directly to force health protection and operational medical readiness. Participants also learned why seemingly simple approaches to snake handling can be dangerous. The Stiletto Snake, for example, possesses a unique, highly flexible fang structure that allows it to strike sideways. Because of this adaptation, it is hard to impossible to hold or pick up a Stiletto Snake safely behind the head. Such examples reinforced that successful management of environmental threats begins with understanding the hazard and avoiding unnecessary exposure. Shwedick also discussed the diversity of reptile biology and behavior. “Sea snakes have a live birth but their close marine relatives, the Sea Kraits, lay eggs,” said Shwedick. “A particularly quirky detail about the venomous lizards Gila monsters is that they sleep on their backs.” These differences illustrate the wide range of species military personnel may encounter across operational environments. The symposium’s most important medical component focused on envenomation recognition and response. “There are three types of snake bites,” said Shwedick. “The first is a strike with no venom, often called a ‘dry bite,’ where the snake strikes defensively but chooses not to inject toxins. The second type involves little venom, resulting in a mild envenomation that may cause severe localized pain and tissue damage but progresses slowly. The third and most dangerous is a bite with a lot of venom, a massive injection of toxins that immediately becomes a systemic, life-threatening medical emergency.” For military medical professionals, distinguishing between these presentations and recognition clinical deterioration can be critical, particularly in remote locations where evacuation and access to antivenom may be delayed. The training emphasized that suspected envenomation requires rapid medical assessment, appropriate consultation, and coordination for definitive treatment. Understanding how to access specialized toxicology and antivenom resources is an important component of preparing military personnel to manage these uncommon but potentially catastrophic emergencies. By incorporating subject matter expertise on venomous reptiles into the MTM curriculum, “Snake Alive!” transforms knowledge of regional wildlife into operationally relevant medical preparedness. The symposium reinforces the broader purpose of the MTM training: ensuring military healthcare professionals can identify environmental and infectious threats, make informed clinical decisions, and protect the health of service members wherever military operations occur. Training opportunities such as “Snakes Alive!” also demonstrate the value of collaboration between NMLPDC, the Uniform Services University, and civilian subject matter experts. These partnerships provide military medical professionals with specialized knowledge that may not be routinely encountered in stateside clinical practice but can become essential during deployments, humanitarian missions, exercises, and contingency operations. Through the Military Tropical Medicine program, NMLPDC continues to develop medical professionals who are prepared not only for the conditions they routinely treat, but also for the unpredictable environmental and clinical challenges of operational medicine. NMLPDC is the cornerstone of Navy Medicine's professional training, leadership development, and education mission; maintaining collaborative relationships with more than 300 military and civilian higher learning institutions while annually supporting 3,000 Federal uniformed services, civilian, and allied foreign military members..

items.title: 673d Security Forces Squadron hosts Alaska Defense Sustainment Training
items.author: A1C Frank Houseton
items.summary: Operating in Alaska requires more than traditional military skills. The state’s rugged terrain, unpredictable conditions and vast distances demand service members be prepared to move, communicate and operate effectively in some of the most challenging environments on earth.
items.body:
JOINT BASE ELMENDORF-RICHARDSON, Alaska – Operating in Alaska requires more than traditional military skills. The state’s rugged terrain, unpredictable conditions and vast distances demand service members be prepared to move, communicate and operate effectively in some of the most challenging environments on earth.

The 673d Security Forces Squadron, based at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, has found a way to address this issue. The Alaska Defense Sustainment Training, a week-long course developing Airmen's survival skills and helping them move and sustain operations in remote and austere conditions.

“The training is important for security forces stationed in Alaska so they know their environment and can have the confidence to go out in various conditions and thrive,” said U.S Alaska Air National Guard Airman 1st Class Thresa Savo, 176th Security Forces defender and ADST cadre member.

The training combines classroom instruction with hands-on scenarios focused on Arctic survival, land navigation, communication, casualty response, transportation and technical movement across challenging terrain.

For U.S. Air Force Staff Sgt. Nevin Larock, an instructor with the 673d SFS, hands-on training is crucial. By combining classroom instruction with hands-on experience, Larock and the training cadre help ensure Alaska-based defenders are ready to operate where the environment itself can become part of the mission.

“We want to see them succeed in training so they can excel at the mission,” Larock said. “They’re being exposed to it before they have to execute it in the real world.”

Larock led instruction during ADST, teaching participants techniques designed to improve mobility, vehicle handling and survival skills in rugged Arctic terrain. The training included all-terrain vehicle operations, safety procedures, rope techniques and navigating steep terrain.

Additionally, the exercise challenged participants to coordinate their movements while safely carrying a simulated casualty, reinforcing the importance of teamwork and communication during evacuation operations. Furthermore, participants practiced tactical combat movements, applying their Arctic mobility skills in a more operational setting and rehearsing how to maneuver as a team while accounting for the terrain around them.

The training also incorporated realistic stressors to help participants understand how fatigue and limited resources can affect their ability to perform during extended operations. “We want to do it in a sense where they’re already sleep deprived, facing possible caloric deficits, when they might be at their lowest—because in combat on deployments, you don’t necessarily get to choose how rested you will be when you’re needed,” said Larock.

Regular iterations of ADST give Airmen an opportunity to learn in a controlled environment, strengthening their ability to respond when those same challenges arise during real-world missions. Training like this continually develops service members to operate effectively across Alaska's unique environment while strengthening the readiness and resilience required for Arctic operations.
