items.title: Global Strike ‘Campaign’ Aims to Speed Up B-1, B-52 Maintenance, Parts Supply
items.author: Steve Losey
items.summary: One year into a new campaign to boost readiness rates for the B-1B Lancer and B-52H Stratofortress bombers, Air Force Global Strike Command is claiming some early wins and planning to forge ahead with more improvements. The post Global Strike ‘Campaign’ Aims to Speed Up B-1, B-52 Maintenance, Parts Supply appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

One year into a new campaign to boost readiness rates for the B-1B Lancer and B-52 H Stratofortress bombers, Air Force Global Strike Command is claiming some early wins and planning to forge ahead with more improvements.

The North Star Readiness Campaign, launched in summer 2025, is mostly focused on coordinating maintenance and supply logistics for two of the most in-demand but stressed fleets in the Air Force. AFGSC is teaming up with Air Force Materiel Command and the Defense Logistics Agency in an effort to streamline the supply of spare parts and engineering support, break down logistical barriers, and improve how depots operate to allow B-1s and B-52s to be repaired and maintained faster.

The drive to improve readiness is needed, officials say, to help keep the B-1 flying through 2037 and the B-52 even longer than that while the Air Force builds out its new fleet of B-21 Raider s. The B-1 fleet’s average age is approaching 40 years old, and the B-52 fleet average is past 60 years old. What’s more, the Air Force has had more and more trouble over the years keeping the jets mission capable.

The Air Force no longer releases statistics on airframes’ mission-capable rates—the percentage of time an aircraft is available and able to carry out its mission—but in 2024, B-52s were available 54 percent of the time, and B-1s were even lower at 43 percent. Both had been on a steady downward trend.

“The North Star Readiness Campaign is our commitment to ensuring the warfighter has the nation’s bomber force ready to go at a moment’s notice,” Global Strike commander Gen. S.L. Davis said in a Sept. 8 statement from the Air Force. “This is a team effort. It brings together the operators at Air Force Global Strike Command, the acquisition and sustainment experts at Air Force Materiel Command, and our logistics partners at the Defense Logistics Agency to focus on one thing: operational readiness.”

In its Sept. 8 release, Global Strike did not detail new mission capable rates for the bomber fleets. But the command did note some progress.

The B-1, for example, has frequently suffered from “mission-impacting part problems.” MICAPs, as they are known, occur when a part that is necessary for an aircraft to be mission capable fails, and the spare or repair part is not available. At the start of the North Star Readiness Campaign, the B-1 fleet had more than 450 MICAPs, the Air Force release states. Now, that figure is down to about 160.

This has allowed maintainers to spend less time working on immediate emergencies on the B-1 and instead concentrate more on high-priority backorders and emerging trends on failures on the aircraft.

Another sign of progress are daily meetings between DLA representatives, supply chain officials, logistics readiness squadrons at the base level, and flightline maintainers to figure out which parts are being delayed and fix problems faster. By clearing procedural logjams, the release states, the command has been able to speed up some shipment timelines from more than a week to two or three days.

The campaign is unfolding at Air Force is increasingly worried about its ability to keep enough bombers in the air—and as some of its key platforms are showing their age.

The B-1 fleet, which now numbers 45 aircraft, was flown extremely heavily and worn out during the Global War on Terror. Over the last five years, the Air Force retired 17 of its most exhausted B-1s, in part to allow maintenance Airmen to concentrate on the healthiest Lancers.

The B-52, meanwhile, is famed for its longevity but is increasingly showing its age. The 75-aircraft fleet’s Pratt & Whitney-made TF33 engines are original, dating back to when the bombers rolled off the production lines, and commonly break. Many of the companies that made spare parts for the B-52 have closed or otherwise stopped making them, forcing the service to find other sources for parts—and even cannibalize other non-flying Stratofortresses for usable parts.

The Air Force is now in the midst of a massive modernization effort for the B-52, which will ultimately see its engines, avionics, radar, cockpit displays, and other key components replaced. This upgrade, which is extensive enough the Air Force will redub the bomber the B-52J, is intended to keep the bombers flying into at least the 2050s.

The Air Force said insight from maintainers who work on these planes every day is crucial to the readiness campaign. Flightline maintainers are providing information that is helping to refine maintenance processes and more quickly move critical parts to where they need to be, the Air Force said.

Chief Master Sgt. Shane Anderson, change management lead for the North Star Readiness Campaign, said one example was the way Airmen built a playbook to allow the “phase maintenance” process—or an extensive maintenance overhaul regularly scheduled for when an aircraft flies a certain number of hours—to be performed much more efficiently, without compromising safety or security.

“The [readiness campaign] started as a concept at the strategic level, but we have also received ideas directly from the flight line,” Anderson said. “They are the ones with the hands-on experience, and we would be remiss if we didn’t leverage their expertise to drive these improvements.”

The campaign also aims to expedite the parts availability for critical B-1 structural and avionics components, while working with AFMC and DLA to “streamline depot-level maintenance cycles.”

“These targeted efforts are designed to maximize the B-1’s operational readiness, ensuring it remains a lethal and highly visible conventional global strike option,” the Air Force said.

The Air Force also said the campaign is helping leaders anticipate future issues that might hurt the bombers’ readiness before they flare up into problems that grind missions to a halt.

The unified approach to improving maintenance is crucial to make sure the strategic bomber fleet remains able to project airpower, the release states.

“By modernizing these incredible platforms and ensuring our maintainers have the parts and support they need, we are sending a clear message to our adversaries and allies alike that the United States’ long-range penetrating strike capability is, and will remain, second to none,” Davis said.

items.title: JBER NCO plays for winning team in Armed Forces softball championship
items.author: A1C Thomas Polk
items.summary: It’s a hot Oklahoma day, and it’s the final game in the 2026 Armed Forces Softball Championship. The men’s Air Force team is up against the Army. It has been a challenging few days leading up to this point–but U.S. Air Force Staff Sgt. Jacob McDonald, representing not only the Air Force as a whole but also his home base of JBER, is sure his team has what it takes to bring home the gold.
items.body:
JOINT BASE ELMENDORF-RICHARDSON, Alaska – It’s a hot Oklahoma day, and it’s the final game in the 2026 Armed Forces Softball Championship. The men’s Air Force team is up against the Army. It has been a challenging few days leading up to this point–but U.S. Air Force Staff Sgt. Jacob McDonald, representing not only the Air Force as a whole but also his home base of JBER, is sure his team has what it takes to bring home the gold.

McDonald is right. Despite fierce competition, as the sun beats down overhead and players bake in the 100-degree heat, and McDonald’s friends and family cheer him on thousands of miles away, the Air Force team secures the win as the 2026 champions.

The Armed Forces Softball Championship is an annual tournament separated into men's and women's brackets, and the 2026 event featured Army, Navy and Air Force teams. This year it was held at Devon Park in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, from Aug. 26 through Aug. 29. The Air Force men’s team had 15 players, selected due to their sports experience, participation in military games and personal references.

For McDonald, his softball career began well before the championship. The noncommissioned officer in charge of the 673d Logistics Readiness Squadron commander support staff at JBER, he used his history in competitive softball, service experience and the support from his friends and family to perform and earn his spot on this year’s team.

He said competing alongside the other branches of the Department of War provided him the opportunity to rise to the challenge and build camaraderie at the same time.

“I started playing competitive softball at my first duty station, Kadena Air Base in Okinawa, Japan, eight years ago,” said McDonald. “Getting the opportunity to represent the Air Force in the Armed Forces Softball Championship has been a goal I’ve set for myself since joining the military.”

While stationed at JBER, McDonald traveled to the Lower 48 often to participate in civilian and military tournaments. In doing so, he gained valuable training, experience, and recognition from other players and coaches.

“This was the first year I got the opportunity to put in an application package, and it was everything I imagined it would be,” he said.

McDonald’s softball and operational experience allowed him to quickly adapt to his new team and work together towards a common goal. Throughout his time at the tournament, he built camaraderie not only with his teammates but also with his competition. “It goes from not knowing each other to ending up being brothers and feeling like family,” said McDonald.

The men’s Air Force team went into the final championship games with a record of five wins and one loss. In the finals, the Air Force faced the Army and came out victorious with a score of 33-18.

While McDonald had his team to rely on at the championship, he also had those back home to cheer him on.

“They're very supportive and responsive, from my leadership all the way to my friends, and especially my wife,” he said. “She was the one who pushed me to do it, and that definitely helped, going out there and knowing that I have as much support as I did.”

Those who know McDonald have spoken to the quality of his character. His supervisor, Master Sgt. Daviea Cowans, quality assurance superintendent of the 673d Logistics Readiness Squadron, said that he is respectful and professional. Even during the live stream of the games, Cowans watched as McDonald “made sure his teammates were looked after,” continuing to display his dedication to his team.

“He is personable, charismatic and cares about the Airmen he supports,” said Cowans. “He always takes on any task and works to the best of his ability.”

McDonald said he took everything that he had learned over the years as an Airman and competitive softball player and highlighted what the Air Force represents: integrity, service and excellence.

“It’s an honor to be able to wear the ‘Air Force’ across my chest and be one of the few selected to go out there and represent not only JBER and my squadron, but the Air Force as a whole,” said McDonald. “It’s a great experience, and there's definitely a lot of pride that goes into that.”

items.title: USAF’s Only Aerial Spray Unit Squeezed by Demand, Aging Equipment, Slow Modernization
items.author: Todd South
items.summary: Over the past few months and peaking in August, crews with the 910th Airlift Wing out of Youngstown Air Reserve Station, Ohio, have been running nighttime, low-flying missions to kill a ubiquitous and deadly adversary that’s plagued Americans for centuries—mosquitoes. The post USAF’s Only Aerial Spray Unit Squeezed by Demand, Aging Equipment, Slow Modernization appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

Over the past few months and peaking in August, crews with the 910th Airlift Wing out of Youngstown Air Reserve Station, Ohio, have been running nighttime, low-flying missions to kill a ubiquitous and deadly adversary that’s plagued Americans for centuries—mosquitoes.

In a given year, crews with the wing conduct 25 recurring missions annually, blanketing thousands of acres with spray to kill mosquitoes carrying West Nile virus; a blue-hued herbicide for invasive plants such as halogeton, which grows on the Utah Test and Training Range; and an oil dispersant for spills such as the 2010 Deepwater Horizon incident.

For decades, the 910th’s C-130H Hercules and analog sprayers have conducted this mission, but the aging aircraft and its equipment have far exceeded their expected use.

The Air Force Reserve has been working since the early 2010s to replace these aging aircraft with C-130Js and their sprayers with more efficient technology.

But like the pesky mosquito, delays in integrating the new Electronic Modular Aerial Spray System and delivering the Boeing-built C-130Js have stymied the modernization effort.

In April, during his final testimony to Congress before retiring, then-Chief of the Air Force Reserve Lt. Gen. John P. Healy praised the unique work of the 910th, whose main mission is to provide tactical airlift—delivering cargo and personnel via airdrop and air-land techniques—and told lawmakers he fears that their spray mission could stall if political leaders and the Department of the Air Force didn’t take action.

Delays in J model deliveries, EMASS compatibility, requirements to divest H models, and aircraft availability concerns means the department could be forced to rely on one plane to service a dozen military sites across nine states. That’s not to mention the possible need for spraying in the event of a major hurricane, overseas disaster, or combat mission that needs to exterminate deadly bugs.

“I predict next year in ‘27, where we’re going to be stuck with only one potential spray system to service the country, and I think that’s an uncomfortable risk with regard to the mission set that they provide,” Healy testified.

Life extensions on the H model aircraft and the integration and delivery of the new EMASS equipment could mitigate the issue, and the wing is hoping to receive four new C-130Js in the coming months, Reserve spokesman Sean Houlihan told Air & Space Forces Magazine. The last of the H models will stick around through 2027, Houlihan added.

the Pentagon faced the prospect of having a single plane to service a dozen military sites across nine states. That’s

But even with the Js now arriving, the long timeline for crew training and certifying the EMASS spray system means that the new Js won’t be able to spray for months.

The Mission

The spray mission predates the Air Force itself; in 1943, the Army Air Forces worked with the Bureau of Entomology and Plant Quarantine to develop technology for a wide-area, aerial-dispersal spray to kill mosquitoes in World War II’s Pacific theater using dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane, or DDT.

The Reserve took over the spray mission from Active-Duty units in 1973 at the tail end of the Vietnam War. In the 53 years since, the Reserve has conducted 10 non-military emergency deployments, spraying more than 7 million acres for pests and insects. Those missions included a 1973 Panama deployment to combat mosquitoes carrying Equine encephalitis, a 1987 mission to reduce Dengue fever-carrying mosquitoes in Puerto Rico, a 1999 deployment to North Carolina and Virginia in the wake of Hurricane Floyd, and a 2005 trip to the Gulf Coast in the aftermath of Hurricanes Katrina and Rita.

The 910th has been the sole unit for this mission since 1992, and as recently as 2009, it had 16 aircraft. Between 2009 and 2014, the wing lost eight planes as the Department of the Air Force decided to retire more of its H models.

Delayed Aircraft

Planning to recapitalize that fleet goes back to at least the fiscal 2020 budget, which saw Congress allocate $730 million for eight C-130J aircraft, four each for the Guard and Reserve. At the time, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported that the Reserve was considering the 910th and the 302nd Airlift Wing in Colorado as potential units for the new aircraft, with deliveries expected in 2023.

More funding for Reserve C-130Js followed in the 2021 and 2022 budgets, and in late 2022, the Department of the Air Force tapped Youngstown as its preferred location for eight C-130Js, setting up the 910th to recapitalize its entire C-130H fleet.

The J model requires two fewer crew members, easing the aircraft’s manning load on all missions. The C-130 crew no longer needs a navigator or flight engineer because its advanced systems perform that work.

The unit received its first C-130J in July 2024 and its second in December 2024. But then things slowed in 2025, as manufacturer Lockheed Martin began integrating a new communications suite because of obsolete components. Deliveries ground to a halt.

Christopher Karns, a Lockheed spokesman, told Air & Space Forces Magazine the firm has finalized certification of the new implementation design and resumed deliveries earlier in 2026. The 910th received its third J model in May.

The company does not determine which Air Force units get planes and when. That’s determined by the service. The 910th had expected its fourth C-130J over the summer, but that has been delayed again until September.

Lockheed expects to return to “historic averages between 16-24 aircraft” in 2026, Karns said. As of late August, there were 40 C-130Js in various phases of production, Karns said.

The delivery delays have had a ripple effect. The 910th has been divesting H models as it takes on new J models, leaving the wing with three C-130Js and four C-130Hs built between 1989 and 1992.

Spraying System

New aircraft are only part of the equation for the spray mission. The Air Force is also trying to field a new spraying system, the EMASS. In 2025, the service awarded a $98.4 million contract to the Battelle Memorial Institute in Ohio to build five EMASS for the Js.

The legacy Modular Aerial Spray System is now 30 years old. It runs four 500-gallon tanks with a 250-gallon flush tank. By contrast, the EMASS can carry up to 3,500 gallons for spraying.

The full, palletized, roll-on/roll-off EMASS kits interface directly with the J model and use the Next Generation Agricultural-Global Positioning System to manage precision, location-based spraying at low altitudes, maximizing pesticide and herbicide use while minimizing collateral or off-target spraying.

But crucially, the digitized, roll-on, roll-off system can’t be used with the legacy H model.

Training and Certification

The combination of a new aircraft model and new spray system has required extra layers of training, testing, certification, and calibration for the 910th.

Training to transition from the C-130H to the J model can take six months to a year at Little Rock Air Force Base, Ark.

Beyond that transition, there’s another layer of specialized training for the spray mission. Pilots typically need at least 500 flight hours before starting spray training, which has aircraft fly as low as 150-300 feet off the ground.

“We do not have a simulator for spray training, so we outfit a vehicle with a lightbar to put on the dashboard,” said Lt. Col. Steve Stroney, 757th Airlift Squadron director of operations and the unit’s most seasoned aerial spray operator. “This is what we use to identify the centerline of a spray swath in the airplane.”

By training with a lightbar on the ground, pilots can get a “low-threat introduction” to visual cues before flying, Stroney said.

After ground training, pilots start local training using the equipment but not yet spraying, working down to 300 feet at night and 100 feet during the day.

Effects

The spray mission’s impact is vast—the 910th services ranges and air installations across the country. It even helps kill many of the legendary sand fleas that munch on recruits at Marine Corps Depot-Parris Island, S.C.

At Minot Air Force Base in North Dakota, Lester Nicholas, 55, has worked the pest control mission both in uniform and as a civilian. Right now, the retired master sergeant works with two Airmen to track and handle every pest across the base’s 8,500 square miles and 150 ICBM launch facilities.

Nicholas spent much of his career at Minot and Grand Forks Air Force Base, N.D. The job chose him.

“I came into the Air Force, and that’s the job they assigned me,” Nicholas told Air & Space Forces Magazine. “That was a long time ago.”

The three-person crew drives trucks with pesticide foggers through some areas of the base, but the harder-to-reach spots where mosquitoes love to live can be tougher. That’s where the 910th comes in.

“We’re kind of limited to the areas, especially the areas that get swampy,” Nicholas said. “Whereas the plane flies above, and the chemical will drift down and get pretty much 100 percent coverage.”

The unit’s data shows that sprays can reduce insect bite counts from up to 200 bites per minute down to less than one, a 91 percent reduction.

Bryan Banfill, a 21-year Air Force veteran who retired in 2024, saw the spraying while stationed at Minot from 2004 to 2013 and now depends on it in his job as the city of Minot’s public works operations director.

The former electronic warfare technician, Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missile program manager, and ROTC instructor didn’t plan on targeting mosquitoes for his day job.

“You know, when I first took this job, I thought for sure I’d learn a lot of neat and interesting facts,” Banfill told Air & Space Forces Magazine. “Mosquitoes, that was definitely not on that list. I had no clue.”

Banfill and his office start tracking mosquito numbers in June. The wetness of the winter and late spring/early summer seasons indicates the likely population, but it always varies.

“We check larval counts, so we actually look at standing bodies of water and what type of increases we’re seeing for larvae,” Banfill said. “Essentially, the pre-hatch for the mosquitoes themselves.”

The city of Minot and the 910th then try to time the spray to kill the adults and reduce the mosquito count later in the summer, when it typically peaks in August.

“We start seeing increases right around the time they’re able to assist us with the spray, the aerial spray itself,” he said.

In July, his team saw about 120 mosquitoes per week, then a spike of more than 2,000 at various locations throughout the city.

“The aerial spray is mainly used, or actually only used, for adulticide,” Banfill said. “So, it is to go ahead and attack the mosquitoes themselves that are already post-hatch.”

items.title: Iran likely to reverse-engineer captured US underwater drone
items.author: Mike Stone and David Jeans, Reuters
items.summary: Iran will almost certainly try to pry open the captured drone’s hardware, but the platform's software does carry built-in defenses, analysts say.
items.body:
MilTech

Iran likely to reverse-engineer captured US underwater drone

An unmanned U.S. submersible Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it captured, Sept. 8, 2026. (IRGC/WANA via REUTERS)

Iran’s capture of a U.S. military underwater drone gives Tehran an opportunity to study and potentially reverse-engineer the vessel, delivering a setback for the Pentagon and drone maker Anduril .

The U.S. military and Anduril have downplayed the significance of the drone falling into Iranian hands. The vessel, a Dive-LD autonomous underwater vehicle designed for long-range surveillance and other undersea missions, is among a new generation of military drones intended to operate for days with little human intervention. Washington has previously treated the loss of advanced drones to Iran as a serious matter.

After Iran captured an RQ-170 Sentinel stealth reconnaissance drone in 2011, then-President Barack Obama publicly asked Tehran to return the aircraft. Iran later claimed it had reverse-engineered the drone and subsequently unveiled domestically produced models that appeared to draw heavily on its design.

More recently, the U.S. military moved swiftly to prevent Iranian forces from taking possession of uncrewed maritime technology. In 2022, a U.S. Navy patrol ship and MH-60S Seahawk helicopter were deployed after an Iranian naval vessel attempted to tow away a Saildrone surface vessel in the Gulf, according to the Navy.

Analysts say Iran is unlikely to gain a decisive military advantage from the captured drone, but the episode nonetheless represents a propaganda victory for Tehran and an awkward setback for Washington’s efforts to project technological superiority.

IRANIAN EMBASSIES MOCK U.S.

Iranian embassies around the world have mocked the U.S. for losing its drone. Iran’s embassy in Ghana, in a post on X, boasted about picking the submersible up in “a strait controlled by people who can hear a shrimp sneeze,” adding that, “Our guys picked it up like a plastic bottle in a fishing net. Fully intact. Still blinking like an idiot. Condolences to whoever was holding the joystick.”

U.S. Navy Capt. Tim Hawkins of U.S. Central Command said the “defective drone was an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment.” Anduril did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

“Of course Iran will take every opportunity as a propaganda win,” said Farzin Nadimi, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. “It can help the (Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps) make better versions of their own designs.”

Iran will almost certainly try to pry open the drone’s hardware, but the drone’s software carries built-in defenses, said Bryan Clark, a senior fellow and director of the Center for Defense Concepts and Technology at the Hudson Institute. Iranian engineers “could definitely reverse-engineer the mechanical systems,” he said, pointing to Tehran’s track record with captured American aircraft.

“Unboxing ceremony by our reverse engineers, tomorrow morning!” Iran’s embassy in Hyderabad wrote on X.

The incident has also highlighted a disconnect between the messaging of Anduril and its customer, the U.S. Navy.

Navy officials said the Dive-LD was an older-model vehicle that suffered a malfunction and was recovered by Iranian forces after being left “dead in the water.”

Anduril has promoted the Dive-LD as “the most reliable and flexible” large autonomous underwater vehicle available, saying it is capable of operating for up to 10 days in demanding conditions. In addition to its use by the U.S. Navy, the Dive-LD was the testbed vehicle for the development of Australia’s new Ghost Shark large underwater drone.

“This is something that Iran has proven very adept at exploiting for its own benefit in terms of seeking to frame the narrative as one of U.S., in this case, ineptitude and their ability to sort of retain control over the Strait of Hormuz,” said Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

items.title: Russia sends bones of medieval warrior prince to Ukraine front to boost morale
items.author: Andrew Osborn, Reuters
items.summary: Bone fragments from the sword hand of a medieval Russian prince who won a famous victory over the Mongols have been sent to the front in Ukraine.
items.body:
Global

Russia sends bones of medieval warrior prince to Ukraine front to boost morale

Bearers carry a case with relics of a medieval Russian prince Dmitry Donskoy during a citywide procession, Sept. 6, 2026. (Sergei Kiselev/Moscow News Agency/Reuters)

Bone fragments from the sword hand of a medieval Russian prince who won a famous victory over the Mongols have been sent to the front in Ukraine to raise army morale in the Russian Orthodox Church’s latest show of support for President Vladimir Putin’s war.

The sarcophagus of Grand Prince Dmitry Donskoy, who died in 1389 and is revered by Russian nationalists for defeating the Mongol Golden Horde at the 1380 Battle of Kulikovo, was uncovered this summer during restoration work at Moscow’s Cathedral of the Archangel inside the Kremlin.

Putin personally inspected what experts said were the prince’s well-preserved remains in August, hailing them as “an absolutely unique and marvellous discovery” which reinforced the foundations of Russian history.

The Russian Orthodox Church, which has backed Putin throughout the conflict, said it had dispatched a fragment of Donskoy’s right hand to Donetsk, one of four Ukrainian regions Putin said he had incorporated into Russia in 2022, a move Kyiv rejected as an illegal land grab.

Referring to Donskoy as “the holy commander,” the Moscow Patriarchate of the Russian Orthodox Church said part of his remains had been sent to the front to stand invisibly shoulder-to-shoulder with Russian troops.

“A fragment of the Grand Prince’s right hand – the very same right hand with which he wielded his sword on Kulikovo Field – has been sent to the front to strengthen the soldiers’ spirits,” it said in a statement.

The relic, held in a small ornate casket beneath toughened glass, will be shown to Russian combat units along the more than 1,000-km front line, it said.

Donskoy, whose name was given to a Soviet tank column funded by the church in World War Two, was declared a saint by the Russian Orthodox Church in 1988.

Patriotic push

The carefully choreographed effort to use his remains in a public relations exercise to boost patriotism and morale comes ahead of a parliamentary election later this month.

Russian military and church officials have presented the discovery as a fortuitous find that could help Russian forces prevail in Ukraine, now in the fifth year of a grinding war.

The tour also comes as Russian forces seek full control of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine and as diplomatic efforts to end the war have yet to yield a breakthrough.

Donskoy’s relics were carried through the streets of Moscow at the weekend in a huge Orthodox procession.

At a ceremony at a World War Two memorial in Donetsk on Tuesday, Sergei Kiriyenko, Putin’s first deputy Kremlin chief of staff, joined military commanders and the Russian-installed regional head in kissing the relic and making the sign of the cross as a priest read a prayer.

“Both our military personnel and the people who live in Donbas need strengthening from above, need God’s help and the blessing of our saints,” Metropolitan Vladimir of Donetsk and Mariupol, a senior Moscow-appointed cleric, said. Donbas is a broader area incorporating Donetsk and neighbouring Luhansk which Russia controls almost in its entirety.

Elsewhere, commanders have presented Donskoy’s remains as evidence that God is on Russia’s side.

The Defence Ministry on Wednesday released footage of troops in the Sverdlovsk region attending a church service carrying icons and Orthodox flags, alongside an interview with a commander who said the relics would support Russia’s victory.

Critics, however, have accused the Church of breaking with religious protocol to please the Kremlin. They have also questioned why Donskoy’s remains, whose location was broadly known for decades, were recovered and venerated only now, 38 years after he was declared a saint.

“By the fifth year of war, the Church leadership in Moscow began to wonder what else it could do to show its support for what Russia terms its ‘special military operation’,” Alexander Zanemonets, an Orthodox priest and historian based outside Russia, wrote in a note for the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center whose director Russia has designated a “foreign agent.”

“It had already sent priests to the front lines, instituted mandatory prayers for Russian victory in every church, and flown icons over cities. A state embroiled in war will try to compel all institutions, including religious ones, to participate in it.”

items.title: NATO allies foil Russian subsea cable sabotage plot
items.author: Sarah McFarlane and Gram Slattery, Reuters
items.summary: The clandestine Russian operation was carried out by Moscow’s GUGI undersea warfare directorate to test a destructive sabotage capability, sources said.
items.body:
Europe

NATO allies foil Russian subsea cable sabotage plot

A sailboat moves near the Svalbard and Jan Mayen islands, part of Norway, in the Arctic Ocean on July 16, 2025. (Sebnem Coskun/Anadolu via Getty Images)

LONDON/WASHINGTON — Deep in Arctic waters near the remote Svalbard archipelago this spring, NATO allies caught Russian subs training to unleash a secret weapon designed to disable critical undersea cables without leaving any fingerprints.

The clandestine Russian operation, described to Reuters by two Western officials, was carried out by Moscow’s GUGI undersea warfare directorate, which used deep-sea submersibles to simulate the deployment of the sophisticated and destructive technology.

A joint operation involving Britain, Norway and the United States tracked and confronted the Russian vessels at sea, said the two officials, speaking on condition of anonymity. The vessels were prevented from completing their exercise and eventually left the area.

Britain and Norway disclosed in April that they had uncovered a covert Russian operation in Arctic waters. But the discovery of the new weapon, the location of the operation and the U.S. involvement have not been reported.

The deep-sea face-off comes at a time when some Western intelligence officials fear the Kremlin is ramping up sabotage operations in Europe and preparing for a conflict with NATO.

Some U.S. intelligence analysts are increasingly concerned Russia may test NATO’s mutual defense pact, known as Article 5, three U.S. officials said. If it does, destroying subsea cables could be a critical part of that effort, the Western officials said.

Cables no thicker than a garden hose, lying on the seabed or buried just below, are critical to global internet connectivity and financial transactions. Their economic and strategic importance has made them targets in past conflicts, including in the First and Second World Wars, when they were critical to delivering orders by telegraph or telephone.

Two 1,400 km subsea fiber-optic cables linking Svalbard to mainland Norway lie as deep as 2,700 meters below the sea’s surface. They carry vast amounts of satellite data downloaded at the SvalSat satellite ground station, the world’s largest and part of NASA’s Near Space Network.

Russia’s Defense Ministry didn’t respond to a request for comment on the incident. The Kremlin consistently denies conducting sabotage operations in NATO countries or plotting any confrontation.

Some Western officials argue that Moscow’s targeting of European states has increased in recent months as the front line in Ukraine has become largely static.

Countries including Poland, Lithuania, and Romania have confirmed various violations. Most recently, an attempted drone attack on the Leipzig/Halle Airport in August triggered a series of responses from Germany, including the closure of a Russian consulate in Bonn and a cultural centre in Berlin.

In August, Central Intelligence Agency Director John Ratcliffe visited intelligence counterparts in Moscow, in part to warn Russia against escalating sabotage operations in Europe, said two people familiar with the matter.

Reuters couldn’t determine if Ratcliffe raised Russia’s covert subsea operations. The Kremlin declined to say what had been discussed or to provide any further details.

Arctic exercise

At the same time as the confrontations at sea, British and Norwegian officials took their findings to Moscow to show they were aware of the new technology – hoping it might make Russia hesitate to use it, the two Western officials said.

Russia didn’t damage any cables. The exercise focused on simulating the deployment of the technology in the event of a conflict with NATO, the officials said. They declined to detail how the technology works.

Asked for comment, NATO referred Reuters to Norwegian and U.K. authorities.

“Through our joint operation, we sent a clear message to Russia that they cannot operate covertly,” Norway’s Defence Minister Tore Sandvik said in a statement.

“We have made it unequivocally clear to Russian authorities that any attempt to target our critical infrastructure will be detected and met with consequences,” he said. “It is in no one’s interest to escalate tensions in the High North.”

Britain’s Defence Ministry pointed to April 9 statements acknowledging attempted covert activities in and near Norwegian and British waters by Russia’s Main Directorate of Deep-Sea Research, known by its Russian acronym GUGI. Washington and London have both imposed sanctions on the secretive directorate.

The White House didn’t respond to a comment request. The CIA declined to comment.

Any escalation between Russia and NATO could quickly underscore the strategic importance of an icy expanse of water between the southern tip of the Svalbard archipelago and mainland Norway known as the Bear Gap, one of the Western officials said.

To reach the Atlantic, Russian nuclear submarines based in the Kola Peninsula would cross the 400-mile-wide stretch of water before passing Norway’s remote volcanic island Jan Mayen.

Britain said this week it deployed forces to Jan Mayen in August alongside Norwegian and U.S. allies for an exercise to demonstrate NATO’s ability to operate jointly in the High North.

Norway plans to have new fiber-optic cable linking Svalbard and Jan Mayen to the mainland by 2028.

‘Burgeoning Russian threat’

NATO allies have focused on subsea infrastructure security since the 2022 destruction of three of the four Nord Stream subsea pipelines supplying Germany with Russian gas. German prosecutors have indicted a Ukrainian man who was a special forces officer at the time of the attack. Ukraine denies any role in the sabotage.

And since 2023, more ships have sailed slowly over or near sensitive subsea infrastructure including pipelines, power cables and telecoms cables to map their location, an activity known as drifting.

Last year, drifting in the North Sea rose 52% to 13,079 vessels from the previous year, data from maritime risk analytics firm Windward showed, while activity in the South China Sea region jumped 88% to 18,401 vessels.

It’s not illegal to survey infrastructure in international waters but security experts see such extensive mapping as preparation for sabotage.

The activity and suspected interference with some cables prompted new initiatives launched in January last year, including NATO’s Baltic Sentry monitoring system and the U.K.-led Nordic Warden, bringing navies together for increased patrols of critical infrastructure.

In the Baltic Sea – one focus area for monitoring – 2025 drifting activity was down 5% to 526 vessels from a year earlier, Windward data showed. It said at least 11 subsea cables had been damaged or cut in the Baltic from October 2023 through the end of last year.

“The current thinking is that Russia and China are probably the most active and critical underwater threats,” said Windward Chief Executive Ami Daniel.

The global network of power and telecoms cables running across seabeds is expanding each year, supported by increases in demand for data and electricity, partly driven by artificial intelligence, and some analysts say Europe remains vulnerable.

“In the last 25 years, Europe did two things simultaneously. It dramatically expanded the extent to which it relies on seabed infrastructure, and it dramatically shrunk its capacity to protect that infrastructure,” said Bruce Jones, a senior fellow with the Brookings Institution. “It’s belatedly rebuilding now, in the face of a burgeoning Russian threat.”

items.title: US radar maker Echodyne mulls European production as drone warfare fuels demand
items.author: Jaroslaw Adamowski
items.summary: The U.S. radar specialist said it's sensing new business opportunities in Europe, where governments are scrambling to up their counter-drone capabilities.
items.body:
Europe

US radar maker Echodyne mulls European production as drone warfare fuels demand

A drone flies near a U.S. soldier with an Echodyne EchoShield radar for drone detection during a media demonstration at the U.S. Army Joint Multinational Readiness Center on Aug. 26, 2026, near Hohenfels, Germany. (Sean Gallup/Getty Images)

KIELCE, Poland — U.S. radar maker Echodyne has announced that Norway’s Kongsberg has selected its MESA radar platform for a broad range of air and surface applications.

Echodyne opened a manufacturing facility in Washington state last July, and is considering establishing a manufacturing presence in Europe to benefit from the booming counter-drone market there.

Eben Frankenberg, the company’s CEO, told Defense News at the MSPO defense show here that Echodyne has longstanding cooperation with Kongsberg. The integration of its radars into the company’s Protector RS4 and Protector RS6 remote weapon stations will further increase Echodyne’s visibility in European markets, he said.

Echodyne’s solutions will make “those remote weapon stations, which weren’t originally designed to counter drone threats, effective at countering drone threats,” Frankenberg said. “And this is something we do with a lot of companies.”

With a surging demand for miniaturized radars that ensure detection and fire-control support for various counter-drone systems in Europe, Echodyne is also considering investing in establishing a manufacturing presence in Europe.

“There’s obviously a big European demand and there’s rightfully some interest from European countries in having more local content,” the CEO said. “We’re thinking about where it would make the most sense.”

In July 2026, Echodyne said it opened an 86,350-square-foot facility under a $40 million investment. The U.S. plant will eventually be able to produce more than 30,000 radar systems per year, according to data from Echodyne.

“Part of the plan with the new facility was that it gives us a template or blueprint to be able to open other new facilities in the future. Because now we know exactly all the machines we need to have, all the workstations, the number of people to equip them,” Frankenberg said. “So it does set us up for that in the future.”

Jaroslaw Adamowski is the Poland correspondent for Defense News.

items.title: Framework for the Opioid Use Disorder Cascade of Care
items.author: Katherine E. Watkins
items.summary: We sought to adapt the framework under the constraints of electronic health record data and identify patient populations at risk for opioid use disorder treatment discontinuity.
items.body:
Adaptation and Application for a Large Municipal Health System

Mariah Kalmin , Christina Crowley , Lia Pak , Colleen M. McCullough , Beth Ann Griffin , Kyle Ragins , Hrishikesh Belani , Katherine E. Watkins

Research Posted on rand.org Sep 10, 2026 Published in: Public Health Reports® (2026). DOI: 10.1177/00333549261467293

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Objectives

Most people with opioid use disorder (OUD) do not receive effective treatments despite their existence. The OUD cascade of care framework can be used to inform quality improvement efforts to address this gap, but data access and linkage requirements may limit its use. We sought to adapt the framework under the constraints of electronic health record data and identify patient populations at risk for OUD treatment discontinuity.

Materials and Methods

We extracted data on patients with OUD from the Los Angeles County Department of Health Services from July 2022 through June 2023. We adapted the cascade of care to include probable OUD diagnosis, receipt of naloxone prescription, and receipt of ≥1 and ≥2 buprenorphine prescriptions. We then stratified and conducted statistical analyses for associations by sex, race and ethnicity, and facility type (inpatient, primary care, emergency, or urgent care).

Results

Of 3881 patients identified with probable OUD, 49% received a naloxone prescription and 30% and 17% had ≥1 and ≥2 buprenorphine prescriptions, respectively, in 1 year. Non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic patients were less likely to receive buprenorphine prescriptions than were non-Hispanic White patients and patients of other or unknown race and ethnicity. We observed larger gaps in care between receipt of ≥1 and ≥2 buprenorphine prescriptions for patients using urgent care and emergency departments compared with patients in other settings.

Practice Implications

This study illustrates substantial gaps between OUD diagnosis and treatment. This adapted framework for the OUD cascade of care can serve as a quality-monitoring tool to aid clinicians and health care administrators in narrowing the treatment gap for people with OUD.

items.title: Mediators of the Effects of an HIV Prevention Advocacy Training Intervention on Prevention Advocacy Among Persons Living with HIV in Uganda
items.author: Stephen Okoboi
items.summary: In a secondary analysis from a randomized controlled trial of a peer advocacy training intervention for PLWH, we examined mediators of intervention effects on HIV prevention advocacy across members of their social network.
items.body:
Glenn Wagner , Laura M. Bogart , Joseph K. Matovu , Violet Gwokyalya , Harold D. Green , Susan Ninsiima , David J. Klein , Stephen Okoboi

Research Posted on rand.org Sep 10, 2026 Published in: Journal of Behavioral Medicine (2026). DOI: 10.1007/s10865-026-00704-z

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Pathways through which advocacy training enhances engagement in advocacy among persons living with HIV (PLWH) are not well understood. In a secondary analysis from a randomized controlled trial of a peer advocacy training intervention for PLWH, we examined mediators of intervention effects on HIV prevention advocacy (i.e., encouraging others to engage in HIV protective behaviors) across members of their social network. A sample of 210 PLWH (105 in each of the intervention and control arms) provided information about their advocacy to their social network members at baseline, and 6-, 12-, and 18-month follow-up. Repeated measures linear regressions showed that PLWH in the intervention group targeted more social network members with advocacy for HIV testing, condom use, pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) use, HIV care, and ART use over the follow-up period compared to those in the control group. In path analysis that examined each mediator in a separate model, reduced internalized HIV stigma and increased HIV knowledge as measured at month 6, each fully mediated the intervention effect on HIV care advocacy; reduced stigma partially mediated the effects on advocacy targeting each of the other four HIV protective behaviors, while increased knowledge partially mediated effects on HIV testing, condom and PrEP use advocacy. Results were unchanged when examining the joint mediation of stigma and knowledge. HIV disclosure and advocacy self-efficacy had no mediating effect. These findings highlight the importance of helping PLWH to cope with HIV stigma and gain knowledge about basic facts and common misconceptions related to HIV, to propel their engagement in advocacy for multiple HIV protective behaviors within their social networks.

items.title: Los Angeles County Public Defender Attorney Workload Study
items.author: Nicholas M. Pace
items.summary: The authors evaluate the Los Angeles County Public Defender’s Office’s Case Complexity System and assess the office’s broader capacity to effectively represent its clients amid growing case complexity and resource constraints.
items.body:
In this report, the authors rigorously evaluate the Los Angeles County Public Defender’s Office’s Case Complexity System, which scores the complexity of individual cases, and assess the office’s broader organizational capacity to effectively represent its clients amid growing case complexity and resource constraints.

Los Angeles County Public Defender Attorney Workload Study

Final Report

Maya Buenaventura , Amy Mahler , James M. Anderson , Nicholas M. Pace

Research Published Sep 10, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

The Los Angeles County Public Defender’s Office (LACPD) is the largest public defense agency in the United States, serving nearly 10 million residents across a vast and diverse region and employing more than 700 attorneys. For an office of LACPD’s scale and complexity, understanding workload demands requires more than simply tracking case counts, which fails to capture how public defense work has evolved given new justice reform legislation in California, expanded diversion programs, and the proliferation of digital evidence.

To better understand attorneys’ time commitments per case type, LACPD leadership sought an independent, data-driven study with two purposes: (1) rigorously evaluate the office’s Case Complexity System (CCS), which algorithmically scores the complexity of individual cases, and (2) assess the office’s broader organizational capacity to effectively represent its clients amid growing case complexity and resource constraints.

To validate whether CCS scores accurately reflect case complexity and workload demands, the authors of this report relied on three independent measures of case complexity and workload demand: a time study that involved attorneys’ self-reported hours during an eight-week period, a Delphi panel composed of experienced LACPD attorneys, and CCS’s algorithmically generated scores.

The authors integrated these quantitative measures with qualitative data from attorney interviews, five years of case management data, and a detailed examination of case assignment practices and support staff use. Through their analyses, the authors synthesize findings and recommend ways that LACPD can continue to improve workload assignments and better serve the people of Los Angeles County.

Key Takeaways

CCS tracks relative case complexity in the aggregate

CCS assigns higher scores to cases that both the time study and the Delphi panel estimated as the most demanding.

There is room to improve alignment in some areas

Most felony cases cluster at the lower end of the CCS scale, and mid-level felony categories with varying workload demands (as indicated by Delphi estimates) often receive similar scores, limiting differentiation.

CCS is early in its implementation, and some refinements would broaden its usefulness

CCS is promising in its design, and addressing data quality and implementation issues would strengthen the scores it produces.

CCS scores are not yet calibrated to be cardinally proportional—a case with a score of 4 does not necessarily reflect twice the amount of attorney hours as a case with a score of 2—so LACPD cannot yet use aggregate scores to determine how many attorney hours a given caseload requires.

Support-staff wait times pull attorneys away from legal work

According to attorneys the authors interviewed, long wait times for support from social workers and paralegals mean that attorneys often take on administrative and case-support tasks.

Recommendations

LACPD could improve CCS data quality by extracting key information from attorneys’ case notes and encouraging consistent entry in the structured Client Case Management System fields that drive scoring.

LACPD should ensure that CCS scores are cardinally proportional using expert elicitation and/or officewide timekeeping and by establishing an annual validation cycle to recalibrate factor weights over time.

LACPD should expand support staff roles where possible and formalize them in diversion support and digital-evidence management, which would allow attorneys to spend more time on legal work.

items.title: Conventional logics, nuclear fears
items.author: Kiran Suman-Chauhan
items.summary: This report examines inadvertent escalation risks between NATO and Russia, analysing how conventional military operations, specifically using deep precision strike weapons, could unintentionally increase the risks of nuclear escalation.
items.body:
This report examines inadvertent escalation risks between NATO and Russia, analysing how conventional military operations, specifically using deep precision strike weapons, could unintentionally increase the risks of nuclear escalation. It identifies key pathways – including C4ISR attacks, counterforce strikes and dual-capable system entanglement – informing NATO defence planning and risk mitigation strategies.

Conventional logics, nuclear fears

Inadvertent escalation risks between NATO and Russia

Paul van Hooft , Mattias Eken , Zsofia Wolford , Artur Honich , Thomas Kenchington , Kiran Suman-Chauhan

Research Published Sep 10, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

This report examines the risk of inadvertent escalation between NATO and Russia, whereby the use of conventional weapons by one side could be misperceived by the other as an intentional existential threat to its nuclear deterrent, regime or society. Unlike deliberate or accidental escalation, inadvertent escalation can arise from the structural entanglement of conventional and nuclear capabilities, doctrinal ambiguity, and the compressed decision-making timelines characteristic of modern warfare. Drawing on a review of Cold War and contemporary nuclear rivalries – including the US–Soviet, Sino-American, Korean Peninsula and India–Pakistan cases – alongside interviews with NATO defence officials, the report identifies four principal pathways through which conventional operations could inadvertently trigger nuclear escalation:

Attacks on command, control, communications and intelligence systems

Counterforce strikes against dual-capable delivery systems

The interaction of missile defence with damage-limitation strategies

Conventional actions perceived as existential threats to regime or societal survival.

The analysis applies these pathways to three key subregions of NATO–Russia confrontation: the North Atlantic and High North, the Baltics and Kaliningrad, and the Black Sea region, highlighting how geography, technology and doctrine combine to create distinct escalation risks in each.

The report finds that these inadvertent escalation risks are likely to be cumulative and entropic, growing more unpredictable the longer a conventional conflict endures. The report calls for greater sensitivity among planners and policymakers to the potential blind spots inherent in conventional campaigns, especially as European NATO member states invest more in long range or deep precision strike. This first report lays the analytical foundation for a subsequent report, which will use scenario-based wargaming to further explore these dynamics and inform policy recommendations for managing escalation risk.

Key Takeaways

Modern networked warfare amplifies inadvertent escalation risks

Inadvertent escalation risks stem from technological, doctrinal and strategic developments in modern networked warfare emphasising high-speed, first-mover advantages through counter-C4ISR operations and precision strikes. Russia combines conventional and nuclear assets with information operations, complicating NATO's ability to interpret its intentions. Similarly, NATO's Multi-Domain Operations concept – reliant on integrated C4ISR, dual-capable missiles and compressed decision making – makes it harder to distinguish conventional from nuclear intent. These risks are inherent to contemporary military doctrine on both sides.

The proliferation of dual-capable systems creates identification problems

The growing number of dual-capable systems – ballistic, cruise and hypersonic missiles, aircraft, submarines and supporting C4ISR infrastructure – entangles conventional and nuclear capabilities. Conventional attacks on such systems could be misread as targeting nuclear assets, creating use-it-or-lose-it pressures, while the use of dual-capable systems for conventional purposes may itself suggest nuclear intent. Peacetime developments such as integrated air and missile defence and counterforce doctrine heighten this risk of misinterpretation.

Certain locations carry disproportionate risk, but escalation accumulates unpredictably

Kaliningrad and the Kola Peninsula are likely to create specific escalation risks, as both sides would struggle to avoid engaging with the military systems, including nuclear-related infrastructure, located there during a conflict. However, the report cautions against focusing too narrowly on specific flashpoints. Escalation risks are inherently entropic, compounding as damage to C4ISR and dual-use assets accumulates over time. The risks present in the opening hours of a confrontation differ markedly from those after days or weeks of sustained fighting, with uncertainty growing throughout.

Recommendations

Integrate escalation-sensitivity into planning

Military planners should embed escalation-sensitivity analysis into campaign design, command exercises and force posture planning, ensuring awareness of how operational choices, such as strikes on C2 nodes, may inadvertently signal existential threats to Russia.

Maintain communication and risk-reduction channels

Military-to-military communication channels, crisis hotlines and confidence-building mechanisms should be preserved even during political confrontation, supported by diplomatic efforts to reaffirm mutual understanding of thresholds and red lines.

Continuously monitor evolving risks

Given escalation risk is dynamic, NATO must continuously monitor and reassess how force modernisation, emerging technologies and AI-enabled systems reshape decision-making timelines and miscalculation potential.

items.title: Iran Damages US A-10, F-15s with Missile Attack on Air Base in Jordan
items.author: Chris Gordon
items.summary: An Iranian ballistic missile attack on a key U.S. air base in Jordan damaged multiple U.S. warplanes, people familiar with the matter confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine. The post Iran Damages US A-10, F-15s with Missile Attack on Air Base in Jordan appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

An Iranian ballistic missile attack on a key U.S. air base in Jordan damaged multiple U.S. warplanes, people familiar with the matter confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine.

One A-10 Thunderbolt II attack aircraft suffered a severely damaged wing and about eight F-15E Strike Eagle fighters were lightly damaged but are considered serviceable after Iran attacked Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan on Sept. 8 Eastern Time.

The damage to U.S. aircraft was first reported by CBS News .

A spokesman for U.S. Central Command did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The attack on the base , known as MSAB, came after the U.S. struck five Iranian tankers Sept. 8, and Iran retaliated by lobbing scores of ballistic missiles at the installation. U.S. and Jordanian forces launched dozens of interceptors at the Iranian missiles. U.S. officials said no American personnel were killed. But Iran was able to harm American materiel. In the hours after the attack, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed it damaged U.S. aircraft at the base.

The U.S. has dozens of warplanes operating from the base, which acts as a key airpower hub for operations against Iran. Tehran has targeted the facility, near the Jordanian town of Azraq, numerous times since the conflict began in February. Three Army Soldiers were killed in a missile attack on the base in July.

items.title: Space Command Maneuvers Satellites Across Multiple Orbits in New Exercise
items.author: Greg Hadley
items.summary: U.S. Space Command maneuvered satellites across low-, medium-, and geosynchronous orbits in an exercise early this month, advancing the command’s push to master dynamic operations in space. The post Space Command Maneuvers Satellites Across Multiple Orbits in New Exercise appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

U.S. Space Command maneuvered satellites across low-, medium-, and geosynchronous orbits in an exercise early this month, advancing the command’s push to master dynamic operations in space.

SPACECOM announced the completion of Apollo Maneuvers 2026 in a Sept. 8 release, a month after commander Gen. Stephen Whiting announced the live-fly exercise to refine tactics and ultimately inform future maneuver warfare doctrine.

The exercise included maneuvers across a vast range of orbits—low-Earth orbit starts at 100 miles above the Earth’s surface, and geosynchronous orbit extends more than 22,000 miles out.

SPACECOM did not specify what assets were used or how far they moved, but Whiting said in August that the command “will take some of our existing satellites and work with partners to demonstrate what are some of the requirements and capabilities to be able to maneuver for advantage, not just maneuver when you have to change your orbital position.”

SPACECOM has been pushing hard to explore maneuver warfare in orbit under Whiting’s leadership. Most operators maneuver their satellites only to maintain orbit, preferring to conserve fuel and extend the spacecraft’s service life. But cheaper launch costs , new refueling spacecraft, and advanced propulsion technologies are causing leaders to rethink that approach.

For military operations, Pentagon space leaders have noted that satellites that cannot maneuver become easy targets. But beyond that, Whiting has argued that SPACECOM needs capabilities not just to run away, but to hold adversaries’ systems at risk.

“To perform, survive, and gain advantage in the space domain, we need maneuverability and survivability in our capabilities,” Whiting said in the release.

The Apollo Maneuvers name is a nod to the Army’s 1941 Louisiana Maneuvers, a series of major battle management exercises designed to test ground tactics during World War II. The exercise also integrated allies who are members of the multinational Operation Olympic Defender and industry players through the Commercial Integration Cell.

“The integration of allied, partner, and commercial capabilities strengthens joint and combined operations and enabled the validation of combined tactics, techniques and procedures,” SPACECOM’s release states.

items.title: General Atomics Offers First Glimpse of Wildfire Drone, Eyed as MQ-9 Successor
items.author: Steve Losey
items.summary: General Atomics has unveiled the first renderings of its Wildfire drone, which it plans to pitch for the Air Force’s hunt for a new, low-cost Massed Modular Aircraft. The post General Atomics Offers First Glimpse of Wildfire Drone, Eyed as MQ-9 Successor appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

General Atomics has unveiled the first renderings of its Wildfire drone, which it plans to pitch for the Air Force’s hunt for a new, low-cost Massed Modular Aircraft .

Wildfire was unveiled in a sizzle reel-type video General Atomics Aeronautical Systems Inc. posted on social media Sept. 9. The video touts more than three decades of the company’s unmanned aerial vehicle development, starting with the Gnat and Predator drones flown in the 1990s up to and including its latest FQ-42A Dark Merlin, before revealing the first three images of Wildfire in short succession.

The images provide hints of the drone’s expected capabilities. One image shows Wildfire carrying four Joint Strike Missiles, which are stealthy cruise missiles, and another shows it with two Long Range Anti-Ship Missiles, or LRASMs.

“The whole point of a flying weapons truck is to come heavy,” General Atomics spokesman C. Mark Brinkley said in response to Air & Space Forces Magazine questions. “Wildfire will be able to carry a minimum of two LRASMs, four JSMs, or some similar configuration of heavy stand-off weapons, across meaningful combat distances.”

Brinkley said the MQ-9A is not be able to carry those payloads, and that they’re twice as much as the Pentagon originally envisioned for MMA. Brinkley said it’s too soon to sat how many Hellfire missiles—which the MQ-9A frequently employs—the Wildfire drone will be able to carry.

A third image shows a swarm of nearly a dozen Wildfire drones bearing down on a group of enemy ships and firing a barrage of missiles at them.

The Air Force envisions Massed Modular Aircraft, or MMA , as a low-cost drone to take on missions now done by General Atomics’ MQ-9A, and wants MMA to be semi-autonomous and able to be sent in groups to overwhelm enemy defenses.

Top Air Force officials told reporters Sept. 3 that they want the MMA’s air vehicle—not counting sensors or other capabilities—to cost no more than $10 million apiece. This would allow MMA to be “attritable,” meaning they would be inexpensive enough to be fielded in large numbers and easily replaced if lost in combat.

The Air Force and the Defense Innovation Unit, when unveiling the MMA concept in July, said losing $30 million drones in battle against an enemy would be unsustainable in a large-scale conflict, and a less expensive option is needed.

The conflict with Iran has cost the Air Force about 45 of its MQ-9 drones. In the Sept. 3 briefing, Air Force officials said the MQ-9 losses were concerning enough to push the service to accelerate its MMA effort. The Air Force and DIU want to have a prototype MMA a year after is contract is awarded and to start fielding it at scale within three years, or as early as 2029.

General Atomics created Wildfire as a clean-sheet design, and said it will be able to achieve all the Air Force’s MMA requirements at a high quality and an affordable price.

Brinkley said Wildfire will be able to exceed the Air Force and DIU’s 8,000 nautical mile ferry range requirement for MMA.

It will be modular, which will allow the Air Force to rapidly add or swap out different capabilities. When asked about Wildfire’s sensing capabilities, Brinkley said it will have “certain features available right out of the box,” but it will be up to the Air Force to decide what modular capabilities it wants to add.

“Modularity is key,” Brinkley said. “We’re showing that now with our Gambit series of uncrewed jets, which includes the XQ-67A Off-Board Sensing Station and FQ-42A Collaborative Combat Aircraft. One design, seamlessly pivoting to various missions. Wildfire will be able to do much the same from an [intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance]/strike lane.”

Brinkley said General Atomics will use its experience on autonomy, artificial intelligence, and machine learning from its work on programs like CCA and the MQ-20 Avenger, “to network dozens of Wildfires together on Day One.”

Brinkley said General Atomics has more than 5 million square feet of manufacturing space it could leverage to build Wildfire, and that the company has produced up to 100 aircraft per year, including MQ-9s.

“We have said from the beginning that we can deliver Wildfires years earlier than the [Air Force and DIU’s original] fiscal 2031 timeline,” Brinkley said. “We can deliver more than twice as many aircraft as originally asked for in the same amount of time. We’re not worried about scaling at all.”

items.title: Elbit Systems’ American subsidiary rebrands as Twenty-Six Defense
items.author: Leigh Giangreco
items.summary: The U.S. arm of Israel's Elbit Systems has rebranded to Twenty-Six Defense, a new name that emphasizes the subsidiary’s American-made brand.
items.body:
MilTech

Elbit Systems’ American subsidiary rebrands as Twenty-Six Defense

A U.S. soldier showcases Elbit America's Enhanced Night Vision Goggle-Binocular (ENVG-B) system. (Elbit America)

The U.S. arm of Israeli-based Elbit Systems has rebranded to Twenty-Six Defense, a new name that emphasizes the subsidiary’s American-made brand.

“Launching Twenty-Six Defense underscores our growth in the American market and reinforces our commitment to supporting U.S. warfighters, wherever the mission takes place,” Luke Savoie, president and CEO of Twenty-Six Defense, said in a company statement on Tuesday.

The number 26 refers to the atomic number for iron and is meant to symbolize “resilience and durability,” Savoie said.

The branding change also comes as American support has become divided in the wake of Hamas’ attack on Israel in October 2023 and the ensuing war in Gaza, which the United Nations classified as a genocide in 2025 .

Headquartered in Fort Worth, Texas, Twenty-Six Defense employs 3,300 people across the United States, according to the company. After General Dynamics sold its tactical aircraft division to Lockheed Martin in 1993, Elbit Systems of America purchased the former General Dynamics manufacturing facility in Fort Worth.

From its Texas headquarters, the company began working on F-16 avionics for the U.S. Air Force. Over the last three decades, the U.S. subsidiary acquired six defense companies, expanding its footprint to include aircraft helmet-mounted display technologies, night vision systems, precision-guided seekers and laser targeting systems.

In 2019, Elbit’s U.S. arm bought Harris Corp’s night vision business as part of an antitrust remedy when Harris and L3 Technologies merged.

Beyond its defense capabilities, Twenty-Six Defense has grown its domestic business in the U.S. as well. In July, the company announced that it scored multiple contracts valued at more than $370 million from the U.S. Customs and Border Protection agency. That work is scheduled through May 2029. The U.S. subsidiary has long provided surveillance systems for CBP along the U.S.-Mexico border .

items.title: Combat Weather Airmen Stressed to Their Limits in Army Competition
items.author: Matthew Cox
items.summary: In the small world of Air Force weather specialists, combat weather specialists are a niche unto themselves, deploying with Army ground units to provide forecasts and, if need be, fight alongside those Soldiers. For Staff Sgt.
