The post Combat Weather Airmen Stressed to Their Limits in Ar
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

In the small world of Air Force weather specialists , combat weather specialists are a niche unto themselves, deploying with Army ground units to provide forecasts and, if need be, fight alongside those Soldiers. For Staff Sgt. Francisco Estrada, the hardest part of the job isn’t the possibility of ground combat, though—it’s briefing Army helicopter pilots on short notice how wind, fog, rain, and other conditions will affect a mission.

Being right about hazardous conditions often means an upcoming flight is scrubbed. Being wrong about them, though, could cause helicopter engines to fail or send an aircrew flying into the side of a mountain.

“Anybody can sit behind a desk and put everything together when they have all the time in the world, but when you are on the fly like you are oftentimes out in the field … it’s really hard to gather everything that you need do it well and do it confidently, when somebody’s asking you, ‘Hey, well, can we can we launch? Can we go?’” Estrada told Air & Space Forces Magazine.

Airmen in this unique career field were tested Aug. 12-13 when combat weather squadrons from across the Air Force participated in Thunder Challenge 2026, a physically and mentally challenging competition that this year put six three-Airmen teams from around the world through two days of high-pressure skill tests at Fort Drum, N.Y.

Competitors marched 10 miles, carrying weapons and 35-pound rucksacks. The competition also included a night land navigation course and a simulated mountain rescue on foot through the thick forested terrain.

Skill stations tested everything from small-arms knowledge to combat casualty care—combat-related tasks these Airmen could need at any time since they are attached to Army combat units. In between these tactical tasks, the combat weather Airmen, known as staff weather officers, or SWOs, also had to prove their technical job expertise by completing tasks ranging from setting up portable weather sensors to a timed weather knowledge test.

Thunder Challenge “is the only competition that measures the lethal combination” of tactical skills as well the “environmental science” knowledge needed operate within Army combat units and advise aviators and combat leaders on how changing weather conditions could impact future missions, Chief Master Sergeant Ronald Buchanan of the Air Force’s 5th Combat Weather Group, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.

“It’s unique because you they go straight from grueling, physical challenges such weighted ruck marches or live-fire stress shooting directly to setting up tactical meteorological equipment, and then from that, using that same equipment or their weather knowledge to deliver an Indo-Pacific-focused forecast brief, not only just under the physical but also under that mental fatigue as well,” Buchanan said.

“These competitions help further prove that we can operate and deliver critical environmental intelligence at the absolute forward edge of any battlefield.”

Estrada, whose team from the 7th Combat Weather Squadron in Germany beat out five other teams to win first place this year, was also part of last year’s winning team at Thunder Challenge. He has been a combat weather specialist for the last three of his seven years in the Air Force. While assigned to the Army’s 12th Combat Aviation Brigade at Katterbach Army Airfield, Estrada has seen a lot of Airmen “get scared” when it comes to preparing an air mission brief on a short deadline with limited data.

During Thunder Challenge, teams had to prepare a brief in about 45 minutes with “very little data, and more importantly, with data from a location that we didn’t know,” Estrada said.

“It’s such a compact timeframe to do that confidently … you have to consider so much. Whether it’s where they’re flying to, their route of flight, are they going over an ocean because at that point, we have to consider what the sea temperatures are like,” Estrada said, adding that headwinds, crosswinds and other conditions that can “make or break their decision to fly, especially when it comes to fuel consumption.”

Normally, SWOs will have at least several hours’ notice, if not a day or two, to prepare a brief and “we’ve had time to kind of do everything and kind of get used to the localized weather pattern,” Estrada said.

Satellite imagery helps with dissecting approaching weather fronts that can bring stormy, wet weather. Topography plays a large role in preparing a brief, Estrada said, especially in the mountains, where low ceilings can be dangerous.

Helicopter pilots have low cloud ceiling minimums they can fly in, “but in those mountains, because they hold so much moisture to trap it all in, it’ll be socked in so you’ll have ceilings go from like 3,000 feet to all of a sudden, your ceilings are on the surface,” Estrada said. “You can’t get through it.”

Army aviators spend a lot of time studying available weather forecasting applications but depend on combat weather Airmen for an unbiased analysis of flying conditions, said UH-60 Black Hawk pilot Capt. Tom Pelkey, who was one of the judges on the air brief portion of the competition.

“You will not launch until the Air Force weather officer gives you a brief,” he said, explaining that Army regulations require it to “ensure that the pilots themselves don’t shop for favorable weather” to suit their mission.

Many factors are needed for a good air brief such as “what’s the moonset going to be if we’re launching at night—like how much illumination? What’s the sea state going to be since we’re flying over water?” said Pelkey, who is assigned to 3rd Battalion, 10th Combat Aviation Brigade at Drum.

Air density is also a critical piece of data helicopter pilots need when planning a mission, Pelkey said. Helicopters need dense air to generate lift through the main rotor blades. Air density decreases with altitude and has an adverse impact on aircraft performance.

“The engine’s going to work based on the density altitude or how much moisture is in the air affected by the temperature, so if it’s going to be hot and moist, my engine doesn’t have much air to beat into combustion,” Pelkey said. “And that’s something helicopter pilots, and even pilots in general, have to be aware of … because that limits us on what the aircraft can carry, how many people we can carry, and what maneuvers we can do.”

When critiquing each team’s air brief, Pelkey said pilots stress that they need combat weather Airmen to provide analysis along with weather data.

“The big thing that we want … the SWOs to understand is, ‘you bring me the weather. All right, so what? What does that mean for my mission exactly?’” Pelkey said. “If we had two routes that we’re going to fly, you need to recommend the route that I’m going to fly based on the weather.”

Sending combat weather Airmen to Thunder Challenge gives leaders an opportunity to gauge the effectiveness of the training that SWOs receive throughout the year, said Col. Staci Coleman, commander of the 5th Combat Weather Group, which commands the 18th Combat Weather Squadron headquartered at of Fort Bragg, N.C., and the 3rd Combat Weather Squadron out of Fort Hood, Texas.

The competition “enables leaders to put the Airmen to the test, so we can see where they’re at with the development of their skills,” Coleman said. “Can they apply their weather expertise and operate as warfighters and make good decisions under pressure? So, we use that as an opportunity to put them under stress just to see how they can respond and to show them where the gaps are in their own training and things that they need to improve on.”

Coleman added that “it shows us where we’re strong and where we need to improve and ensures that we’re building combat-ready Airmen who are ready for the fight.”

To 1st Lt. Isabel Weiss, participating in the competition was a great experience for her “very junior team,” since it was “totally different from what most people think of when they think of the Air Force and when they think of weather support.”

“I think a lot of people think of computer people just looking at models, but it was a really intense competition, and we got to go into the Army combat skills that we’ve learned, and also we got to show our other proficiency,” said Weiss, who is part of an 18th CWS detachment that’s attached to the Army’s 3rd Combat Aviation Brigade at Fort Stewart, Ga. “We were into it; I thought it was amazing.”

Her team came in fourth place, which she is “very proud of” since “we were brand new to this type of competition environment,” said Weiss, who was named Fittest SWO from her combined score on the fitness test, 10-mile ruck march, and mountaineering portion of the competition.

Her team trained at Fort Stewart for the night land navigation, but the course at Drum was “very hard, and it was pitch black,” Weiss said. “We only had red light headlamps, and two of our headlamps died.”

“We were in the trenches for sure, but that was great,” she said. “I really do like this tactical stuff. … We had our face paints on, we had our bulletproof vests and helmets, sleeping outside, shooting weapons; it was just a really cool thing that you don’t get to do very often with the Air Force.”

The competition was also great on-the-job training for her junior Airmen teammates, Weiss said.

“I think the first time that they go to an exercise, or when they get ready for deployment, they’re going to be so familiar with the equipment, when it’s used, how it’s used, and then just working in a high-pressure situation—I think it’s a really unique thing that I’ve never heard of an Airman experiencing so early in their career.”

For Estrada, the hardest field skill was the mountain rescue portion of the competition that required teams to locate a dummy casualty and move “him” through steep, wooded terrain on a “Skedco,” which is a special stretcher equipped with straps for securing a casualty that can be lowered down steep inclines by ropes.

“We had to assess him for any injuries or any wounds, and … then we had to move him in Skedco from point A to point B,” Estrada said. “I think it might have been a good 100 meters, long enough to just be exhausting.” Teams then had to lower the casualty down one cliff and up to the top of another steep rise, he said.

Estrada said he will likely compete in next year’s competition as well. “It gives you an opportunity to kind of gauge where you’re at versus like your peers,” he said. “And I think there’s something rewarding about that—seeing all your effort, all the dedication that you put into your skillset to kind of become a better forecaster, a better combat weather team. There’s something so gratifying about that, that it’s hard to kind of walk away from.”

items.title: Hypersonic Aircraft Startup Adding Anduril’s Autonomy Software for 2027 Flight
items.author: Todd South
items.summary: Startups Anduril Industries and Heremus have agreed to integrate Anduril’s autonomy software onto Hermeus’ hypersonic demonstrator aircraft “Quarterhorse”—uniting two technologies that have drawn keen interest and investment from the Air Force. The post Hypersonic Aircraft Startup Adding Anduril’s Autonomy Software for 2027 Flight appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

Startups Anduril Industries and Heremus have agreed to integrate Anduril’s autonomy software onto Hermeus’ hypersonic demonstrator aircraft “Quarterhorse”—uniting two technologies that have drawn keen interest and investment from the Air Force.

The firms announced the deal Sept. 3 and said they plan to fly the Quarterhorse Mk 2 aircraft using the Lattice autonomy system in 2027.

Hermeus is attempting to build a reusable aircraft that can reach hypersonic speeds, defined as Mach 5 and above, and has received funding and support from the Air Force. Quarterhorse has yet to go that fast—company officials say they’re targeting supersonic speeds, or Mach 1-plus, as the next step in their test campaign—but adding autonomy software could enable faster control of the aircraft as it flies around a mile per second.

At the same time, preparing the software for the platform will take time.

“We will spend the rest of this year on a build-up from software in the loop to integration testing to hardware in the loop and validation testing, then we’ll go toward flight,” Brett Darcey, vice president for mission autonomy at Anduril, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.

Anduril is already refining its autonomy software, dubbed Lattice, for the Air Force’s Collaborative Combat Aircraft program. The firm is competing with Shield AI and Collins Aerospace on that front. Anduril is also building its FQ-44A Fury drone as one of the CCA airframes, along with General Atomics’ FQ-42A Dark Merlin.

But while Anduril has experience with the CCA program, CCAs aren’t meant to be supersonic nor hypersonic like Quarterhorse. The speeds at which that aircraft will operate will require beyond human-like decision-making speeds. The Autonomy Government Reference Architecture that serves as the baseline for most contractor’s autonomy software requires that Quarterhorse be able to fly itself “through all regimes of flight, which would include the jump to supersonic,” Darcey said.

That means human operators will tell the software to fly at a certain velocity, and the software will be responsible for taking the steps to execute the command.

“That probably means we’re going to do a lot of software and hardware in the loop testing, and a lot of independent validation of what we are doing on the route generation side, and appropriately, I think the monitoring of execution of those routes when we’re at those high speeds on the build-up phase all the way to flight,” Darcey said.

That step-by-step approach is necessary as companies work to build trust in the software’s ability to control the aircraft’s flight and other taskings for its human operators.

Tactics, techniques, and procedures are still developing and evolving to build that trust between human and machine, but Darcey was quick to note that in the development stage there can be too little trust; at times, there can also be too much.

He likens it to using an actual horse in warfare. Horses are independent, thinking creatures that can also be trained to do certain things. Cavalrymen would build their trust in the “human-horse system” over time, instead of just jumping on a horse and going to war.

A key difference between autonomy software and an actual horse, though, is that the software has built-in debrief functions that will tell the user what it did and why. And as developers of the software, sharing that data with their company partners and the Air Force provides transparency for the process, Darcey said.

CCA and Mission Autonomy

In February , Anduril’s developmental YFQ-44A flew with two different mission autonomy software suites on the same aircraft during the same flight, using both Lattice and Shield AI’s Hivemind suite.

“We do have an advantage with Fury,” Darcey said. “That kind of deep platform knowledge definitely is useful.”

But Darcey was quick to point out that the company isn’t tying all its software thinking to its own platform, or even to a single platform. The software used in the CCA program must also be viable for a wide range of aircraft types, based on USAF requirements.

“One of the big challenges with mission autonomy is it has to be generally built so it can do the mission requirements of multiple platforms at once,” Darcey said.

Quarterhorse

Hermeus conducted its first flight with the Mk1 model in May 2025 and then flew its Mk 2.1 demonstration vehicle in another flight in March.

That flight ran from Spaceport America past White Sands Missile Range, N.M., with operators piloting the aircraft from a ground-based flight deck, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported.

The Mk 2 aircraft is roughly the size of an F-16 fighter.

The company won a $1.5 million contract in 2020 for a future hypersonic Presidential and Executive Airlift fleet via AFWERX, an Air Force innovation arm within the Air Force Research Laboratory.

In 2021, Hermeus won a $60 million Strategic Funding Increase contract via AFWERX and the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center

The Defense Innovation Unit awarded Hermeus a $23 million contract in 2023 for technologies related to the unit’s larger goal of creating a Hypersonic High-Cadence Airborne Testing Capabilities program.

items.title: UK Armed Forces pay tribute to late King of Norway at his funeral in Oslo
items.summary: Royal Marines and British Army personnel attended the funeral of King Harald V of Norway on Wednesday.
items.body:
Royal Marines and British Army personnel attended the funeral of King Harald V of Norway on Wednesday.

20 Royal Marines provided a marching detachment lining the route of the funeral procession in Oslo. Personnel from 1st Battalion, The Yorkshire Regiment, also attended as part of the UK’s tribute.

The late King, who died on 28 August, maintained a dedicated 45-year relationship with the British Armed Forces as an Honorary Colonel in the UK Royal Marines and an Honorary General in the British Army. He met with UK Commando Forces leadership every year and maintained a sharp, active interest in the Corps.

King Harald V’s father, King Olav V, was appointed an Honorary Admiral in the Royal Navy in 1958. In 1961, he and his son, the then Crown Prince Harald, were hosted onboard the Royal Navy aircraft carrier HMS Hermes during her regional engagement visit to Oslo.

The then Crown Prince Harald was appointed Honorary Colonel of the Royal Marines in March 1981 by Her Late Majesty Queen Elizabeth II, the first such appointment involving a member of a foreign Royal household in the Corps’ history. He paid his first visit to the Royal Marines that October, touring CTCRM Lympstone and RM Bickleigh, where he watched a cliff assault by 40 Commando and a demonstration of jungle warfare training by 42 Commando.

His connection with the Royal Marines continued throughout his reign. In 2018, he visited Royal Marines from X Company, 45 Commando, at Vaernes Camp in Norway during Exercise Trident Juncture, NATO’s largest collective defence exercise in a decade, where he was briefed on the Corps’ role in the exercise and joined celebrations marking the Royal Marines’ 354th birthday.

items.title: Saab tapped to continue work on Sweden’s next flagship fighter jet
items.author: Linus Höller
items.summary: The Swedish government has tapped Saab to continue work on a next-generation fighter jet concept, keeping a wholly domestic iron in the fire.
items.body:
Europe

Saab tapped to continue work on Sweden’s next flagship fighter jet

A Saab JAS-39E Gripen performs at the Flight Days 2026 event in Malmen, Linkoping, Sweden, on Aug. 22, 2026. (Pradeep Dambarage/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

VIENNA — Saab has received a new contract worth approximately SEK 2.9 billion (roughly $303 million) from Sweden’s Defense Materiel Administration, FMV, to continue conceptual work on the country’s future fighter system, the company announced in a statement Wednesday.

The deal’s work period runs from 2026 to 2028, with options extending into 2029 and 2030, and builds on agreements signed in 2024 and 2025.

According to Saab, the work covers flying and ground-based demonstrators, advanced studies and the development of future system concepts for both manned and unmanned platforms. The company says the program is meant to strengthen Sweden’s capabilities in systems integration, autonomy, signature adaptation, propulsion and digital development, while reducing technical risk and preserving “freedom of action” for future decisions on the country’s air combat capability.

Lars Tossman, head of Saab’s Aeronautics business area, said in the statement that FMV’s continued confidence in Saab is “crucial to further develop and demonstrate new technologies that will be central to future fighter system.”

The order is the third in a series of awards tied to Sweden’s Koncept för Framtida Stridsflyg (KFS) program, also referred to as Vägval stridsflyg, which is intended to shape the country’s air power beyond 2040. The initial contract was signed in March 2024, followed by a SEK 2.6 billion extension in October 2025 covering 2025 to 2027. That earlier phase included plans for a flying demonstrator, with concept and technology development originally set to wrap up by the third quarter of 2026 and initial flight tests to follow in 2027.

Saab has previously outlined a family of concepts under its F-series branding, including a crewed fighter alongside subsonic and supersonic uncrewed platforms of varying weight classes and form factors.

The KFS was launched after Sweden withdrew from the British-led Team Tempest project, which would later become GCAP, in 2023, opting instead for its own domestic development.

Saab plays a crucial role in Sweden as the country’s only manufacturer of fighter jets, and its aircraft have made up the backbone of the Swedish air force for decades. Currently, the Saab Gripen plays this role.

Linus Höller is Defense News' Europe correspondent and OSINT investigator. He reports on the arms deals, sanctions, and geopolitics shaping Europe and the world. He holds master’s degrees in WMD nonproliferation, terrorism studies, and international relations, and works in four languages: English, German, Russian, and Spanish.

items.title: Iran and US hit tankers in biggest wave of attacks on shipping since war began
items.author: Enas Alashray, Idrees Ali and Jana Choukeir, Reuters
items.summary: Recent attacks by the U.S. and Iran have shattered a month of relative calm, with both hitting military, shipping and energy assets.
items.body:
Mideast Africa

Iran and US hit tankers in biggest wave of attacks on shipping since war began

Iranian crude oil carriers after being struck. U.S. Central Command says it targeted the carriers after attempted Iranian missile attacks on a U.S. Navy warship over the past two days. (U.S. Central Command via Reuters)

Iran said on Wednesday it had attacked 10 ships near the Strait of Hormuz after the U.S. sank five Iranian oil tankers, in the biggest declared wave of tit-for-tat attacks on shipping by both sides since the start of the six-month-old war.

At least one seafarer aboard a tanker was reported killed and another listed as missing. The attacks sent the price of oil surging, with the international Brent crude benchmark breaching $100 a barrel for the first time since July.

Iran also said it had fired ballistic missiles at a base used by U.S. forces in Jordan. Attacks by both sides since the end of August have shattered a month of relative calm, with the U.S. and Iran hitting military, shipping and energy assets.

The Revolutionary Guards said they would sharply escalate their response to any further attacks, and if the enemy struck two or three Iranian targets, Iran would respond by hitting 20. Iran would soon release maps of a new, much larger off-limits zone at sea that would extend as far as the Arabian Gulf off Chabahar on the far reaches of Iran’s coast near Pakistan, the Guards said.

Recent days have also seen an escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen, a second theatre of war that threatens global energy supplies from the Middle East.

Video shows Iranian tankers ablaze

The Americans said they destroyed five Iranian oil tankers overnight, releasing video of ships ablaze before they sank. The U.S. military’s Central Command called its attacks a response to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targeting a U.S. Navy warship twice with ballistic missiles over the previous two days. No Americans were harmed, the U.S. said.

Washington has announced a new policy of attacking Iranian tankers in retaliation for fire that threatens its warships. Iran says it is using new, more capable missiles to attack U.S. ships.

“Iran continues to try to hit U.S. naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters during a visit to Colombia.

After Iran announced its strikes in response, saying it fired on two U.S. ships and eight tankers, reports indicated vessels had been hit in waters near several neighbouring countries.

One seafarer was killed aboard the oil products tanker Hercules Star while at anchorage off Dubai and another crew member was missing, the vessel’s charterer, Peninsula, said. Maritime security sources said it may have been hit by a drone.

The British maritime security agency UKMTO described a vessel in the vicinity that was listing, possibly taking on water after being struck by a projectile. Reuters could not immediately determine whether this referred to the same ship. Two Iraqi port officials said a tanker carrying 2 million barrels of fuel oil, the New Andros, had caught fire after being struck by a drone in Iraqi waters. There were no reports of casualties among the 22 crew.

The UKMTO said it had received reports of several merchant ships struck by disabling fire in the northern Gulf and Gulf of Oman, on either side of the strait. It was not immediately able to confirm casualties or environmental impact.

Iran also threatened oil tankers in Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports, according to a statement carried by state media. A maritime security source reported a liquefied natural gas tanker was damaged in the Emirati port of Khor Fakkan.

The IRGC also said on Wednesday it had fired ballistic missiles at a base used by U.S. forces near Al Azraq, in eastern Jordan. Jordan said its air defences had intercepted 18 of the 20 Iranian missiles, with two falling in unpopulated areas and no casualties. A U.S. official said Iran’s strikes in Jordan were ineffective and all American troops were accounted for.

Video filmed in Ash-Shajarah, in northern Jordan, and verified by Reuters showed flashes lighting up the night sky.

Strait choked off

Iran has largely choked off transit through the strait that carried a fifth of global oil before the war.

Washington has responded with a blockade of Iranian ports, and says it has been able to guide many tankers through the strait, although independent monitors say the extent to which oil is escaping has become increasingly difficult to assess. Preliminary data showed just six ships crossing with transponders on over the last 24 hours.

Escalating combat between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-aligned Houthi movement that controls most populated parts of Yemen has created additional uncertainty for energy markets. A Saudi-backed government based in the south of Yemen has launched a multi-pronged assault on areas controlled by the Houthis, who have threatened Saudi shipping in the Red Sea.

On Tuesday, the Houthis launched an attack on four cities in Saudi Arabia, causing huge fires at oil installations that were visible from space. Saudi authorities said 73 people were wounded. The Saudi Press Agency released footage showing homes severely damaged and injured patients in hospital.

A source in Pakistan, which signed a mutual defence pact with Riyadh last month, said Saudi Arabia had carried out retaliatory strikes on Yemen. The Houthis say dozens of people have been killed in Saudi airstrikes, which Saudi Arabia has not confirmed.

HTML

Operational Low Flying Training Timetable 21 September to 25 September 2026

Details

Timetables for operational low flying ( OLF ) training by RAF fast jets and Hercules aircraft. These timetables cover 3 tactical training areas ( TTA ) only. These are:

LFA 7(T): central Wales

LFA 14(T): northern Scotland

LFA 20(T): the borders of southern Scotland and northern England

When the TTA is not in use, there may be other flying activity in the area. The MOD is unable to provide a timetable for all low flying activity as the information can very quickly become outdated due to weather conditions and training requirements.

items.title: Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard MP's speech at Mansion House Defence and Security event
items.summary: Minister Pollard highlighting the importance of collaboration between government, industry and private finance, to strengthen UK deterrence and drive economic growth.
items.body:
Lady Mayor, thank you very much for hosting this event today and good afternoon, everyone. It’s a real pleasure to be with you today.

Under this one roof we have many leaders and decision makers needed to spark that next generation of defence innovation that we need to keep our country safe and support our allies. So, thank you for giving up your valuable time to be here.

I’m honoured that I get to speak as warm up act to my friend, the Ukrainian Ambassador. I’ve spent a lot of time in Kyiv over the past two years in particular, and the courage of the Ukrainian people is something that we must honour not just in words but in the actual support that we provide for their frontline, for their nation, for the innovators and we do that by not just sending equipment to Ukraine but by partnering, innovating and developing new technologies together.

I know that there are people in this room whose work is not theoretical in that regard and you are making a big difference to our friends in Ukraine so thank you for what you do.

Now, we meet at a point where global geopolitics is more fragile, more disruptive and more changeable. And that means we need an entirely new system of warfighting and deterrence, which means more innovation and new approaches with new weapon systems that revolutionised the battlefield.

Certainly, the way that the United Kingdom would now fight is fundamentally different today than it was at the point when Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine only those four and a half years ago. We’re learning the lessons from Ukraine by supporting them, but that means changing the way that the United Kingdom operates.

Now, our most urgent mission right now is to transform Britain’s defence posture and turbocharge innovation. Many of the most critical advances in defence right now are coming from tech startups and tech scale-ups. Agile businesses which are seizing the opportunities on offer and driving change at speed. And so today our challenge is this: how can we get better at finding, funding and firing up the most creative minds and enterprise to get the best technology into the hands of our armed forces and those of our allies as fast as possible.

Now it was just over two years ago that this government took office and we inherited a defence programme which to be honest and to be frank was unfit to counter the dangers that we now face. We are moving towards warfighting readiness and in doing so we must discard the warm comfort blanket that we are used to in Britain, of polishing old things and pretending that that will protect us. If our technology and kit will not work in Ukraine, I do not want it in our armed forces. That is an opportunity for new technology, new thinking, new weapons to be brought to the fore. And in designing new technology, we need to design for the conflicts of today and the battles of tomorrow.

Now, our supply chains are critical to that. An industry that works in our supply chains know how painfully slow, wasteful and costly the procurement the MOD previously undertook was. We are changing that. I think it was especially true for those small businesses and scale-ups with amazing products who struggled sometimes to find the right buyer within the MOD.

Now since that time, we’ve produced a new blueprint for a completely different type of military and a different type of procurement. We published our Strategic Defence Review, Defence Industrial Strategy and Defence Investment Plan to build a more resilient and warfighting-ready military, backed by a world-class supply chain and we’re bringing industry into the heart of defence the fundamental enabler of everything that we are trying to achieve. To not only make our country more secure, but also more successful and prosperous, by creating high-quality defence jobs, skills and opportunities in every postcode.

I used to be incentivised by the MOD press office to say defence is an engine for growth in all my interviews, they used to be encouraging me to do it. With Andy Burnham in Downing Street I now say re-industrialisation, but the fundamental truth is there. Investment in defence creates good jobs. It provides opportunities in particular for our young people and we should be unafraid and unapologetic of saying that truth loudly. Defence spending is an engine for growth. It is a way of re-industrialising. It is a way of creating opportunity. It also keeps us safe.

Now to make our country more secure and more successful we need to create more high quality defence jobs, skills and opportunities. Now if we are to do that SMEs in particular, scale-ups, are really important. Within the MOD, we’ve reformed our system with a new National Armaments Director, Rupert Pearce, coming from a FTSE 100 company, bringing a new corporate approach and energy to the way that we procure.

We’ve established the Defence Office of Small Business growth to help remove those obstacles to entry, cut red tape, and roll out a 50% increase in spend from the MOD with medium and small-sized firms by Summer 2028. That’s moving an extra two and a half billion pounds into the pockets of SMEs by changing the way we procure, making it easier for small businesses to enter our supply chain.

We’ve published our SME Action Plan to set out what we will do so we can be held accountable for that change, and that supports start-ups, scale-ups, and other companies to be able to grow. And helping small firms navigate the routes to funding is something crucial if you want to get the best out of them. At a national level our Defence Office for Small Business Growth provides the guidance for those routes, removes duplication when we find it and clarifies the entry points where necessary.

At local levels I’m really pleased that the rollout of regional defence and security clusters have been so successful with more regions developing them, creating new regional routes to tailor support for businesses and bring together localised networks of major suppliers, devolved and local governments and importantly provide a forum for investors to meet them and support them as well.

Now, Ukraine has shown us the way to innovate at lightning speed because of the necessity of the war that they are fighting. And as we learn from Ukraine’s lead, defence must harness the resources that Britain possesses not just across tech and engineering sectors, but across finance, consulting and academia as well - to help create, inspire and deliver the change that we need. And finance is obviously key to our topic today.

Now, the government is already increasing defence spending. As a defence minister, of course, I would like more defence spending. But it’s not just from the taxpayer that there’s opportunities for investing in defence. It’s how you crowd in private capital, how you use the institutions, the networks, the structures of the City of London and the UK’s place at the heart of global financial trade, to bring more private capital into defence, creating more good jobs and more deterrence. Now, public investment will remain central to that mission as we increase our defence capabilities. But in a more dangerous world, we need to build more capacity now, rather than just wait for the increase in defence money that we know is coming over the next 10 years.

So that’s why the Defence Investment Plan sets out the priority areas that we will invest in both now, and later to provide the certainty for investors to understand what type of technologies, what areas of defence will the government invest in, where we also seek investment from the private sector.

And we need to work hard to make sure that Defence and our colleagues in the investment community speak the same language. Because I think, at the moment, there’s a risk that we sometimes speak past each other. And speaking the same language with the same necessary data will increase our ability to deliver.

Now, Britain has long prospered when government, industry and finance have worked together and our task today is not to reinvent the finance sectors, but a way of bringing us together to create that new partnership for today’s era.

Now, the prize is significant, not just stronger national defence and security, but a more innovative defence sector and a growing market that helps re-industrialise, but also an opportunity to export to our friends as well. Because it’s not just the United Kingdom that’s investing in defence. Our allies in NATO and further afield are doing the same.

Now, in the Defence Investment Plan, we announced a Defence Investment Unit because investors need a clearer interface with defence and defence needs financial expertise to turn priorities into market-facing propositions, speaking the same language.

Following the autumn budget this year, we will publish the Defence Finance Investment Strategy to set a clear framework for how government and responsible private capital can work together in support of security, resilience and growth. And in December, we will also hold a defence investment summit to turn strategy into delivery and bring together government, industry and investors to accelerate the flow of capital into priority defence capabilities.

Now, before I finish, I want to set out that this is not a theoretical game. This is happening right now and we need to make it easier for it to happen more frequently. In May, 13 British startups were awarded contracts of up to £4 million as part of the Defence Unicorn Fund programme. Kraken Technologies, as one of them, which manufactures maritime uncrewed surface vehicles, has since gone on to raise $175 million in a Series B funding round off the back of a $1 billion valuation. Green Jets is another British firm which has secured significant funding from capital. It was just one of three firms selected by the Ministry of Defence to develop a low-cost drone interceptor. Both Kraken and Green Jets received funding from the National Security Strategic Investment Fund and NATO Innovation Fund, while the British Business Bank also financed Kraken. And JET Connectivity, a small business which builds novel 5G and 6G communications tools was the only British firm to be admitted to the procedures NATO Diana mission track programme earlier this year from over three and a half thousand participants.

That was fantastic recognition of British innovation at its best, but I know it’s just the tip of the iceberg. There are so many other British, brilliant British companies that we need to be able to support as well.

Now, it is in these uncertain times that not only do friends stand together, which is why the support that we offer in Ukraine is long lasting, is serious and will not change no matter what threats Putin throws at us. It is also in these uncertain times that we need to make it easier to bring private capital and public investment together to create the new defence technologies that we need to keep our nation safe.

But let me finish with a final thought. Today we will not only get a clearer view of the potential on offer in the growing defence industry in the UK, and advice on how you can access more of that market. We also get a chance to keep Britain secure in a more dangerous world. Defence needs to be a national endeavour. A whole of society endeavour, a whole of government endeavour. It is the responsibility of the Ministry of Defence to lead that, but it is not the responsibility of the Ministry of Defence alone. To keep our nation safe, we need every part of society, every part of government and industry to step up to support that resilience, that innovation, and that drive to keep us all safe. Because as we can see from our friends in Ukraine, where deterrence fails, not only is it more and more expensive in treasure and lives and lost opportunity. It’s something that, as everyone here, we must take steps to avoid. That is why deterrence matters. That’s why increasing our deterrence matters with new technologies. But if deterrence fails, we must be ready to fight, and we must be ready to win. And all of you in this group can play a part in doing so.

Thank you for what you’re doing here today, and thank you Lady Mayor for bringing us all together.

items.title: Ministry of Defence policies to tackle unacceptable behaviour
items.summary: Policies and measures to tackle unacceptable behaviour across Defence, including ways to respond and report it.
items.body:
Defence support: bullying, harassment or discrimination - Guidance for Defence personnel on how to raise concerns about bullying, harassment or discrimination and get support.

Defence support: sexual offences - Guidance for Defence personnel on how to report sexual offences and get support at home and overseas.

The Ministry of Defence (MOD) is taking decisive steps to tackle unacceptable behaviour and ensure a safe, respectful environment for all who serve the nation.

Unacceptable behaviour has no place in Defence and will not be tolerated. These behaviours do not reflect the high values and standards upheld by the vast majority Defence personnel, whether in the British Army , Royal Navy , Royal Air Force , or Civil Service .

Defence is taking action

Defence’s commitment is underpinned by the Raising our Standards Programme (RoS), which was established to prevent and tackle unacceptable behaviour and cultural issues that undermine the values and standards across Defence.

Since 2021, Defence has introduced a series of measures to provide clear and robust guidance to civilian and military personnel on preventing and addressing incidents.

Prevention

Defence is committed to preventing unacceptable behaviour at the earliest opportunity through training, education, and robust policies. These measures aim to set clear expectations, prevent incidents, and build confidence that unacceptable behaviour will be addressed effectively.

Addressing Violence Against Women and Girls (VAWG): A programme is underway to deliver targeted actions to tackle VAWG in Defence, with lessons being used to inform wider action.

Zero Tolerance policies to Unacceptable Sexual Behaviour: Three Zero Tolerance policies have been introduced to ensure these behaviours are rooted out: a Victim/Survivor Focused Approach Policy, a policy on Sexual Offences and Sexual Relationships Between Instructors and Trainees, and the Sexual Exploitation and Abuse Policy (JSP 769).

Training and Education: All Defence personnel are required to complete a variety of training packages on standards of behaviour and how to identify and address unacceptable conduct.

Domestic Abuse Action Plan: Outlines Defence’s commitment to addressing domestic abuse, supporting affected personnel, and ensuring that appropriate action is taken against perpetrators.

Reporting

Everyone working in Defence is encouraged to call out or report behaviour that falls short of Defence’s high standards and ​values.

To support personnel reporting, Defence has established independent mechanisms to ensure complaints and serious criminal offences are handled appropriately.

The Defence Serious Crime Command (DSCC): Investigates allegations of serious criminal wrongdoing across the Armed Forces, and is outside the single Service chain of Command.

Victim Witness Care Unit (VWCU): The VWCU, part of the DSCC, provides comprehensive care and support to victims and witnesses of serious crimes. It ensures that victims are aware of their options in line with the Code of Practice for Victims of Crime .

Tri-Service Complaints Team: Investigates the most non-criminal serious complaints, such as bullying, discrimination and harassment, outside the single Service chain of command.

Service Complaints App and Civilian My Complaints App: Faster, easier and simpler ways for Service Personnel to raise Service Complaints and for civilians to raise unacceptable behaviours complaints or more general grievances.

Confidential reporting channels are available 24/7 for military and civilian personnel: The Bullying, Harassment and Discrimination (BHD) helpline provides emotional support, guidance, or practical advice from trained BHD advisers 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year. It operates independently from Defence and outside the chain of command or line management structure, and can be used anonymously and is confidential. The Confidential Hotline is the primary point of contact for raising concerns and a source of authoritative and impartial advice and guidance on all aspects of the Raising a Concern (Whistleblowing) Policy and Procedure in JSP 492. The team will review and identify the most appropriate route to resolve concerns. Everyone who works in Defence can use it.

The Bullying, Harassment and Discrimination (BHD) helpline provides emotional support, guidance, or practical advice from trained BHD advisers 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year. It operates independently from Defence and outside the chain of command or line management structure, and can be used anonymously and is confidential.

The Confidential Hotline is the primary point of contact for raising concerns and a source of authoritative and impartial advice and guidance on all aspects of the Raising a Concern (Whistleblowing) Policy and Procedure in JSP 492. The team will review and identify the most appropriate route to resolve concerns. Everyone who works in Defence can use it.

In addition to the independent mechanisms above, a full list of ways to informally and formally respond and report instances can be found by searching ‘Reporting Unacceptable Behaviour’ in Defence internal communication channels.

Enforcement

The JSPs and Raising a Concern policy demonstrate that supporting victims/survivors is a Defence priority. They also provide personnel with greater confidence to raise complaints and believe action will be taken without fear of it impacting them or their career for doing so.

Every allegation is investigated, with appropriate, consistent, and robust consequences for people whose behaviour falls below the high standards of conduct the MOD demands. This can include administrative, disciplinary, criminal action, or termination of employment and/or discharge from the Armed Forces.

Defence have also introduced mechanisms that ensure we are transparent in our actions, learn from feedback and continually improve.

Armed Forces Sexual Harassment and Sexualised Behaviours Survey: Conducted to gather experiences and perceptions of sexual harassment and sexualised behaviours among service personnel and will provide vital data to inform preventative programmes.

The Defence Serious Crime Command (DSCC): Investigates allegations of serious criminal wrongdoing across the Armed Forces, and is outside the singe Service chain of Command.

Defence Voices Panel: Providing a platform for Defence personnel to share their experiences and views, helping shape our policies and practices.

External Challenge Panel: Bringing in external experts to provide independent scrutiny and advice on Defence’s approach to tackling unacceptable behaviour.

Independent Armed Forces Commissioner: Former Air Commodore Polly Miller-Perkins CBE was appointed the UK’s first ever Armed Forces Commissioner in March 2026. They will act as an independent champion and direct point of contact for personnel and their families and have unprecedented powers to investigate welfare issues and raise concerns that impact service life, including equipment, housing, and unacceptable behaviours.

Service Police Complaints Commissioner: Providing independent oversight of complaints made against the Service Police, ensuring investigations are fair and impartial.

Support and advice

Defence is committed to supporting those affected by unacceptable behaviour through a range of internal and external channels.

For further information:

access Defence support: bullying, harassment or discrimination - Guidance for Defence personnel on how to raise concerns about bullying, harassment or discrimination and get support.

access Defence support: sexual offences - Guidance for Defence personnel on how to report sexual offences and get support at home and overseas.

search ‘Call it out - Reporting Unacceptable Behaviour’ on internal systems

JSPs that help tackle and prevent unacceptable behaviour

Joint Service Publication (JSP) documents are produced by the MOD and some are publicly available. Defence personnel can find a full list of JSPs on internal systems by searching ‘JSPs’.

JSP 763: The MOD Behaviours and Informal Complaints Resolution Policy - a guide for all MOD service and civilian personnel on behaviours and the informal complaints resolution process.

JSP 831: Redress of individual grievances: service complaints - a guide for MOD service and civilian personnel on the application of policy for service complaints.

MOD’s Raising a Concern Policy

The Ministry of Defence raising a concern policy ensures that individuals’ concerns are addressed and resolved at the right level and as quickly and effectively as possible. It reassures individuals of protection from victimisation when raising concerns.

items.title: Defence support: bullying, harassment or discrimination
items.summary: Guidance for Defence personnel on how to raise concerns about bullying, harassment or discrimination and get support.
items.body:
This guidance is for Armed Forces personnel, civil servants, contractors, and their families and friends.

If you have experienced a sexual offence, visit Defence support: sexual offences .

Defence personnel can find additional guidance on how to recognise and respond to unacceptable or criminal behaviour and access support on the Call it Out hub on Defence Gateway .

If you have experienced unacceptable behaviour including bullying, harassment, sexual harassment or discrimination, support is available.

This page explains how you can raise a complaint and get support.

Unacceptable behaviour has no place in Defence and concerns will be taken seriously.

You may wish to:

seek advice

resolve the issue informally

make a formal complaint

Support is available whatever approach you choose.

If illegal or criminal behaviour has occurred, this should be reported to the Service Police , MOD Police or civilian police as soon as possible.

If you are unsure if what you’ve seen or experienced is unacceptable behaviour, you can read the definition of the behaviours in Behaviours and informal complaints resolution (JSP 763) - GOV.UK .

Raise a complaint

Seek informal resolution

In some circumstances, concerns can be resolved informally. Early action can help stop issues escalating, address misunderstandings and restore working relationships.

Informal resolution does not mean the matter is less important or will not be taken seriously. The main difference is that informal processes are often simpler and can help resolve issues more quickly.

Service or civilian personnel may wish to:

speak directly to the person, if you feel comfortable doing so

seek advice or intervention from a manager or Chain of Command, adviser or another trusted person

use local support, mediation or advisory services available within Defence

You can choose to make a formal complaint at any time.

For more information read Behaviours and informal complaints resolution (JSP 763) .

Defence personnel can also find more detailed information on the Call it Out hub on Defence Gateway .

Service Complaint

Current and former members of the Armed Forces can make a Service Complaint if they believe they have been wronged on a matter that arises under service law.

This can include complaints of bullying, harassment, discrimination and biased, improper or dishonest behaviour.

You can:

complete the Service Complaint Form on the My Complaint app, accessible via Defence Gateway , or:

submit a Service Complaint in writing using the form found at Annex F of JSP 831 Part 2 - GOV.UK

For more information read the guidance on the Armed Forces Service Complaints process - GOV.UK or at Redress of individual grievances: service complaints (JSP 831) - GOV.UK .

Civilian Formal Complaint

Defence civil servants, contractors, consultants and agency workers can raise formal complaints or grievances about bullying, harassment, discrimination or victimisation through the MOD Civilian Formal Complaints Process.

You can use the My Complaints App on Defence Gateway to:

submit a formal complaint

submit an anonymous complaint

record an incident, even if you do not wish to make a complaint at that time

If you cannot access the app, contact the DBS HR Advisory and Casework Service:

civilian personnel enquiry centre: 0800 345 7772 (UK) or +44 1225 747772 (Overseas), 8am to 4pm Monday to Friday

submit a form via the Digital Workplace (DWP)

Email: peopleservices@dbs.mod.uk

Support is available whether or not you choose to make a complaint.

Get support

Support is available whether or not you choose to make a formal complaint. You may want advice, help understanding your options, or simply someone to talk to before deciding what to do next.

You do not need to make a formal complaint to access support. Different services can provide practical advice, emotional support and information about the options available to you.

Available to all personnel:

Local support

If you would prefer to speak to someone directly, support is available through local Defence networks.

You can speak to:

a friend or colleague

your manager or Chain of Command

welfare staff

a diversity and inclusion adviser

staff networks

a padre or chaplain

a Trade Union representative (civilian personnel only) for advice and support on workplace issues and complaints processes.

If you choose to inform your Chain of Command about a sexual offence, their duty of care means they must tell the Service Police.

Bullying, Harassment and Discrimination Helpline

A confidential helpline is available for military personnel, civil servants and contractors.

Trained advisers can provide emotional support, practical advice and guidance on the support available to you. The helpline is open 24/7, 365 days a year and offers a safe, anonymous space to discuss concerns.

Telephone: 0800 014 2381 (UK) or +44 330 008 5942 (Overseas)

Confidential hotline

If you have concerns about wrongdoing, misconduct, illegal activity, safety risks or behaviour that falls below the standards expected in Defence, you can seek confidential advice and guidance for raising a concern and whistleblowing in Defence.

Email: Confidential-hotline@mod.gov.uk

Further information can be found in the MOD Raising a Concern Policy .

Defence Victim and Witness Care Unit

The Defence Victim and Witness Care Unit (VWCU) provide support for victims and witnesses of serious crime committed by people who are under service law in the UK and overseas.

It is independent of the chain of command and you can self-refer.

Victim Liaison Officers (VLOs) can explain what support is available, help you access services and make sure your views are understood.

Helpline: text or call 07974 074259.

Available Monday to Thursday, 8am to 4pm, and Friday, 8am to 3:30pm, excluding bank holidays.

Email: People-DSCC-VWCUGroup@mod.gov.uk

For more information visit the Victim Witness Care Unit GOV.UK page.

Support for Service personnel, veterans and their families:

The Armed Forces Commissioner

The role of the Commissioner is to provide independent and impartial oversight of the Service Complaints system for members of the UK Armed Forces.

It is also to act as a direct point of contact for serving personnel and their families who can raise general service welfare concerns that may impact on their service lives and their ability to serve.

telephone: 0300 369 0689

enquiry form

email: contact@scoaf.org.uk

For more information visit the Armed Forces Commissioner website.

Aurora New Dawn

Aurora New Dawn is a charity that provides free and confidential support for UK Armed Forces personnel and their families, including those deployed overseas. It is independent from Defence and the Chain of Command.

The specialist team can support you if you are experiencing domestic abuse, sexual violence or stalking.

Call the helpline or WhatsApp: +44 (0)333 0912 527

Helpline hours (GMT): 9am to 3pm, Monday to Friday.

WhatsApp service (GMT): Tuesday 9am to 3pm, Wednesday and Thursday 5pm to 8pm, Sunday 10am to 2pm.

For more information visit the Aurora Dawn Armed Forces website.

SSAFA Safe to Serve

SSAFA, the Armed Forces charity, is a source of support for serving personnel, veterans and their families.

SSAFA Safe To Serve is a dedicated support service for women currently serving in HM Armed Forces who are experiencing bullying, discrimination, harassment, or sexual harassment. It is outside the military Chain of Command.

Telephone: Speak directly to an advisor by calling + 44 800 260 6722

Webform: Use the webform to send a message

WhatsApp: Send a message securely on +44 203 807 4400

If you are not a woman currently serving in HM Armed Forces but you would like to speak to SSAFA, please contact SSAFA Forcesline online or telephone +44 800 260 6780 (9am to 5pm Monday to Thursday and 9am to 4pm on Friday).

Veterans UK

Veterans UK provides support and guidance for veterans, former members of the Armed Forces, and their families.

It can provide information on welfare support, compensation schemes, pensions and other services available to the veteran community.

call: 0808 1914 218

For more information visit Veterans UK .

Support for civilians and contractors:

Employee Assistance Programme (EAP)

If you are a civilian, the Employee Assistance Programme (EAP) is a confidential service available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. It can help with personal or work-related issues. EAP will not share any information with your employer or managers.

Helpline:

0800 731 8629 (UK)

+44 330 008 5959 (outside the UK)

contact form

For more information, visit the Workplace wellbeing website.

If you are deployed or based overseas:

If you are overseas, you can access the same support options as in the UK.

Bullying, Harassment, and Discrimination Helpline: +44 330 008 5942

Confidential Hotline for whistleblowing: confidential-hotline@mod.gov.uk

SSAFA Safe to Serve - WhatsApp: +44 203 807 4400

Aurora New Dawn - Helpline and WhatsApp: +44 (0)333 0912 527.

Employee Assistance Programme - +44 330 008 5959

Other support organisations

If you prefer to seek support outside of Defence, specialist organisations can provide information, advice and practical support.

General advice and support

The Samaritans

Help at Hand

items.title: Defence support: sexual offences
items.summary: Guidance for Defence personnel on how to report sexual offences and get support at home and overseas.
items.body:
This guidance is for Armed Forces personnel, civil servants, contractors, and their families and friends.

It explains how to:

report a sexual offence

get medical help

get support

You don’t have to make a report at all to receive support.

Report a sexual offence

If you or someone else is in immediate danger in the UK, call 999.

You can report a sexual offence to either the civilian police or the Service Police.

If you are unsure which organisation to contact, either organisation can explain your options and help you access support. You will be listened to without judgement.

It doesn’t matter whether the offence happened recently or in the past.

Civilian police

If you are in immediate danger in the UK, call 999.

If you have a hearing or speech impairment, use the textphone service 18000, or text if you’ve pre-registered with the emergency SMS service .

If you are in danger and you can’t speak or answer questions:

call 999

press 55 when prompted and your call will be transferred to the police

Pressing 55 only works on mobiles and doesn’t allow the police to track your location. If you don’t press 55, your call will be ended.

If it is not an emergency, call 101.

Service Police

The Service Police is responsible for policing armed forces personnel and civilians subject to service discipline.

You can report the incident to the Service Police in the UK or overseas if the incident involves a person who is subject to Service Law or a civilian subject to service discipline.

You can:

call the Service Police Crime Bureau on 02392 285 170 or 0331 145 7630

attend or call a local Service Police station (the Service Police Crime Bureau will be able to provide a location and contact details)

Specially trained officers will provide support, explain your options, and make sure your needs and wishes are considered.

The Defence Serious Crime Command (DSCC) is an independent, professional and global Service Police force with jurisdiction to investigate serious crime committed by those subject to Service law, in the UK and overseas.

Give information anonymously

If you have information about a sexual offence, you can give information anonymously to Crimestoppers.

Call on 0800 555 111

Fill out an anonymous form

If you have experienced a sexual offence and wish to report a crime, you should contact the police directly to get support and advice.

For more information visit the Crimestoppers website.

Get medical help

Medical centre

Your local medical centre or GP practice is a safe place to ask for help.

Medical staff can provide physical and mental healthcare, refer you to specialist services and support your wellbeing at work.

They will not normally share information unless there is a risk of serious harm to you or someone else.

NHS Sexual Assault Referral Centre

A Sexual Assault Referral Centre (SARC) is a specialist NHS service for anyone who has been raped, sexually assaulted or abused.

You can contact a SARC without reporting to the police. You can go at any time, and do not have to go alone.

Find your nearest sexual assault referral centre

SARCs can offer medical, practical and emotional support. They have specially trained doctors, nurses and support workers to care for you.

Services are free and available to everyone regardless of gender, age, the type of incident, or when it happened.

Services include:

crisis care

medical and forensic examination

emergency contraception

sexual health support

access to a sexual assault advisor

referral to mental health support and sexual violence support

For more information visit NHS help after rape and sexual assault .

Get support

You can access support whether or not you choose to make a formal report.

There is no wrong way to seek support.

Different services can provide information, practical help and emotional support, depending on what you need.

Defence personnel can find more guidance on how to recognise and respond to unacceptable or criminal behaviour and get support on the Call it Out hub on Defence Gateway .

Available to all personnel:

Local support

If you would prefer to speak to someone directly, support is available through local Defence networks.

You can speak to:

a friend or colleague

your manager or Chain of Command

welfare staff

a diversity and inclusion adviser

staff networks

a padre or chaplain

a Trade Union representative (civilian personnel only) for advice and support on workplace issues and complaints processes

If you choose to inform your Chain of Command about a sexual offence, their duty of care means they must tell the Service Police.

Defence Victim Witness Care Unit

The Defence Victim Witness Care Unit (VWCU) provide support for victims and witnesses of serious crime committed by people who are under service law in the UK and overseas.

It is independent of the Chain of Command and you can self-refer.

Victim Liaison Officers (VLOs) can explain what support is available, help you access services and make sure your views are understood.

Helpline: text or call 07974 074259.

Available Monday to Thursday, 8am to 4pm, and Friday, 8am to 3:30pm, excluding bank holidays.

Email: People-DSCC-VWCUGroup@mod.gov.uk

For more information visit the Victim Witness Care Unit GOV.UK page.

Independent Legal Advisors scheme

The Independent Legal Advisors (ILA) scheme provides free, independent legal advice and guidance for eligible Service and civilian personnel aged 18 or over, where a reported sexual offence is being investigated within the Service Justice System.

The scheme can help you understand the justice process, your legal rights, what to expect during an investigation, how personal information may be requested or used, and the options available if you are unhappy with how your case has been handled.

The ILA will not tell you what decisions to make or advocate on your behalf. Their role is to give you the information and advice you need to understand your options and make informed choices.

Accessing the scheme is voluntary. Referrals can be made by organisations supporting you, including the Service Police, Defence Serious Crime Command or the Victim Witness Care Unit, and will only be made with your consent.

Support for Service personnel, veterans and their families:

Aurora New Dawn

Aurora New Dawn is a charity that provides free and confidential support for UK Armed Forces personnel and their families, including those deployed overseas. It is independent from Defence and the Chain of Command.

The specialist team can support you if you are experiencing domestic abuse, sexual violence or stalking.

Call the helpline or WhatsApp: +44 (0)333 0912 527

Helpline hours (GMT): 9am to 3pm, Monday to Friday.

WhatsApp service (GMT): Tuesday 9am to 3pm, Wednesday and Thursday 5pm to 8pm, Sunday 10am to 2pm.

For more information visit the Aurora Dawn Armed Forces website.

Veterans UK

Veterans UK provides support and guidance for veterans, former members of the Armed Forces, and their families.

It can provide information on welfare support, compensation schemes, pensions and other services available to the veteran community.

call: 0808 1914 218

For more information visit Veterans UK .

Support for civilians and contractors:

Employee Assistance Programme (EAP)

If you are a civilian, the Employee Assistance Programme (EAP) is a confidential service available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. It can help with personal or work-related issues. EAP will not share any information with your employer or managers.

Helpline:

0800 731 8629 (UK)

+44 330 008 5959 (outside the UK)

contact form

For more information, visit the Workplace wellbeing website.

If you are deployed or based overseas:

If you are deployed or based overseas, support arrangements may be different from those available in the UK.

Contact the local Service Police in the first instance and they can explain the support and services available to you. If local Service Police support is not available, contact the Service Police Crime Bureau on 02392 285 170 or 0331 145 7630 for advice and support.

Defence medical staff can provide advice on the support and care available in your location.

You can also access support from:

items.title: Getting a Security Clearance Doesn't Have to Be So Intimidating: Q&A with Sina Beaghley
items.summary: The security clearance process can be difficult and time-consuming but the government has made big strides in improving it. Sina Beaghley, a senior international and defense researcher at RAND, has provided much of the research underpinning that effort.
items.body:
Getting a Security Clearance Doesn't Have to Be So Intimidating: Q&A with Sina Beaghley

Commentary

Sep 9, 2026

Sina Beaghley has worked for years to solve a problem that could keep good candidates from considering government service.

Intelligence officers, members of the military, and other key government employees and contractors have to undergo security screening. The process can be difficult and time-consuming. A few clicks on the internet, and prospective candidates can find countless stories of people stuck in security-clearance limbo.

Yet the government has made big strides in modernizing and improving the process. Beaghley , a senior international and defense researcher at RAND, has provided much of the research underpinning that effort. She and her research teams have also developed plain-English guidance to make the process less intimidating. Do applicants need to report past marijuana use? Yes. Will seeking treatment for a mental health concern automatically disqualify them from a federal position? No.

Beaghley came to RAND from the National Security Council staff, where she led the security review following a massive leak of classified documents in 2013 by then-contractor Edward Snowden. She has also worked at the National Counterterrorism Center, the Pentagon, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Treasury Department.

What's at stake in efforts to improve the security clearance process?

This is really about recruiting and retaining the best candidates for government service, especially those who can be trusted with federal security clearances. These are the people the government needs to execute its missions. But if the clearance process is too cumbersome, it's going to discourage them from even applying. It can also cause confusion, which opens the door to a lot of misinformation when people turn to the internet for advice.

What are some of the most common examples of misinformation you've found?

People think that things like student debt or foreign travel will disqualify them from getting a job that requires a federal clearance. But the reality is that there are very few issues that automatically disqualify someone. When there are concerns, what the government looks for is mitigating factors.

So maybe you had a drug problem, but you sought treatment and haven't touched drugs for years. That's something where the government will have to decide: Is this person a risk? Or have they mitigated the problem, and we can trust them?

Another big misperception is with dual citizenship . We found a really widespread perception that dual citizens can't get a security clearance. One hundred percent not true. In fact, the U.S. government wants people who have foreign experience and expertise in some of these key national security positions. They can make the government more effective in executing international policy. But they do, clearly, need to display loyalty to the United States.

Where would you make changes?

The government has been working for years now to improve this process, and it's done a lot already. But it's not all the way there yet . You ask almost anyone who's gotten a security clearance, and unless they've never traveled, have no foreign contacts—have absolutely no reportable situations—they're going to have stories about how long it took or how difficult it was.

At RAND, we've really focused on improving the experience for applicants. So, for example, putting everything in plain language so people can understand it. Making sure the instructions are consistent across agencies. The idea is to improve recruitment and retention, and that requires people who are willing to go through the process. The process can't be such a nightmare that people don't even want to embark on it.

The reality is that there are very few issues that automatically disqualify someone.

What advice would you give someone considering a job that requires vetting?

My best advice: Be honest. Most issues have mitigating factors that the government will look at. But if you're not honest, then the issue becomes your personal conduct. The government will say, “You weren't honest here, so how can we expect you to be honest in the future?”

And then, don't let the process intimidate you. Understand that it's not necessarily going to be the quickest and easiest process, but there are resources out there that can help. Our RAND team developed a toolkit that includes a step-by-step guide so people know what to expect. It has tips for completing the vetting questionnaire ( PDF ) , section by section, explaining what to include and what not to include. And we tried, as much as possible, to put it all into plain English.

You've been through the process a few times. What was your experience like?

I was actually just updating my security clearance as I was writing our most recent report on this. And I had to call a support hotline twice and ask for help because parts of the process were so unclear. And that's for me, who's supposed to be an expert here! Fortunately, someone did answer my questions and helped me make sure I was providing the correct information. So that's progress in improving the applicant experience, and I'll take that!

items.title: Anduril doubles down on Poland with autonomous aircraft pitch for F-35, Apache
items.author: Jaroslaw Adamowski
items.summary: U.S. tech company Anduril is pitching two drone types to accompany Poland's envisioned fleets of F-35 fighter jets and Apache attack helicopters.
items.body:
Europe

Anduril doubles down on Poland with autonomous aircraft pitch for F-35, Apache

A general view of the Anduril Fury, an autonomous air vehicle, displayed on March 28, 2025, in Avalon, Australia. (Asanka Ratnayake/Getty Images)

KIELCE, Poland — U.S. defense-technology company Anduril Industries has teamed up with Poland’s state-run defense giant PGZ for local assembly and production of the surface-launched Barracuda-500M cruise missile. Pending ongoing negotiations with the Polish Ministry of National Defence, the producer is also pitching its Fury autonomous combat aircraft and the Thunder autonomous attack rotorcraft to Poland in an effort that could make the nation their first European user.

Brian Moran, the company’s vice president for Europe, told Defense News at the MSPO defense show here that, while advancing the Barracuda project in partnership with PGZ, the company is also offering two autonomous aircraft to accompany the country’s envisioned fleets of Lockheed Martin’s F-35 fighter jets and Boeing’s AH-64E Apache attack helicopters .

“One of the flagship programs for Anduril has been collaborative combat aircraft, CCA, where our Fury has been chosen by the United States Air Force as a program of record,” Moran said. “With Poland getting its F-35s, Fury is tailor-made to partner with an F-35 as a loyal wingman and as a force multiplier to keep men and women in uniform out of harm’s way.”

In addition to 32 F-35 jets, the first of which arrived in Poland last May, Warsaw is also awaiting the delivery of 96 Apache helicopters. With the latter program in mind, Anduril is in talks with Polish officials over a potential sale of the Thunder drone, following its unveiling at July’s Farnborough Airshow.

“In July, we launched Thunder which is an autonomous collaborative platform for the Apache attack helicopter,” Moran said. “And just like Fury operating with an F-35, with Poland getting all these Apaches, having Thunder is a force multiplier, especially as Poland will have to train a lot of pilots for 96 Apaches.”

Deliveries of the 96 helicopters with related gear and weapons are scheduled to begin in 2028. Once the copters are supplied to the country, Poland’s military is expected to be the second-largest user of the Apaches in the world after the United States.

Last year, the Polish defense ministry signed a $300 million contract to lease eight AH-64D Apaches from the United States in anticipation of the planned deliveries.

Jaroslaw Adamowski is the Poland correspondent for Defense News.

items.title: US Navy’s next-generation fighter decision to be unveiled soon, sources say
items.author: Mike Stone, Reuters
items.summary: The program, currently unnamed but designated F/A-XX, has been buffeted by delays and funding disputes for years.
items.body:
Air Warfare

US Navy’s next-generation fighter decision to be unveiled soon, sources say

Aerial view of the United States military headquarters, the Pentagon, Sept. 28, 2008. (Jason Reed/Reuters)

The Pentagon has decided which company will make the U.S. Navy’s next-generation stealth fighter and could announce the winner in the coming weeks or sooner, two people briefed on the matter said.

Boeing and Northrop Grumman are competing for the contract, which previous programs of similar scope suggest could be worth tens of billions of dollars over its lifetime.

The program, currently unnamed but designated F/A-XX, has been buffeted by delays and funding disputes for years. Some Pentagon officials had sought to delay it by up to three years, citing concerns about engineering and supply chain capacity. Congress pushed back, earmarking $750 million for F/A-XX in the massive tax-cut and spending bill signed into law in 2025 and an additional $1.4 billion in fiscal 2026.

With China rapidly fielding advanced combat aircraft — including ones Beijing describes as sixth-generation — the stakes of further delay are high, leaving the Navy without a modern fighter capable of operating from carriers in the 2030s and beyond, potentially undermining its ability to project power in contested environments, a U.S. official has said.

A Pentagon spokesperson said, “We continue work to award the F/A-XX contract in the near future. There is no additional information at this time.”

The carrier-borne fighter jet will be the centerpiece of the Navy’s Next Generation Air Dominance family of systems, intended to replace the aging F/A-18E/F Super Hornet fleet that has been in service since the 1990s.

It is expected to feature advanced stealth capabilities, improved range and endurance, and the ability to integrate with uncrewed combat aircraft and the Navy’s carrier-based air defense systems. The first production jets are expected to enter service in the 2030s, while F/A-18s are expected to remain in service into the 2040s.
