items.title: 25 Years After 9/11: Lessons for Securing the Homeland
items.summary: Reflecting on 25 years since the September 11 terror attacks, RAND experts answer questions about protecting soft targets, the role of the TSA, mitigating risks from emerging technologies, and more.
items.body:
Commentary

Sep 8, 2026

The Tribute in Light rises above the New York skyline from the Brooklyn waterfront across the East River in New York, on September 9, 2025

Friday marks 25 years since the September 11 terror attacks. Americans are spending the week remembering those who lost their lives and honoring the first responders and others who sprang into action to help. The attacks cast a long shadow, stretching beyond Ground Zero, the Pentagon, and Flight 93 to transform not just the United States but the world.

RAND experts are reflecting on one of the most enduring aspects of this transformation: what we've learned about homeland security in the quarter-century since the attacks. Below, our researchers answer questions about protecting soft targets, mitigating risks from emerging technologies, and more.

What has stayed with you most about September 11, 2001? How did that day shape the way you think about protecting the homeland?

Heather Williams My professional trajectory has been shaped by many events, but it was set in motion by September 11. The attacks led me to focus on the Middle East and to join the U.S. Intelligence Community. That day stays with me as a reminder that solidarity is interwoven into the American fabric. This is comforting as we grapple with the current national divisions.

My thoughts on September 11 as a policy expert are more nuanced. Policymaking is so difficult because bureaucracy is complex and people are naturally resistant to change. September 11 allowed leaders to overcome much of the resistance, and I lived the positive effects of the Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act. At the same time, the reactionary nature of those changes created a patchwork of organizations working on homeland security, largely focused on terrorism as the threat.

That enterprise is now reorienting toward today's multi-hazard environment but without the catalyst that September 11 provided. Like many others, I'm motivated to build the necessary protective institutions before another tragedy strikes.

Ryan Consaul I think back to the tremendous sense of patriotism and unity born from the great tragedy of 9/11. Sadly, that unity has given way to controversy and division. Congressional oversight remains diffuse, and past bipartisan efforts to enact meaningful legislation to protect the homeland have given way to more-partisan priorities. Given the multitude of threats we continue to face, we need to stand together to tackle ongoing and emergent homeland security challenges.

Given the multitude of threats we continue to face, we need to stand together to tackle ongoing and emergent homeland security challenges.

What have we learned in the years since 9/11 about how best to protect soft targets? What does the evidence say about safeguarding communities from mass attacks by nonstate actors and others?

Brian Jackson For protecting soft targets, we often think first about technology: cameras, weapon-detection systems, or other physical protection measures. But some of the most effective protection comes from the community working together to identify and respond to potential threats. This is called behavioral threat assessment and management, or BTAM, and it's now one of the ways that the majority of K–12 schools , many workplaces, and some police departments or community safety efforts protect themselves. Teams respond when someone's behavior suggests they may become violent. Much of what the teams using this approach do doesn't look like security. For example, they might get the people referred to them into counseling or other programs to redirect them from whatever is moving them toward violence.

BTAM is effective, but it relies on everyone buying in. You can't intervene with a kid who's reading violent websites or making threats if their classmate doesn't let the teacher know what's happening or if the kid's parent refuses to let the child work with a counselor. Building and maintaining trust is tough. We tried to use this approach in the years after 9/11; it was a central part of efforts to respond to radicalization to violent extremism. But because many of the other counterterrorism approaches undermined trust with key communities, the strategy was never able to strengthen homeland security as much as it could have.

John Hollywood The evidence supports starting with layered security strategies in which multiple measures work together to improve the chance that an attack will be stopped or at least mitigated.

These security layers start with prevention. Tips from the public to police or on-site security have often helped to foil plots. Look for warning signs that incorporate a strong motivation to attack with concrete actions to prepare. Things like creating attack plans; researching how to attack; seeking to learn from extremists (including traveling to receive paramilitary training); accumulating large quantities of weapons or materials used in the construction of improvised explosives; and probing or breaching potential attack sites. Be aware that most motivations for mass attacks have been personal rather than ideological or partisan.

For on-site security, focus on the basics. Cases where attackers had direct access to a large crowd have tended to have the highest lethality, so consider how to put distance, barriers, and crowd movement between would-be attackers and crowds. Access-control systems—notably exterior and interior door locks, secured windows, and securable entryways—have all been effective and efficient. However, all require training and maintenance.

Be aware that most motivations for mass attacks have been personal rather than ideological or partisan.

Bystanders and security have stopped attacks. Groups of bystanders tackling shooters has been extremely effective. Again, training can make responses even more effective. That said, training needs to be low-stress and empowering without causing psychological injuries.

For communities, use interagency teams to support prevention, security training, and response planning. We need to establish and fund teams responsible for both educating the public about what to report and conducting diligent follow-up on reported cases. (Brian mentioned an approach for doing so, BTAM, above.) We then need to ensure advance planning and joint training with those agencies that will respond locally to a mass attack.

For many Americans, the creation of the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) and changes to airport screening remain among the most visible legacies of 9/11. What has research found about the TSA?

Kelly Klima Research over the past 25 years suggests that TSA has played a vital role in reducing the risk of terrorist attacks against U.S. aviation. Since 9/11, there has been no successful terrorist attack on a U.S. commercial flight that passed through TSA screening. This record reflects a layered defense-in-depth approach to screening passengers, baggage, and cargo, alongside intelligence, law-enforcement, and industry partners.

TSA has also balanced security with the need to move millions of travelers and large volumes of cargo efficiently and at reasonable cost. The passenger fee is less than $6 per flight, and the total TSA budget (which includes the development and procurement of screening technology) is about $8 billion in 2026.

That balance of security and reasonable cost continues to improve through better physical and chemical screening technologies, changes in checkpoint design and procedures, and risk-based approaches that focus attention where it's needed most.

But the threat continues to evolve. Terrorists and insiders may seek to conceal firearms, explosives, or other weapons in new ways. Emerging cyber and other nontraditional threats require constant assessment. Continued investment in advanced detection technologies, process redesign, and responsibly developed AI can help TSA identify threats more accurately and quickly, strengthen aviation security, and improve the passenger experience.

Continued investment in advanced detection technologies, process redesign, and responsibly developed AI can help TSA identify threats more accurately and quickly.

Williams Americans associate TSA with the blue shirts they encounter at the security checkpoint, but the organization has a broader mandate than many realize. One of the other programs TSA manages is the Security Threat Assessment for multiple security credentials, including the Transportation Worker Identification Credential (TWIC) and Hazardous Materials Endorsement for commercial driver's licenses. RAND research has found that TSA generally executes these programs effectively, at cost, and with timely resolution, in a way that reduces internal threats. For example, TWIC applicants who have no flags for possible disqualifying factors could find a physical card in their mailbox less than six days later.

Many anti-terrorism technologies and capabilities require collaborations between government and the private sector. What have we learned about how to effectively navigate those partnerships?

Thao Liz Nguyen One of the enduring lessons is that the development, maturation, and operational adoption of anti-terrorism technologies can proliferate in well-structured public-private collaboration. After 9/11, the Support Anti-terrorism by Fostering Effective Technologies Act of 2002, enacted as part of the Homeland Security Act of 2002, established the Office of SAFETY Act Implementation and created a statutory framework for evaluating and incentivizing anti-terrorism technologies. From a technology-evaluation perspective, the SAFETY Act not only encourages innovation in the abstract but applies a rigorous process to assessing technical performance, operational utility, and real-world deployment considerations of mature technologies to emerging capabilities.

Designation and Certification protections under the SAFETY Act have helped mature the market for proven security technologies and services by reducing liability uncertainty and signaling that a capability has undergone meaningful DHS review. At the same time, the Developmental Testing and Evaluation Designation protection has been especially important for emerging technologies, because it allows developers to generate operational evidence, refine concepts of use, and test performance in relevant environments before a capability is fully fielded.

What we've learned is that effective public-private partnership requires more than funding or policy encouragement; it requires credible evaluation pathways, clear incentives for participation, and mechanisms that help bridge the gap between innovation, validation, and scalable adoption for anti-terrorism technologies.

The development, maturation, and operational adoption of anti-terrorism technologies can proliferate in well-structured public-private collaboration.

Of course, new technologies have also transformed the threat landscape. Let's start with unmanned aerial systems, commonly known as drones. How have drones emerged as a potential threat to people and infrastructure, and what do we know about how to mitigate that threat?

Brendan Toland Drones have rapidly emerged as a threat because these systems have become more capable and more available. Parallel advances in a series of technologies (batteries, electric motors, precision manufacturing, optics) have shrunk the airframe for drones, increased their speed and endurance, and lowered their cost. Additionally, improvements in lightweight cameras, guidance via GPS waypoints, and wire-guided control have made it more difficult to detect and take over hostile drones. Finally, drones come in various forms. This lets bad actors select a drone that is optimal for the intended objective, whether that's maintaining an eye in the sky or delivering compact items (contraband, bombs) virtually anywhere at speed.

As part of RAND's work operating the Homeland Security Operational Analysis Center, we evaluated the capabilities of commercially available drones. We found that these systems continue to lower in cost while improving on operationally relevant metrics, such as speed, flight time, and payload capacity. We also developed several high-threat scenarios in which bad actors could use drones to threaten the homeland, including bombing a federal building or delivering a chemical agent outside a major sporting event. Looking across the market, we found more than 500 systems capable of conducting at least one of our high-threat scenarios. This number has only grown in the six years since our research was conducted.

The speed of drones and the ability to launch these systems from virtually anywhere constrains the response time for those working to defend the homeland. In our more recent simulation modeling, we found that defenders had only seconds to a few minutes to detect and defeat incoming drones, depending on the situation. If the adversary uses a drone to provide aerial surveillance, then in many cases the onboard camera enables a stand-off range that undermines detection. Any effective defense requires deploying layered mitigation capabilities in advance, putting these capabilities in the hands of trained personnel, sharing detection information across the homeland security enterprise, and empowering defenders on the ground to make quick decisions.

Christopher Scott Adams Advances in drone technology have made the threat more salient, but the homeland security enterprise has some tools to help mitigate that threat. The Preventing Emerging Threats Act and the SAFER SKIES Act have given key counter-drone authorities to federal and state/local/tribal/territorial law enforcement, respectively. These include permissions, under certain circumstances, to intercept communications between drones and their operators, track and monitor drone flights, and disable, down, or destroy potential threats.

These authorities have allowed DHS and its partners to invest in counter-drone technologies. At RAND, we've advised our DHS sponsors on the requirements for effective counter-drone capabilities and the right technology mix. This analysis has informed ongoing counter-drone investments at the border and in defense of major events, such as the World Cup and the Olympics.

Advances in drone technology have made the threat more salient, but the homeland security enterprise has some tools to help mitigate that threat.

Across these assessments, we've found a few consistent effective practices to mitigate, though not eliminate, the threat. First, defense-in-depth is key; having multiple types of sensors and effectors (kinetic and non-kinetic) in the same location gives the best chance of detecting and defeating a variety of drone threats. Second, defenders need to plan ahead. This includes resolving authorities issues, developing rules of engagement that are well understood by all operators, and creating information-sharing agreements across responsible agencies. Third, employing automation in defense can provide the speed to respond to a similarly automated threat.

What about artificial intelligence? For example, concerns are rising that AI could enable biological attacks. What do we know about this emerging risk and how best to mitigate it?

Steph Guerra Historically, biological attacks have been rare, unsuccessful, and difficult to execute. That's because of the technical, operational, and motivational barriers that bad actors face. But AI is increasingly able to lower these barriers by democratizing biological expertise, driving laboratory workflows, raising the ceiling of biological novelty, and circumventing existing biosecurity controls like gene synthesis screening . At RAND, we seek to assess these capabilities to help inform policy action that reduces the risk of misuse while still enabling beneficial scientific innovation.

Our team recently published a biosecurity strategy for the AI era to prevent AI-enabled biological attacks. The strategy is deliberately layered, because different mitigations stop different threat actors. For example, access controls like gene synthesis screening may stop a lone terrorist, but they probably can't stop a state bioweapons program. But a state program might be deterred from developing bioweapons by credible attribution and rapid response capabilities. Each layer is critical, but only having one is insufficient.

We know AI capabilities in biology are advancing fast, but thankfully the most hazardous thresholds haven't yet been crossed. That gives us a narrow window to build protective infrastructure before misuse becomes demonstrably easy.

Nguyen Detection technology is being pushed to do more than it was originally built for. This is true for any emerging unforeseen threat. As AI lowers the barrier to entry of designing novel biological agents or even modifying existing ones, screening systems must improve at spotting unusual patterns, not just known signatures stored in their static reference libraries. In practice, that means detection equipment needs to keep pace with new compounds, new delivery methods, and changes in how material may be packaged or concealed.

The challenge is that detection is only as good as the data, calibration, and reference libraries it relies on, so if the libraries are outdated, then the equipment can miss something that doesn't look like the “expected” threat. That's why DHS and other stakeholders should continue investing in research, development, testing, and evaluation; field testing; and recalibration of sensors and screening tools. We also need to think about how these systems are integrated across layers of screening, because no single device is going to catch everything. We need to invest in innovative detection systems and the algorithms behind them so they can stay adaptive and agile as threats evolve.

David Luckey The convergence of AI with advances in biotechnology and chemistry represents one of the most significant emerging risks to homeland security since 9/11. AI is rapidly lowering technical barriers in synthetic biology, genomics, and chemical engineering. This means that malicious actors could potentially leverage AI tools to design, synthesize, or optimize biological or chemical agents with unprecedented speed and precision.

This risk is not hypothetical. AI-driven platforms can already assist in protein folding, gene editing, and even the design of novel chemical compounds. Used by a bad actor, these capabilities could be repurposed to engineer pathogens or toxins that evade current detection and mitigation strategies. The dual-use nature of AI in life sciences poses unique governance and oversight challenges; the same tools that accelerate medical breakthroughs can also facilitate weaponization.

Mitigating this risk almost certainly requires a multi-layered approach that includes strengthening oversight, promoting responsible innovation, enhancing detection and response, and building cross-sector partnerships. Effective mitigation will likely depend on seamless collaboration between government, industry, and the research community. Proactive risk assessment, horizon scanning, and anticipatory governance are essential to stay ahead of adversaries who might exploit AI for catastrophic ends.

Proactive risk assessment, horizon scanning, and anticipatory governance are essential to stay ahead of adversaries who might exploit AI for catastrophic ends.

Twenty-five years later, what lesson from 9/11 feels most urgent in your work today?

Jackson Responding to threats requires thinking about how we will maintain defenses in the long term, even when the need to respond is most urgent.

The human and financial costs of 9/11 were catastrophic, and so there was pressure to do everything possible to make sure that such a tragedy couldn't happen again. As time passed, it became clear that the costs of all the security and other measures added up over time—and that one of the most effective responses to that specific threat (reinforcing airplane cockpit doors) was one of the cheapest. While government needs to spend to protect the nation, the more expensive security measures are, the harder they are to maintain over time.

Though thinking about the cost-effectiveness of security may seem odd when we're concerned about the risk of disasters like 9/11, doing so is critical, particularly since it's often much cheaper for attackers to try something new than it is for defenders to update protections.

Hollywood We need to stay vigilant but not overreactive.

This means maintaining a focus between overreaction to what have been extremely rare events and inattention to ongoing threats. Similarly, we must avoid getting distracted by a single part of the threat (e.g., focusing on a specific ideology when most attacks are personally motivated) or by a single security technology. Instead, what's needed is a strategic, layered approach that counters the full range of violent threats. Perhaps most importantly, vigilance means maintaining and developing partnerships between the public, security groups, and local, state, and federal agencies to provide ongoing prevention and protection.

Luckey It's imperative to have imagination and adaptability in the face of evolving threats.

9/11 exposed the dangers of “failure of imagination,” specifically the inability to anticipate how adversaries might exploit emerging or unexplored vulnerabilities. Today, as we confront the intersection of AI and biological or chemical weapons, that lesson is more urgent than ever.

Our adversaries are agile, opportunistic, and increasingly technologically sophisticated. The tools of mass disruption are no longer confined to nation-states or well-resourced groups; they're becoming accessible to a broader spectrum of actors. This reality demands that we continually reassess our assumptions, update our risk models, and foster a culture of innovation and vigilance across the homeland security enterprise.

I'm reminded daily that security is a dynamic process, not a static end state. The post-9/11 era amplified the value of intelligence sharing, public-private partnerships, and resilience. But it also illuminated that the next threat might not look like the last. Our greatest asset is the ability to anticipate, adapt, and act—before the unimaginable becomes reality.

items.title: Novel technologies for security-sector governance and management
items.author: Elizabeth Moisan
items.summary: RAND Europe scoped technology use in security-sector governance and management, mapping opportunities and risks from real-world cases and distilling lessons and good practices to embed good governance in the adoption and use of these tools.
items.body:
RAND Europe conducted a scoping study to explore the use of technologies in security sector governance and management (SSG/M) with the aim of examining opportunities and risks stemming from use cases identified through the research, as well as identifying lessons learned and good practices to foster good-governance efforts when leveraging technological solutions in the security sector.

Novel technologies for security-sector governance and management

Pauline Paillé , Sarah Winder , Elizabeth Moisan

Research Published Sep 8, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

RAND Europe conducted a scoping study on the implications of novel technologies for security-sector governance and management (SSG/M) supported by the Security and Stabilisation Department of the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO).

The study explored how emerging solutions such as artificial intelligence (AI), biometrics, machine learning and enhanced surveillance systems are being adopted by security-sector actors and how their use affects public acceptability and consent, institutional accountability, financial sustainability and ethics.

Through a targeted literature review and semi-structured interviews with key stakeholders, the study investigated how technologies can strengthen efficiency, effectiveness and transparency across SSG/M while introducing significant risks, including privacy and data-protection concerns, algorithmic bias, opaque decision making, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, and challenges related to data sovereignty and reliance on private suppliers. The study identified cross-cutting lessons and good practices to guide responsible adoption and foster good governance by emphasising early engagement with end users, adaptation to local context, clear data governance, layered human oversight of automated processes, complementary internal policies and external regulation, and continuous training.

Key Takeaways

Exploring novel technologies and their impact on SSG/M

Nine technology areas were identified as being increasingly used in SSG/M: Augmented Reality/Virtual Reality (AR/VR), Automated decision support, Biometrics, Blockchain, Digital ID platforms, Data management solutions, Satellite imagery, Social media monitoring, and Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs).

These solutions can provide gains in efficiency, effectiveness, situational awareness, and, where designed transparently, strengthened accountability and traceability. However, there are also cross-cutting risks to consider: privacy and data-protection concerns, algorithmic bias and opaque models, cybersecurity and data-sovereignty vulnerabilities, exclusion of digitally marginalised groups, and diluted accountability when private vendors or automated systems shape decisions.

Enhancing good-governance practices for the use of technology in SSG/M

Six cross-cutting practices were identified to embed governance into the full technology lifecycle in the context of SSG/M: 1. Co-design with end users and communities to ensure fit-for-purpose tools and accountability 2. Justify and adapt adoption to local context, infrastructure and perceptions, anticipating misuse 3. Assess need and balance risk appetite and tolerance, including lifecycle costs, while governing data provenance, ownership and cross-border sharing 4. Move beyond human-in-the-loop to multilayered oversight that counters automation bias, allows time to intervene and clarifies responsibility 5. Pair internal policies with external regulation and oversight (transparent approvals, logging/auditing, public consultation and after-action reviews) for accountability 6. Provide continuous and dedicated training for operators and leaders to support the use of technologies in SSG/M.

Recommendations

There is a need to bring key stakeholders together, including private-sector companies developing technological solutions as well as state and non-state actors involved in the delivery and management of security services. Relevant actors from adjacent sectors who are also using these technologies, such as humanitarian or disaster-response bodies, could also benefit from widespread engagement.

Technological solutions evolve very rapidly and often simultaneously across contexts. As a result, there are limited opportunities to learn from past or ongoing experiences in other contexts in order to replicate good practices and avoid pitfalls that may have been previously identified in different settings .

SSG/M good-governance principles should be embedded when considering the use of technologies. To do so, the principles of good governance outlined above should form part of the requirements when considering technological solutions for the provision and management of security services. In addition, the development of a risk-assessment model could be used across fragile contexts to assess the suitability of these technological solutions.

items.title: An analysis of Veterans’ and Reservists’ participation in the labour market
items.author: Linda Slapakova
items.summary: This RAND Europe research explores UK Veterans’ and Reservists’ participation in civilian labour markets, including economic participation, underemployment and barriers to, and facilitators of, good employment outcomes.
items.body:
This RAND Europe research explores UK Veterans’ and Reservists’ participation in civilian labour markets, including economic participation, underemployment and barriers to, and facilitators of, good employment outcomes. While Veterans and Reservists have similar employment rates and hourly wages to non-Veterans they face distinct labour market challenges, including barriers at the individual, employer and structural level.

An analysis of Veterans’ and Reservists’ participation in the labour market

Catherine Galley , Sean Flanagan , Linda Slapakova

Research Published Sep 7, 2026

Includes Executive Summary; Supplementary Annex

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Approximately 960,000 working-age Veterans and 30,000 volunteer Reservists live in Great Britain, and they participate in the labour market at broadly comparable levels to the wider civilian populations. However, the nature of their economic activity often differs: Veterans are over-represented in sectors such as manufacturing, transport, construction and public administration. Despite the high employment rate, some Veterans and Reservists also face barriers to securing meaningful work and some Veterans and Reservists experience underemployment where their skills and experience are not being fully utilised.

Despite growing policy attention, including the 2026 Veterans’ Strategy commitment to ensuring Veteran’s skills are properly recognised and utilised, and that these skills contribute to UK national security, there are significant evidence gaps on Veterans’ and Reservists’ participation in the labour market. Research has historically focused on whether individuals are in employment, overlooking phenomena such as underemployment and positive economic contributions.

To address these gaps, RAND Europe was commissioned by the Office for Veterans' Affairs, via the Armed Forces Covenant Fund Trust, to conduct a mixed-methods study combining statistical analysis of three national datasets (the Census, Annual Population Survey, and Family Resources Survey) with an international literature review and stakeholder interviews. This report presents new evidence on the employment profile and earnings of Veterans and Reservists, underemployment and the barriers and facilitators to Veterans and Reservists gaining successful employment, informing five recommendations for the OVA.

Key Takeaways

Veterans and Reservists have similar levels of employment and hourly wages to comparable non-Veterans

The data shows that Veterans and Reservists have similar levels of employment and hourly wages to non-Veterans with similar characteristics, indicating that Veterans and Reservists do not face systemic labour market disadvantage. However, Veterans and Reservists are concentrated in different industries and occupations to non-Veterans, making them vulnerable to economic shocks in different ways to non-Veterans.

Employers increasingly recognise that Veterans and Reservists bring valuable skills to the labour market

However, some Veterans and Reservists still face challenges in translating their skills and qualifications and having them recognised in civilian workplaces, and can face barriers to employment at the individual, employer and structural level. These barriers include poor awareness and understanding of the Armed Forces, military roles and skills among hiring managers and other decision makers, and a lack of clear policies to support Veterans and Reservists consistently.

Underemployment remains an underexplored but potentially significant issue for both Veterans and Reservists

The limited evidence suggests that underemployment may affect a substantial number of Veterans, particularly during their transition from military service to civilian life. For Reservists, underemployment is more complex and can occur in both their military and civilian roles.

Minority subgroups within the Veteran community tend to experience the disadvantages faced by their non-Veteran counterparts

Female, ethnic minority, and disabled/poor-health Veterans generally experience similar labour-market disadvantages as their non-Veteran peers with the same characteristics, rather than being either protected or uniquely disadvantaged by Veteran status alone.

Recommendations

This report makes five recommendations for the Office for Veterans’ Affairs:

Continue providing through-life career support to Veterans and Reservists with a focus on encouraging engagement and exploring promising avenues for strengthening support.

Continue to promote understanding of military service among employers and the broader public, focusing on gatekeepers (e.g. hiring managers) as well as senior leadership.

Ensure policymakers and service providers consider regional differences and ensure that policies and support are inclusive to all members of the Armed Forces community.

Monitor trends and shocks impacting the labour market and work with other stakeholders across national and local government, industry and the third sector to effectively align support provision.

Work with stakeholders across the sector to address priority evidence gaps and ensure the continued inclusion of Veteran and Armed Forces identifiers in large-scale national surveys.

items.title: AI Can Now Design Viruses. We Need Biosecurity Guardrails Now
items.summary: As AI advances, the risk of engineered viral bioweapons is growing. The window to prepare is now—by building a layered, resilient system of defense.
items.body:
Commentary

Sep 4, 2026

By Steph Guerra

This commentary was originally published by Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists on September 4, 2026.

“Nature is the world’s worst bioterrorist” is a common maxim in the field of biosecurity, a reference to the idea that naturally emerging pathogens cause far more deaths than any biological attack a terrorist could carry out. But the trope may soon be outdated. In an article published Aug. 6 in the journal Science , scientists demonstrated that trained AI models can design novel viruses as well as—if not better than—nature itself.

Their experiment created viruses that infect bacteria, not humans. Still, much like the multiple AI models that escaped their test environments to hack other networks this summer, these newly revealed capabilities give biosecurity experts like me pause. How do we keep enabling legitimate scientific progress, while also preventing AI from assisting in the creation of biological weapons?

As AI capabilities advance, viral bioweapons could become much easier to design and produce and could cause even more harm than the weapons used in the past. Consider that almost all the bioterrorist attacks in our modern era have involved substances like anthrax or ricin. While they’ve harmed dozens of people at a time, the illnesses these attacks caused weren’t transmissible between humans. Designing novel viruses, on the other hand, could enable biological attacks that spread, infections that leap from person to person and that could even spark a pandemic. To prevent this outcome, we need to build mechanisms for restricting access to the tools, data, and materials that might allow someone to misuse emerging capabilities in this way. And we should also go further by building defenses that can deter nefarious activity in the first place. …

The remainder of this commentary is available at thebulletin.org .

items.title: Tomorrow's Victory and the Army of the Future: Forecasting the Next Steps in Ukraine's Military Evolution
items.summary: Ukraine’s military has changed substantially since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. Will its next evolution be shaped by traditionalists or technologists?
items.body:
Commentary

Sep 3, 2026

Ukrainian soldiers practice operating a ground-based drone (UGV) during a training session at the 10th Corps’ drone school, Kharkiv

By Jacob Parakilas and Oliver Gill

Amidst a changing strategic context which has seen Russian fortunes recede from their high water mark, Ukraine’s armed forces are facing another inflection point. The Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) of 2026 bear little resemblance to the army which faced Russia's initial seizure of Crimea, the force which fought Russian-backed separatists in Donbas from 2014–2022, and even the force that turned back Russia’s attempt to decapitate Ukraine in February 2022. That army, which just over a decade ago was still defined by its Soviet legacy, has emerged today as something new: a hybrid force, in which legacy organisational structures and Soviet-era kit work alongside imported doctrines, arms from Western partners, and increasingly domestically produced equipment and experimental methods.

But like the war itself, that force has not reached a static final form. It remains a work in progress , adapting to circumstance as Ukraine continues to defend its sovereignty against Russian aggression. The question we ask here is: if Ukraine’s armed forces are a substantial evolution relative to the beginning of the war, what form will they take on next?

The choice facing Ukraine's forces is far from a binary between East and West. As the full-scale war enters its fifth year, with its character still changing, the AFU continues to be tasked with building, deploying, and improving its existing capabilities while simultaneously developing innovative organisational structures, tactics, and doctrine to use them most effectively.

Two camps have emerged into view this last month, each associated with a senior official whose disputes became highly public and controversial. A traditionalist camp, personified by recently relieved Chief of the General Staff Oleksandr Syrskyi, highlights the way in which Ukraine’s forces succeeded in holding the frontline against a materially and numerically superior adversary with an often-overlooked reliance on traditional tactics and weapons ( PDF ) . A reformist camp, symbolised by equally recently dismissed Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, champions technological superiority and suggests more fundamental restructuring to better leverage novel weapons, unconventional tactics, and reformed procurement practices favouring decentralisation, SMEs, and increased transparency. Put simply, this reflects a struggle of the old guard against the next generation.

One could interpret the dismissal of the senior figures in both camps as a sign that Ukraine’s leadership is trying to find a middle path, but the fundamental questions of how to continue the AFU’s evolution in the face of ongoing Russian assaults is unlikely to disappear. And as General Syrskyi’s successor Mykhailo Drapatyi assumes the role of Chief of the General Staff of the AFU, it is worth first questioning the validity of this framing. The distinction between Old and New, static and manoeuvrable, traditional and novel, is perhaps an oversimplification. The public rivalry between General Syrskyi and Fedorov cannot be viewed simply as a difference of opinion on military management, divorced from the political and cultural context from which both men have emerged. For the future of the AFU, it is far more useful to view these two sides as a contest between theories of victory and governance — and about what kind of force posture and approach to military management best achieves that end goal.

If Ukraine’s armed forces are a substantial evolution relative to the beginning of the war, what form will they take on next?

The Unmanned Systems Forces: The Command of the Future?

Within the AFU, the Unmanned Systems Forces (USF) stand out as a source of pride for their technological and technical mastery of asymmetric warfare with attritable, adaptable tools ( PDF ) . The USF make up just two percent of the military’s personnel strength yet are responsible for roughly 30 percent of Russian losses , having irrevocably changed the character of the battlefield. Converting the AFU into a vehicle for a massively expanded USF is one possibility. That said, the remaining 98 percent of personnel (what might be termed the "traditional army") are just as essential, still accounting for the remaining 70 percent of Russian losses. To achieve full effect, hold the line, and sustain Ukraine's valiant defence over the past four years, both the “traditional” and “novel” camps have had to work together, regardless of friction, every step of the way. This is not as outlandish as it might seem at first blush. After all, it was under General Syrskyi's tenure that the world's first Unmanned Systems Force was codified as a branch of the armed forces .

But what would be the implications of either camp—the Traditionalists or the Technologists—taking the lead on the AFU’s future? To structure this discussion, we consider four areas of potential change: unit structure, training, recruitment, and procurement. And for the purposes of this thought exercise, our assumption is a relatively steady state over the next two years, with no ceasefire and a constant level of ongoing hostilities with Russia.

Scenario One: Traditionalist Retrenchment

In this scenario, the General Staff fend off radical transformation while continuing an approach of large-scale but selective integration of emerging technologies. Doing so has preserved interoperability with NATO, avoiding the unknown vulnerabilities that radical restructuring might introduce, and leant into a narrative of battlefield success and national effort to keep the ranks filled with volunteers.

Unit Structure

Over the course of the full-scale war, traditionalists have consistently favoured fielding the maximum number of brigades . As fresh recruits complete basic training, they continue to be more or less evenly distributed across all active units, rather than being preferentially assigned to higher-performing or more combat-effective formations.

Despite efforts to centralise command and control into a Corps structure , the AFU has continued to centralise decision-making at the General Staff level. As in previous years, brigades subordinated to this new corps structure remain non-contiguous across the frontline — a complicating factor that has continued to require constant intervention from the General Staff.

Training Structures

Under General Syrskyi's tenure, General Basic Military Training was extended from 30 to 51 days for standard entry into the Ground Forces . Under this regime, all soldiers are first trained as infantrymen, only later being potentially trained as Uncrewed Systems (UxS) operators. Given the prevalence of Russian infiltration tactics , and the subsequent risk of finding themselves in direct small-arms engagements, this approach persists. Moreover, despite Technologist aspirations toward full battlefield automation , human spotters and ground troops have remained essential for taking and holding positions. Centralised training ensures all personnel master foundational soldiering skills, enabling tactical movement and combined-arms discipline. In this scenario, technical expertise has remained a specialist force enhancer rather than the central organising principle of individual training.

Recruitment

In a war of attrition, with frontline ground forces bearing the cost of holding the line, waves of mobilisation have continued to be key to maintaining a viable force. As training structures continue to emphasise infantry skillsets, voluntary recruitment, which was already struggling to meet demand, has become increasingly inadequate. Despite public protest and frustration, more coercive forms of mobilisation and conscription have become necessary to fill the ranks.

Procurement

Legacy systems, alongside a staggering scale of unmanned systems production, have remained the potent toolkit that has frozen the frontline against the Russian invaders. Innovation has been rewarded where it guarantees immediate return on investment. Contracts for procurement, refurbishment and upgrading of legacy systems have continued to scale consistent with trends from previous years, and large scale contracts continue to be awarded at the discretion of the General Staff, with more decentralised procurement and production of unmanned systems remaining the exception rather than the rule.

Assessment

The Traditionalist theory of victory emphasises the need to preserve traditional offensive capability—the weapons and tactics which allowed Ukrainian forces to retake territory around Kharkiv and the city of Kherson in 2022 and punch into Kursk in 2024. In this now dominant view, over-reliance on unmanned systems, and the temptation of autonomous kill-chains that seek to separate weapon operators from danger, risks only prolonging the war. Only by eventually driving the invaders from occupied territory by manoeuvre can the war be ended justly. Offensive action by assault units, with uncrewed systems in a crucial but supporting function, remains indispensable.

This model has minimised structural risk by reinforcing combined-arms fundamentals and adapting new technology and tactics wholesale once they are proven, not before. While UxS and medium-range strike platforms offer unprecedented operational agility, they cannot independently solve every tactical problem. Heavy artillery, armoured breachers, and conventional strike assets have remained indispensable for reducing hardened, protected infrastructure. By treating UxS as a preparatory enabler used to clear logistics, destroy enemy electronic warfare and soft targets, or degrade enemy air defences ahead of ground manoeuvre, this approach has maintained operational balance while avoiding command duplication.

In a war of attrition, with frontline ground forces bearing the cost of holding the line, waves of mobilisation have continued to be key to maintaining a viable force.

Scenario Two: Technologist Transformation

In this scenario, the Technologist camp is ascendant and leans fully into an emerging model—operationally, technologically, and organisationally. At the front line, human soldiers do less of the fighting directly; increasingly, the role of traditional frontline specialists (riflemen, machine gunners, etc.) shifts toward guarding strongpoints and securing rear areas to protect logistics and communications functions. ISR, defensive fires, short-range strike, and even ground assault are increasingly handled by remote and autonomous systems, with humans serving as a backup force rather than leading the charge. This has reduced AFU personnel's exposure to enemy direct fire and allows volunteers who might otherwise be unfit for frontline duty to continue contributing to combat operations. However, it has also destabilized existing structures, increased turnover at higher ranks, and opened opportunities for Russian forces to exploit seams in Ukrainian defences—both physically and informationally. The AFU's rapid transformation also risks outpacing NATO's own force-transformation efforts, creating new obstacles to interoperability .

Technologists have pursued corps structure reforms more thoroughly and centralizing command and control into coordinated hubs. High-performing brigades and corps have been further rewarded with recruits and materiel, while underperforming commands are gradually dissolved, with personnel redistributed to units under more effective leadership. Under this model, newer formations like the USF have been formalised as primary drivers of combat power. Tactical tasking has shifted away from traditional combined-arms brigades toward specialised autonomous units, with more offensive roles almost entirely delegated to autonomous platforms. Greater effort is directed toward strategic asymmetry—targeting enemy logistics at mid-range, and industry, supply chains, and military and energy infrastructure at long range and strategic depth. Where predominantly human formations undertake offensive operations, they do so in discrete, carefully bounded circumstances, helped by close collaboration with robotic systems and only in areas where systematic preparation has maximised their odds of success and survival.

Taking the Unmanned Systems Force's approach as indicative of the broader Technologist model, Ukrainian soldiers have continued to train first and foremost as infantry. Drone operators emerge from a unified fighting culture of frontline soldiers, not the reverse. That said, experimentation with and adoption of UxS has been more deliberately integrated into standard Basic Training, preparing soldiers to support unmanned systems-led operations. Defensive tactics, rather than the perceived costliness of offensive training, become the predominant skillset.

Under the Technologist approach, greater effort has gone into reforming recruitment along more practical lines. Conscription has been reimagined as an invitation to serve during defined, limited service periods, paired with a narrative emphasis on survivability as a core institutional value. Such a structure has built significant goodwill among the general population, but has not produced the raw numbers that mass mobilisation would, further driving reliance on UxS and novel tactics and reducing the AFU’s ability to surge forces to shore up weak points in the line or to contain enemy breakthroughs.

Market forces have increasingly squeezed out manufacturers previously protected by unregulated contracts. Innovation has surged as small- and medium-sized enterprises seize smaller contracts on the periphery, while the Ukrainian and European drone-primes of tomorrow have consolidated market share and continue scaling up. Ukrainian firms have become increasingly viable players on the global defence market, but demand for their products has created some tension as the government tries to balance sustainable export success with continuing to feed the needs of the AFU.

The Technologist theory of victory runs in a markedly different direction to the Traditionalist approach. Under this approach, unmanned systems offer asymmetric advantage and create distance between operators and the enemy. Offensive operations, rather than serving as the key to victory, become momentary and opportunistic—such as the recent pushes in the south following the whitelisting of Ukraine-based Starlink terminals, which triggered connection and communication failures on the Russian side. This camp instead pursues a theory of victory built on unrestricted technological dominance in the operational domain, particularly through medium- and deep-strike capabilities against Russian logistics and industrial infrastructure, gradually degrading the enemy's ability to wage war. Preserving human life, even at the cost of static defence, allows attritable forces to absorb the brunt of punishment. Victory, in this view , comes through economic and logistical collapse rather than decisive battlefield action.

The question is whether [a] robotic integration ends up proving that the fundamentals of war have changed … or that war changes slowly and victory comes from paying heed to fundamentals.

Conclusion

A senior officer in the USF advised the authors not to reduce the question of the AFU’s future to a simple dichotomy between old and new ways of doing things, especially regarding force structure. Unmanned systems, he explained, are a single tool in the commander’s toolbox. Increasingly essential, but still just one capability among many that must be used together and selected carefully to achieve full operational success. Unmanned systems alone cannot take a heavily fortified position; yet in the Ukrainian battlefield of 2026, it is not possible to accomplish that task without them. Those systems are essential for harassing enemy infantry, armour, and logistics at short-to-medium range, and for destroying other soft targets—but heavy artillery and armour are still needed to destroy hardened targets, and infantry is still needed to move in and hold a position once cleared. This, indeed, is the purpose of Ukraine's domestic C2 system, DELTA: to link the full range of military capabilities together via live feed and to put the most appropriate tool to any given battlefield task. Whichever theory of victory Ukraine ultimately pursues, unmanned systems and traditional military hardware will need to be used in tandem to achieve it.

The distinction between traditional and novel approaches may be more clearly evidenced not in force structure itself, but in approaches to military culture and command (USF brigades, for instance, are largely staffed by recently recruited civilians at the command level), in approaches to recruitment, training, and procurement, and in differing theories of victory: combined manoeuvre and large-scale breakthrough versus attritional, asymmetric harassment of strategic and economic objectives.

Indeed, the distinction between the Unmanned Systems Forces (13 out of over 100 total AFU brigades) on one hand, and the land forces, National Guard, and territorial defence forces on the other, is again not as clear-cut as it may seem. While the Unmanned Systems Forces pioneer new technologies, procurement practices, and force structures, all of Ukraine's forces—land, territorial defence, and National Guard alike—use unmanned systems to varying degrees and in different ways.

The question is whether this robotic integration ends up proving that the fundamentals of war have changed and that revolutionary rather than evolutionary approaches are necessary for victory—or that war changes slowly and victory comes from paying heed to fundamentals. At this stage, the question is not yet answered, but the ultimate shape and fate of the AFU will be our strongest evidence one way or the other.

items.title: Buying Time Against AI Proliferation
items.author: Tobias Sytsma
items.summary: The author describes a formal model of artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and proliferation that focuses on the demand for AI capability.
items.body:
Much of today’s policy debate over artificial intelligence (AI) revolves around instruments designed to change the costs of access to AI; this report describes a formal model of AI adoption and proliferation that focuses on the demand for AI capability.

Buying Time Against AI Proliferation

The Economics of Governed Access

Tobias Sytsma

Research Published Sep 3, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Much of today’s policy debate over artificial intelligence (AI) focuses on efforts to change the costs of access to AI—to shift relative costs such that AI adoption is steered toward channels that society can monitor and away from channels it cannot.

Policy analysis has concentrated on the supply side of this problem, with such mechanisms as export restrictions, licensing requirements, and controls on computing hardware. But where AI capabilities end up depends on the choices of organizations and individuals about what to adopt and through which channels, and it is on this demand side that cost-shifting instruments operate. This demand side of the problem has received far less systematic analysis.

This report addresses this gap with a framework for judging when cost-shifting steers adoption as intended, when it accomplishes little, and when it backfires and makes proliferation worse. The author details a formal model in which AI adoption is driven by relative costs across access channels, and governance instruments operate by manipulating those relative costs. The central question is: When policy changes the relative cost of AI access, how do users reallocate across governed and ungoverned channels, and under what conditions does that reallocation reduce, fail to affect, or accelerate uncontrolled proliferation of AI?

Key Takeaways

Compliance burdens on governed AI access channels can make uncontrolled AI proliferation worse

Raising the cost of controlled frontier access without corresponding pressure on ungoverned alternatives can redirect user adoption toward ungoverned access channels. In simulations conducted by the author, this occurred in roughly one-quarter of relevant scenarios.

Whether AI access governance can sufficiently delay or suppress ungoverned access growth depends on three demand-side conditions

Three indicators predict whether policies can suppress ungoverned AI access: (1) how responsive adopters are to cost differences across channels, (2) how effectively policy can raise the cost of ungoverned AI access, and (3) how costly it is for users to switch between access channels.

AI access governance policies are no longer able to shift users toward governed access channels once AI capabilities are sufficiently strong

Once AI capabilities become sufficiently valuable to users, policies that attempt to shift the relative costs of governed vs. ungoverned AI access lose their traction. Once AI capabilities advance far enough, no policy evaluated in the modeling framework can suppress ungoverned access.

The distinction between AI capability dynamics and access-cost dynamics matters for governance of the technology

A framing centered on capability thresholds implies that governance should track and respond to specific technical milestones; a framing centered on price dynamics implies that governance should track and respond to the cost of access. The latter may be more observable, more amenable to policy intervention, and more predictive of who adopts what and through which channels.

items.title: U.S. Army Yuma Proving Ground hosts Arizona Commanders Summit
items.author: Mark Schauer
items.summary: With the purpose of sharing information and building relationships, military commanders and senior leaders from across Arizona gathered for a day of discussions at U.S. Army Yuma Proving Ground (YPG) on Sep. 2, 2026. The summit, the first hosted by YPG Commander Col. Charles Seaberry, was the first held on post since 2022.
items.body:
Effective communication is a vital commodity, something of which one can never have too much.

With the purpose of sharing information and building relationships, military commanders and senior leaders from across Arizona gathered for a day of discussions at U.S. Army Yuma Proving Ground (YPG) on Sep. 2.

The summit, the first hosted by YPG Commander Col. Charles Seaberry, was the first held on post since 2022.

“It gives me an opportunity to meet my fellow commanders in Arizona,” said Seaberry. “It is good to collaborate and learn about the creative things they are doing that I could potentially leverage with YPG. I think we are going to have a lot of opportunities to synergize our initiatives and be less duplicative in areas where we are resource constrained.”

The Arizona Commanders Summit is a semi-annual event in which commanders and senior leaders from YPG, Marine Corps Air Station-Yuma, Fort Huachuca, Luke Air Force Base, Davis-Monthan Air Force Base, the Arizona National Guard’s Papago Park Military Reservation, and other Arizona and California-based military units along with local and state government representatives to discuss mission and installation sustainment. Though not a decision-making body, the group hears presentations on key topics throughout the day.

“I like the ability to go to all of the installations and see what they are like,” said Chas Buchanan, Director of the 56th Range management Office at Luke Airforce Base. “Seeing the remoteness of some of the installations and the challenges they face that are different than those we face in Phoenix really helps get the broader picture.”

The forum was an opportunity to compare challenges and network to share assets to accomplish the mission. For example, although YPG’s primary mission is conducting developmental testing of military equipment, the post also supports military training exercises. YPG is also part of the recently announced Army Permissive Test Range Expansion Initiative, which prioritizes commercial access to specialized environments ideal for testing unmanned aerial systems (UAS), counter-UAS technologies, long-range fires and low-cost interceptors at several facilities, including West Cibola Range, a newly opened component of YPG within YPG’s existing boundaries.

“That has dramatic implications into the future,” said Yuma Mayor Douglas Nicholls, who attended the event. “As we bring the amazing capabilities of YPG to bear for private industry, I think it will be a gamechanger for us for years to come.”

Multiple attendees noted the support the proving ground enjoys from the greater Yuma community, as well as the important role YPG plays in ensuring our nation’s defense. Nicholls gave a comprehensive presentation about what the city of Yuma offers early in the event.

“The military is important to our community and as a representative of the city I want to let everyone in the state know that Yuma is a community committed to the defense of our nation and preparing our warfighters,” said Nicholls. “It’s part of what makes Yuma, Yuma.”

items.title: When Disaster Strikes, Could AI Help? Q&A with Jessica Jensen
items.summary: Disasters are more frequent, more severe, and more costly. Pressure is mounting on emergency managers and the organizations that support them. Senior policy researcher Jessica Jensen discusses how artificial intelligence could help carry some of that burden.
items.body:
When Disaster Strikes, Could AI Help? Q&A with Jessica Jensen

Commentary

Sep 2, 2026

Evacuations in the Ravenswood neighborhood due to flooding after days of heavy rain in Indianapolis, Indiana, August 15, 2026

When disaster strikes, the public sees the most visible parts of the response: evacuations, first responders, rescue operations, and recovery efforts. But behind the scenes is a much larger network of people working to help communities manage through chaos.

That job is getting harder. Disasters are more frequent, more severe, and more costly. Pressure is mounting on emergency managers and the organizations that support them.

In a new RAND study supported by the Markle Foundation as part of the AI for Disasters and Emergencies Initiative (AIDE) , senior policy researcher Jessica Jensen and her RAND colleagues examined how artificial intelligence could help carry some of that burden.

Over more than two decades, Jensen has helped emergency management rethink how communities prepare for, respond to, and recover from increasingly complex disasters. Now, she is exploring how AI could help a field that's already stretched thin adapt to even greater demands.

What could AI realistically help emergency managers do—and how could that improve outcomes for communities?

AI can help with prediction and modeling, including when events are likely to occur and how severe impacts may be. It can also help bring together data from different groups, so people better understand what is happening during a disaster. If AI is used well, it can help communities get the right help at the right time without inefficiency or duplicated effort, ultimately saving lives.

Before disasters happen, emergency managers spend a lot of time on routine work like preparing plans, creating outreach materials, and managing grants. AI can speed up much of that work. That allows emergency managers to spend less time behind their desks and more time doing important public-facing work—helping people prepare, building community relationships, and focusing on the things that lessen disaster impacts.

If AI is used well, it can help communities get the right help at the right time without inefficiency or duplicated effort, ultimately saving lives.

Your team identified more than 1,000 AI-enabled products relevant to emergency management. What do these tools do, and what surprised you about your findings?

We were shocked by the number of tools out there. We thought we might find dozens. Instead, we found 1,179.

A lot of them support response. They support situational awareness, hazard monitoring, damage assessment, information sharing, and more. But the market is uneven, with more tools for response than for preparedness or recovery.

A big challenge facing emergency managers is that many of the products are very narrow. For example, many offer one piece of insight, but they do not connect different information streams or help create a fuller picture. That creates what we call a stacking problem. People would need to use multiple tools and would have to connect them. The products also tend not to facilitate interorganizational coordination, a hallmark of emergency management task areas.

What are the biggest barriers to using these tools—and what will it take for emergency management to adopt them more widely?

As we found, it's not that the tools do not exist. It is whether organizations have the capacity to evaluate them, buy them, integrate them, and keep using them over time.

A lot of these products require technical expertise. Often, you need someone with an IT background to set the tool up and provide ongoing support. Many jurisdictions don't have that kind of staffing. Many products also require internet connectivity, which can become an issue during response. A significant number depend on another product to work. And pricing is often hard to find—which makes procurement difficult.

Then you add privacy or cyber concerns, and the reality is that many offices are already stretched thin. One issue by itself may be manageable, but taken together, they can be overwhelming.

This is also where there is room for progress. Technology companies can design products more specifically for this field and prioritize transparency on pricing, access, and technical requirements—which will drive better adoption. Policymakers can make decisions about governance, procurement, and funding that make adoption easier. And emergency managers can build more familiarity with what these tools can do and where their limits are.

In your research, what role did large language models (LLMs) and AI chatbots play in emergency management today?

We found they could be especially useful for administrative and communication tasks in emergency management. They can help summarize reports, draft materials, translate information, and process large amounts of text more efficiently.

Those kinds of general-purpose tools stood out as one place the field may be able to realize benefits quickly, since they have broad capabilities, are user-friendly, and already available to some jurisdictions. For more complex emergency management tasks, though, there is still more research and real-world testing that needs to be done to determine LLMs effectiveness.

This study was supported by the Markle Foundation's AI for Disasters + Emergencies (AIDE) Initiative. How critical is philanthropic support in a fast-moving area like this?

One of the most important things philanthropies can do is bring together technology companies, the user community, and the researchers developing the underlying technologies, and facilitate conversations about how to balance everyone's interests. That convening role—and the ability to sustain those conversations—can make the difference between tools that sound promising and tools that actually help communities. That is exactly what the AIDE Initiative is doing—bringing the right people together to explore how AI can better support disaster preparedness, response, and recovery.

The AIDE Initiative is bringing the right people together to explore how AI can better support disaster preparedness, response, and recovery.

You've dedicated your career to emergency management. What's kept you in the field so long?

I've known I wanted to serve this field since I was 14. Around that time, a regular at the restaurant where I worked would talk about his job helping communities and organizations recover after disasters. What stayed with me was how many different people and systems have to come together to help a community heal.

Now, years later, this work feels even more meaningful. There is an incredible opportunity in emergency management to keep evolving the practice to better serve communities. And I care deeply about the people who do this work. They are hardworking, passionate, and committed—even when resources are scarce and the demands keep growing. In a world of increasing disasters and rising impacts, that work matters enormously. It's what keeps me going.

items.title: A Standardized Framework for Assessing High-Risk Life Sciences Research
items.author: Elizabeth Cameron
items.summary: Recent federal policies establish funding prohibitions and review requirements for certain high-risk life sciences research. The authors advise that federal agencies adopt an objective decisionmaking framework for dangerous gain-of-function research.
items.body:
Defining Objective Criteria That Can Facilitate Expert and AI Reviews of Dangerous Gain-of-Function Research

Matt Sharkey , Adeline E. Williams , John P. Tarangelo , Barbara Del Castello , Christopher Rodriguez , Celine Robinson , Graham Griffin , Skye A. Miner , Rebecca Moritz , Tyler Hoard , et al.

Published Sep 2, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Two recent federal policies establish funding prohibitions and research review requirements for certain life sciences pathogen or toxin research. Based on the definition of dangerous gain-of-function research (DGOF), the authors recommend that relevant federal agencies adopt an objective, transparent decisionmaking framework with defined DGOF criteria. This framework builds on previous RAND work to assess high-risk research.

items.title: Countering Model Distillation
items.author: Brian A. Jackson
items.summary: Artificial intelligence model distillation (training new models on outputs of more capable ones) could affect U.S. frontier model advantage. New policy tools could augment such technical countermeasures as raising costs or reducing model quality.
items.body:
Limits and Alternatives

Michael J. D. Vermeer , Brian A. Jackson

Expert Insights Published Sep 2, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Artificial intelligence model distillation (that is, the process of training a new model on the outputs of a more capable one) poses a growing challenge to efforts to preserve the U.S. frontier model advantage. In this paper, the authors examine whether technical counter-distillation measures are likely to be sufficient to deter distillation. They argue that technical measures alone (such as by materially raising the cost of distillation or substantially reducing the quality of the resulting models) are unlikely to change the underlying incentives that make distillation attractive and that broader policy tools might be needed.

items.title: Super Garuda Shield 26 kicks off with multinational partners ceremony
items.author: PO2 Alfredo Marron and SGT William Rogers
items.summary: Super Garuda Shield 26 (SGS 26) began with an opening ceremony Aug. 31 2026, in Bandung, bringing together service members from Indonesia, the United States and 13 partner countries for a multinational exercise focused on strengthening relationships, interoperability and readiness.
items.body:
SOUTH SUMATRA, Indonesia — Super Garuda Shield 26 (SGS 26) began with an opening ceremony Aug. 31 2026, in Bandung, bringing together service members from Indonesia, the United States and 13 partner countries for a multinational exercise focused on strengthening relationships, interoperability and readiness.

Approximately 5,000 combined armed forces personnel are scheduled to participate in SGS 26 from Aug, 31 to Sept. 11 at multiple training locations across Indonesia, including Bandung, Bataraja and Lampung.

The U.S. Pacific Command-sponsored exercise demonstrates the shared purpose of participating nations while enhancing interoperability and providing realistic training in a variety of climates, terrains, and environments.

“SGS 26 is building valuable relationships and readiness with our Indonesian and multinational partners through challenging and realistic training,” said Maj. Gen. Patrick Ellis, commanding general of the 4th Infantry Division, “We are excited to work side by side with our partners this year to ensure we remain ready to rapidly respond to any contingency or crisis.”

SGS 26 provides opportunities for professional exchanges that strengthen partnerships through shared learning and training. Training includes engineering construction activities, staff training exercises, airborne operations, jungle training, air assault operations, a large field training exercise and combined arms live fire exercises, a Stinger missile live fire exercise, and a High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (HIMARS) live fire exercise.

The variety of training events allows participating forces to share their respective experiences and expertise while developing a better understanding of how partner nations plan, coordinate and execute military operations.

U.S. Army, Airforce, Navy and Marine Corps personnel will train alongside their Indonesian hosts and regional allies and partners to sharpen tactical readiness, test joint command-and-control systems and strengthen their ability to operate together. Training alongside partner nations builds the collective trust and interoperability necessary to strengthen defense relationships and support shared interests throughout the Indo-Pacific.

Beyond improving technical and tactical capabilities, SGS 26 provides opportunities for service members from participating nations to build professional relationships. Those relationships can improve communication and mutual understanding among forces that may work together during future operations, contingencies or crises.

Super Garuda Shield has developed into an important venue for multinational cooperation and professional exchange. Each iteration provides participating nations an opportunity to build upon existing partnerships while creating new relationships among service members throughout the region.

The United States’ participation in SGS 26 reflects its enduring defense relationship with Indonesia and its commitment to working alongside allies and partners. By training together, participating forces build the collective trust and interoperability necessary to respond to shared challenges and uphold their shared interest in a free and open Indo-Pacific.

Ellis reinforced the importance of building these partnerships during SGS 26 saying, “the trust that is required to execute these operations cannot be built in a briefing room; it is built in the mud, in the surf, in the cockpits, and in the operational command centers.”

Throughout the nearly two-week exercise, participating forces will continue training together across Indonesia, strengthening professional relationships and improving their ability to operate as a combined and joint force.
